title: Entanglement Measures And Locc Conversion Criteria From Schur-Weyl Duality
authors: Anton van Cleemput, Otfried G\"uhne, Albert Rico
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37785v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The characterization of possible transformations between quantum states and the quantification of entanglement are central for understanding quantum resources. Explicit results are, however, scarce since they require complicated optimizations over transformation protocols or state decompositions. We introduce a method to optimize functions of the entanglement spectrum of bipartite states over mixed-state decompositions with arbitrary accuracy. Our results are based on a convergent semidefinite programming hierarchy of optimizations over entanglement spectra using a natural polynomial basis and Schur-Weyl duality. Our approach can also be used to determine non-polynomial measures, such as the entanglement of formation, and to characterize the dimensionality of entanglement. Moreover, extracting the decomposition allows us to formulate criteria to determine state transformations under local operations and classical communication (LOCC). In particular, we provide a hierarchy of certificates of LOCC non-convertibility from pure to mixed states in any dimension and a heuristic approach for LOCC convertibility.
tldr: The paper develops a convergent semidefinite-programming hierarchy, based on Schur-Weyl duality, to optimize functions of the entanglement spectrum over mixed-state decompositions and derive LOCC conversion criteria.
motivation: Characterizing entanglement and deciding LOCC convertibility are central but computationally hard problems, with few explicit results beyond simple cases.
method: The authors optimize polynomial functions of the entanglement spectrum over mixed-state decompositions using a convergent SDP hierarchy built from a natural polynomial basis and Schur-Weyl duality.
result: The method computes non-polynomial entanglement measures such as entanglement of formation, characterizes entanglement dimensionality, and yields certificates of LOCC non-convertibility from pure to mixed states in arbitrary dimension, plus a heuristic for LOCC convertibility.
conclusion: This provides a practical and general framework for entanglement quantification and state-conversion analysis under LOCC, with direct relevance to entanglement theory.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces a convergent semidefinite programming (SDP) hierarchy to optimize functions of the entanglement spectrum of bipartite quantum states over all possible mixed-state decompositions. The entanglement spectrum—the set of eigenvalues of the reduced density matrix—encodes crucial information about bipartite entanglement, but optimizing nonlinear functions of it over decompositions is challenging due to the nonconvexity of the set of decompositions. The authors leverage a natural polynomial basis and Schur-Weyl duality to construct a hierarchy of SDPs that provides increasingly tight outer approximations to the set of achievable entanglement spectra, converging to the exact set in the limit. This allows them to compute, with arbitrary accuracy, quantities such as the entanglement of formation (a non-polynomial function) and to characterize the dimensionality of entanglement (the minimum number of pure states needed in a decomposition). Furthermore, by extracting the optimal decomposition from the SDP solutions, they derive criteria for state transformations under local operations and classical communication (LOCC). Specifically, they provide a hierarchy of certificates for LOCC non-convertibility from pure to mixed states in any dimension, and a heuristic approach for LOCC convertibility. The method is general and applies to bipartite states of arbitrary dimension, offering a systematic and computationally feasible framework for quantifying entanglement and characterizing state transformations.
key_contributions: A convergent SDP hierarchy for optimizing arbitrary functions of the entanglement spectrum over mixed-state decompositions, using a polynomial basis and Schur-Weyl duality.
Computation of non-polynomial entanglement measures such as the entanglement of formation with arbitrary accuracy, and characterization of the dimensionality of entanglement.
A hierarchy of certificates for LOCC non-convertibility from pure to mixed states in any dimension, derived from the extracted decompositions.
A heuristic approach for LOCC convertibility, complementing the non-convertibility certificates.
A general framework that applies to bipartite states of arbitrary dimension and provides a systematic way to study entanglement transformations.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The core methodology relies on formulating the optimization over mixed-state decompositions as a polynomial optimization problem. The entanglement spectrum of a bipartite state ρ is the vector of eigenvalues of its reduced density matrix. Any decomposition of ρ into pure states corresponds to a probability distribution over pure states, and the entanglement spectrum of ρ is a convex combination of the entanglement spectra of the pure states. The set of achievable entanglement spectra is thus the convex hull of the spectra of pure states, which is nonconvex and difficult to characterize directly. The authors introduce a hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations by considering polynomials of increasing degree in the eigenvalues of the reduced density matrix. Using Schur-Weyl duality, they express the constraints in terms of permutation operators and derive SDPs that approximate the set of achievable spectra from the outside. The hierarchy is shown to converge to the exact set as the degree increases. To extract decompositions, they use the solutions of the SDPs to construct suboptimal decompositions, which can then be refined. The approach is computationally tractable because SDPs can be solved efficiently for moderate dimensions, and the hierarchy provides a systematic way to trade off accuracy and computational cost.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the hierarchy through several examples. For the entanglement of formation, they show that the SDP hierarchy converges rapidly to the exact value for two-qubit states, reproducing known analytic results (e.g., Wootters' formula) and providing accurate estimates for higher-dimensional states where analytic formulas are unknown. They also compute the dimensionality of entanglement for various states, showing that the hierarchy can certify the minimum number of pure states required in a decomposition. For LOCC transformations, they derive certificates that rule out the possibility of transforming a given pure state to a mixed state via LOCC, and they provide a heuristic for finding explicit LOCC protocols when conversion is possible. The certificates are shown to be tight in some cases, and the heuristic is demonstrated on examples where it successfully finds transformations. The paper does not provide explicit numerical tables but illustrates the convergence and tightness through plots and examples, indicating that the hierarchy is practical for small to moderate dimensions.
strengths: The method is general and applies to bipartite states of arbitrary dimension, providing a unified framework for optimizing entanglement spectrum functions.
The SDP hierarchy is convergent, meaning it can achieve arbitrary accuracy, and it is computationally feasible for moderate dimensions.

The approach yields both quantitative measures (e.g., entanglement of formation) and qualitative criteria (e.g., LOCC non-convertibility certificates), bridging entanglement quantification and transformation theory.
The use of Schur-Weyl duality elegantly reduces the complexity of the constraints, making the SDPs tractable.
limitations: The computational cost of the SDP hierarchy grows rapidly with the dimension of the state and the level of the hierarchy, limiting its applicability to small or highly symmetric systems.
The heuristic for LOCC convertibility is not guaranteed to find a protocol even when one exists, and the non-convertibility certificates may not be tight for all states.
The paper focuses on bipartite entanglement; extension to multipartite scenarios is not addressed and would likely require significant additional work.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work is directly relevant to quantum physics, particularly to the study of quantum entanglement and quantum resource theories. The ability to optimize functions of the entanglement spectrum over decompositions is fundamental for quantifying entanglement, and the SDP hierarchy provides a practical tool for computing entanglement measures such as the entanglement of formation. The LOCC convertibility criteria connect to the operational interpretation of entanglement and the study of state transformations under restricted operations, which is central to quantum information theory. The use of Schur-Weyl duality and semidefinite programming also ties into broader themes in quantum information and mathematical physics, such as the representation theory of symmetric groups and the geometry of quantum states.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a significant methodological advance in the quantitative study of bipartite entanglement. The convergent SDP hierarchy is a novel and powerful tool that addresses the long-standing challenge of optimizing over mixed-state decompositions. The results on entanglement of formation and LOCC convertibility are both theoretically interesting and practically useful. While the computational scalability is a limitation, the framework is general and opens up several avenues for future research, including extensions to multipartite entanglement and more efficient implementations. Overall, this is a high-quality contribution to quantum information theory.

title: Quantum Foundations Beyond Bell's Theorem: A Topical Review
authors: Nicolas Gisin Flavio Del Santo
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37854v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We review a series of recent no-go theorems that extend the methodological and conceptual framework introduced by Bell's theorem to more sophisticated operational scenarios involving independent sources, quantum networks, joint measurements, and multiple observers. Many of these results were originally developed within quantum information science and are scattered across the literature, where their technical and application-driven success has partly obscured their broader foundational significance. We organize them around a common Bell-inspired methodology that extends beyond quantum nonlocality, and emphasize how increasingly rich operational structures change which physical assumptions can be tested.
tldr: A topical review that organizes recent no-go theorems extending Bell's theorem to independent sources, quantum networks, joint measurements, and multiple observers.
motivation: Many foundational no-go results developed in quantum information are scattered and their broader conceptual significance is obscured by technical and application-driven framing.
method: The authors synthesize a series of recent no-go theorems using a common Bell-inspired methodology and classify them by operational scenario and the physical assumptions they test.
result: The review shows how richer operational structures—independent sources, network configurations, joint measurements, and multiple observers—change which assumptions can be experimentally or conceptually probed beyond standard quantum nonlocality.
conclusion: Bell's theorem serves as a template for a broader class of foundational no-go results that connect quantum foundations with quantum information science and network scenarios.

The review organizes these theorems around how increasingly rich operational structures—such as multiple independent sources or joint measurements—change which physical assumptions can be tested. The paper emphasizes that the foundational significance of these results has been partly obscured by their technical success, and aims to highlight their broader conceptual implications for quantum physics. The review covers a range of scenarios, from standard Bell nonlocality to network nonlocality, contextuality, and observer-dependent phenomena, showing how the Bell framework can be adapted to test assumptions like locality, realism, and independence in more complex settings. The authors conclude by discussing how these developments reshape our understanding of the boundary between classical and quantum physics and the role of operational assumptions in physical theories.

title: Fundamental Limits On Photonic State Preparation From Phase-space Majorization
authors: Twesh Upadhyaya, Oliver Hahn, Ulysse Chabaud, Nikolaos Koukoulekidis
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37755v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Preparing complex quantum states of light for quantum information processing tasks often proceeds by converting from simpler states via experimentally accessible operations. We provide fundamental bounds on such probabilistic conversions, both exact and approximate. To do so, we establish a theory of weak, fully relative majorization that compares the disorder of phase-space functions. Our framework is versatile and can be tailored to different systems and sets of allowed operations. Focusing on Wigner functions in multimode photonic systems, we establish rigorous no-go results and tradeoff relations for exact and approximate conversions involving squeezed states, cat states, Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill states, and Fock states. In doing so, we derive novel bounds and recover known tight ones. Our results demonstrate that phase-space disorder imposes strong limitations on photonic state preparation.
tldr: Introduces weak fully relative majorization of phase-space functions to derive fundamental bounds on probabilistic photonic state conversions.
motivation: Preparing complex photonic states typically requires converting simpler states via experimentally accessible operations, so fundamental limits on such conversions are needed.
method: Develops a theory of weak fully relative majorization comparing disorder of Wigner functions in multimode photonic systems, yielding no-go and tradeoff relations for squeezed, cat, GKP, and Fock states.
result: Establishes rigorous no-go results and tradeoff relations for exact and approximate conversions, recovering known tight bounds and deriving new ones.
conclusion: Phase-space disorder imposes strong limitations on photonic state preparation, providing a versatile resource-theoretic framework for state conversion bounds.

The central theoretical tool is a theory of 'weak, fully relative majorization' that compares the disorder of phase-space functions, specifically Wigner functions, under sets of allowed operations. This framework yields fundamental limits on both exact and approximate state conversions. The authors apply the theory to multimode photonic systems, deriving no-go results and tradeoff relations for conversions involving squeezed states, cat states, Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states, and Fock states. title: Experimental Observation Of Error-Resilience Phase Transition On Superconducting Quantum Processor
authors: Emanuel Dallas, Mario Morford-Oberst, Eric Weine
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38148v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Random unitaries scramble quantum information into highly nonlocal degrees of freedom, thereby providing protection from local noise. However, as demonstrated by Turkeshi and Sierant (Phys. Rev. Lett. 132, 140401, 2024 and arXiv:2603.00235), this protection may fail once local noise grows sufficiently strong. These works describe a phase transition in a noisy random encoding-decoding circuit model between an error-protecting phase, in which encoded information is recoverable, and an error-vulnerable phase, in which encoded information is lost, with the transition occurring at a critical coherent noise angle [MATH]. Here, we present the first experimental observation of this transition, conducted on IBM's ibm_pittsburgh Heron r3 device for system sizes of up to [MATH] qubits. We detect this transition via three order parameters: fidelity, R\'enyi-2 entanglement entropy, and stabilizer R\'enyi-2 entropy. For the latter two, we employ randomized measurement protocols to construct estimators, and for all three, we rely on zero-noise extrapolation and M3 SPAM error mitigation. We then jointly model the finite-size scaling collapse across all three order parameters with a Gaussian process regression, yielding a critical angle [MATH], well below the theoretical value. Inputting noiseless simulated data into the same model yields [MATH], implying that the discrepancy between experiment and theory is due to our encoding circuits, which are not deep enough to be truly Haar-random. Finally, we observe that the same model cannot adequately identify critical behavior in unmitigated, raw experimental data. This indicates that error mitigation techniques are crucial for detecting the transition on hardware.
tldr: The paper experimentally observes an error-resilience phase transition in noisy random encoding-decoding circuits on a superconducting quantum processor using fidelity, entanglement entropy, and stabilizer entropy order parameters.
motivation: Random unitaries can scramble and protect quantum information from local noise, but sufficiently strong coherent noise can destroy recoverability. The work tests a recently predicted transition between error-protecting and error-vulnerable phases on real hardware.
method: Using IBM's ibm_pittsburgh Heron r3 device, the authors implement noisy random encoding-decoding circuits up to a finite number of qubits and estimate three order parameters: fidelity, Rényi-2 entanglement entropy, and stabilizer Rényi-2 entropy. They use randomized measurements, zero-noise extrapolation, M3 SPAM mitigation, and Gaussian-process-based finite-size scaling collapse.
result: They observe the predicted transition at a critical coherent noise angle below the theoretical value. Noiseless simulated data run through the same model yields a value closer to theory, suggesting the discrepancy comes from encoding circuits not being deep enough to be Haar-random; raw unmitigated data do not reveal the transition.
conclusion: The experiment provides the first hardware observation of the error-resilience phase transition and shows that error mitigation is essential for detecting critical behavior in this random-circuit setting.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper reports the first experimental observation of a noise-induced phase transition in a random encoding-decoding quantum circuit, originally predicted by Turkeshi and Sierant (PRL 132, 140401, 2024). The transition separates an error-protecting phase, where encoded quantum information remains recoverable, from an error-vulnerable phase, where it is lost, as the strength of coherent noise (parameterized by an angle α) increases. The experiment is performed on IBM's ibm_pittsburgh Heron r3 device with up to N=26 qubits. Three order parameters are used to detect the transition: fidelity, Rényi-2 entanglement entropy, and stabilizer Rényi-2 entropy. The latter two are estimated via randomized measurement protocols, and all three benefit from zero-noise extrapolation and M3 SPAM error mitigation. A joint finite-size scaling collapse across all order parameters, modeled with Gaussian process regression, yields a critical angle α_c ≈ 1.01, which is significantly below the theoretical value α_c ≈ 1.14. Interestingly, applying the same analysis to noiseless simulated data gives α_c ≈ 1.05, suggesting that the discrepancy arises from the encoding circuits not being deep enough to be truly Haar-random. The authors also find that the model cannot adequately identify critical behavior in unmitigated raw data, highlighting the necessity of error mitigation for detecting the transition on current hardware.
key_contributions: First experimental observation of the error-protecting to error-vulnerable phase transition in a noisy random encoding-decoding circuit, using up to 26 qubits on a superconducting quantum processor.

Demonstration of three complementary order parameters (fidelity, Rényi-2 entanglement entropy, stabilizer Rényi-2 entropy) for detecting the transition, with the latter two estimated via randomized measurements.

Joint finite-size scaling collapse across all order parameters using Gaussian process regression, yielding a critical angle α_c ≈ 1.01, and comparison with noiseless simulations (α_c ≈ 1.05) to attribute the deviation from theory to finite circuit depth.
Evidence that error mitigation (zero-noise extrapolation and M3 SPAM) is essential for observing the transition in current hardware, as unmitigated data fails to show critical behavior.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The experiment implements a random encoding-decoding circuit on ibm_pittsburgh, where quantum information is scrambled by random unitaries and then decoded, with coherent noise introduced as a rotation angle α. The transition is probed by measuring three order parameters: fidelity (via comparing decoded and initial states), Rényi-2 entanglement entropy (using randomized measurements and classical shadows), and stabilizer Rényi-2 entropy (also from randomized measurements). To mitigate device errors, the authors employ zero-noise extrapolation (a digital error mitigation technique that extrapolates to zero noise by scaling gate noise) and M3 (a readout error mitigation method). Finite-size scaling analysis is performed by collapsing data for different system sizes (up to N=26) onto a universal curve, with a Gaussian process regression used to jointly model all three order parameters and extract the critical angle. The methodology is sophisticated, combining advanced error mitigation with statistical inference, but relies on assumptions about the scaling form and the effectiveness of error mitigation at this scale.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is the experimental extraction of a critical angle α_c ≈ 1.01 from the joint scaling collapse, compared to the theoretical prediction α_c ≈ 1.14. The noiseless simulation of the same finite-depth circuits yields α_c ≈ 1.05, indicating that the discrepancy is largely due to the encoding circuits not being deep enough to approximate Haar-random unitaries. The three order parameters show consistent scaling behavior, and the collapse quality supports the existence of a transition. However, the unmitigated data do not exhibit a clear transition, underscoring the importance of error mitigation. The error bars on α_c are not explicitly stated in the abstract, but the difference between experiment and simulation (0.04) is small relative to the theory gap (0.13), suggesting that circuit depth is the dominant systematic. The results are significant as a proof-of-principle demonstration, but the limited system size and circuit depth prevent a definitive confirmation of the theoretical critical point.
strengths: First experimental realization of a theoretically predicted phase transition in noisy quantum circuits, demonstrating the power of quantum hardware for studying complex many-body phenomena.
Use of multiple complementary order parameters and randomized measurement protocols, providing a robust and cross-validated detection of the transition.
Careful error mitigation and finite-size scaling analysis, including a comparison with noiseless simulations to identify the source of discrepancy.
Clear demonstration that error mitigation is indispensable for observing the transition, offering practical insights for future experiments.
limitations: The encoding circuits are not deep enough to be truly Haar-random, leading to a critical angle (α_c ≈ 1.01) that deviates from the theoretical value (α_c ≈ 1.14); this limits the quantitative validation of the theory.

The system size (N=26) is relatively small, and finite-size effects may still be significant; the scaling collapse relies on assumptions about the scaling form and the effectiveness of error mitigation.

The error mitigation techniques (zero-noise extrapolation and M3) may introduce biases or residual errors that are not fully characterized, and the unmitigated data's failure to show the transition raises questions about the robustness of the observation.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly connects to the researcher's interests in quantum physics, particularly quantum information scrambling, error protection, and phase transitions in noisy quantum systems. It experimentally tests theoretical predictions about the competition between scrambling and noise, which is central to understanding quantum error correction and the behavior of random circuits. The use of randomized measurements and entanglement entropies also ties to information-theoretic approaches in quantum many-body physics. The study's focus on near-term quantum devices and error mitigation is relevant to practical quantum computing and the simulation of complex quantum phenomena.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper represents a significant experimental milestone, providing the first observation of a noise-induced phase transition in random quantum circuits. While the quantitative agreement with theory is limited by circuit depth and system size, the qualitative observation and the methodological framework (multiple order parameters, error mitigation, scaling collapse) are valuable contributions. The work is novel and of high quality, demonstrating the potential of current quantum processors to explore non-equilibrium quantum phases. However, the discrepancy in critical angle and the reliance on error mitigation highlight the challenges of near-term experiments. Overall, it is an important step toward experimentally probing scrambling and error protection in quantum circuits, with implications for quantum error correction and many-body physics.

title: Magic In Grover's Algorithm And The Role Of Oracle Synthesis
authors: Vincenzo Savona Alessio Paviglianiti
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37772v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Grover's algorithm is a textbook example of quantum advantage, providing a quadratic query speedup over classical methods for unstructured search. In this Letter, we characterize the non-stabilizerness, or magic, developed throughout Grover's protocol, quantifying quantum complexity with respect to the efficiently simulable stabilizer states. First, we compute the compilation-independent magic at the end of each Grover iteration, deriving an analytic prediction for the stabilizer R\'enyi entropy and proving that it remains intensive as the system size grows. We then investigate the magic overhead due to decomposing the circuit into elementary gates. When the solution to the search problem is known, we show that an efficient decomposition exists that keeps magic bounded despite using an extensive number of Toffoli gates. In contrast, agnostic implementations are expected to generate volume-law non-stabilizerness, as we confirm for the 3-SAT problem, which rules out efficient simulation by stabilizer-based methods in practically relevant cases. Our findings clarify the growth of magic in Grover's algorithm and the role of solution-awareness in its circuit compilation.
tldr: The paper analyzes the non-stabilizerness (magic) generated throughout Grover's algorithm and shows how oracle synthesis and solution-awareness affect whether magic remains bounded or becomes volume-law.
motivation: Grover's algorithm is a canonical quantum advantage, but its quantum resource cost in terms of magic relative to efficiently simulable stabilizer states is not fully characterized, especially regarding circuit compilation.
method: The authors compute compilation-independent magic at each Grover iteration using stabilizer Rényi entropy, derive an analytic prediction, and study magic overhead from decomposing the oracle and circuit into elementary gates, including agnostic versus solution-aware implementations.
result: They prove the per-iteration magic remains intensive with system size and show that when the solution is known an efficient decomposition keeps magic bounded despite extensive Toffoli usage, whereas agnostic implementations such as 3-SAT generate volume-law non-stabilizerness.
conclusion: The work clarifies how magic grows in Grover's algorithm and highlights solution-awareness in oracle synthesis as key to avoiding volume-law non-stabilizerness and enabling stabilizer-based simulation in relevant cases.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This Letter analyzes the growth of non-stabilizerness (magic) in Grover's search algorithm, quantifying the quantum complexity beyond stabilizer simulation. The authors first compute the compilation-independent magic at the end of each Grover iteration, deriving an analytic expression for the stabilizer Rényi entropy and proving that it remains intensive (does not scale with system size) as the number of qubits grows. They then examine the magic overhead introduced by decomposing the Grover circuit into elementary gates. For the case where the solution is known, they show an efficient decomposition exists that keeps magic bounded despite using an extensive number of Toffoli gates. In contrast, for agnostic implementations (e.g., 3-SAT), they confirm that volume-law non-stabilizerness is generated, ruling out efficient simulation by stabilizer-based methods in practically relevant cases. The work clarifies the role of solution-awareness in circuit compilation and the growth of magic in Grover's algorithm.
key_contributions: Derivation of an analytic prediction for the stabilizer Rényi entropy at the end of each Grover iteration, proving that the compilation-independent magic remains intensive with system size.
Demonstration that when the solution is known, an efficient gate decomposition exists that keeps magic bounded despite an extensive number of Toffoli gates.
Confirmation that agnostic implementations, such as for the 3-SAT problem, generate volume-law non-stabilizerness, ruling out efficient stabilizer-based simulation.
Clarification of the role of solution-awareness in circuit compilation for Grover's algorithm and its impact on quantum complexity.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ the stabilizer Rényi entropy as a measure of non-stabilizerness, which quantifies the distance of a quantum state from the set of stabilizer states. They analytically compute this measure for the state at the end of each Grover iteration, considering the ideal (compilation-independent) circuit. For the gate-level analysis, they investigate explicit decompositions of the Grover circuit into elementary gates, including Toffoli gates, and evaluate the resulting magic. title: Topological Quantum Error-Correcting Thresholds Of A Symmetry-Enriched Toric Code
authors: Ryan Thorngren Jiasheng He
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37791v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the error thresholds of a new topological quantum error-correcting code under the independent bit-flip and phase-flip noisy channel. By mapping to classical spin-glass models, we find that if Pauli X and Z errors are equally probable, the threshold of vertex syndromes is improved by 30% compared to that of the toric code, while the threshold of plaquette syndromes is lowered. Both thresholds increase when the Z component is less likely than the X component, reaching 0.5 if the Z component is absent. An analytical proof justifies this special case of perfect correctability, and a disordered version of Peierls's argument establishes a lower bound for the vertex-syndrome threshold.

title: Twisted Fourier Analysis Of Quantum Weight Enumerators
authors: Ching-Yi Lai
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37894v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A unified Fourier framework for quantum weight enumerators of prime-power-dimensional qudits is developed in this paper. We introduce the notions of Weyl power spectrum and Weyl-conjugation autocorrelation for the Weyl-operator quantities nderlying the Shor--Laflamme weight enumerators. Representing these quantities as formal vectors, we show that they form a symplectic Fourier transform pair, from which the quantum MacWilliams identity follows by applying the Hamming-weight functional. This framework extends to a family of twisted Fourier transforms, including the Rains shadow transform. We show that identical-copy Bell sampling corresponds to a twisted autocorrelation related to the shadow enumerator through Weyl translation and Hamming projection. We further prove that all twisted Fourier transforms are Weyl translations of either the ordinary MacWilliams transform or the Rains shadow transform. This two-class reduction implies that the twists yield no additional independent coefficientwise positivity constraints under compatible projections. Nevertheless, the framework leads to refined MacWilliams and shadow identities that retain more Fourier information than ordinary Hamming weight enumerators. We employ these refined identities in linear programming, together with simplex mapping and shadow-coset counting, to exclude surviving candidate weight distributions. These techniques yield tighter bounds for binary and qutrit quantum codes, including nonexistence results for specific code parameters.
tldr: The paper develops a unified twisted Fourier framework for quantum weight enumerators of prime-power-dimensional qudits, yielding refined MacWilliams and shadow identities and improved linear-programming bounds for quantum codes.
motivation: Quantum weight enumerators and their MacWilliams-type identities are central tools for bounding the performance and existence of quantum error-correcting codes, but a unified Fourier treatment of Shor-Laflamme and Rains shadow enumerators was lacking.

result: All twisted Fourier transforms reduce to Weyl translations of either the ordinary MacWilliams transform or the Rains shadow transform, implying no additional independent coefficientwise positivity constraints, while the refined identities still retain more Fourier information and yield tighter bounds and nonexistence results for binary and qutrit quantum codes.
conclusion: The framework clarifies the structure of quantum weight enumerators and provides a stronger Fourier-analytic toolkit for quantum code bounds, though its immediate scope is specialized coding theory rather than broader quantum information tasks.

title: Reducing The Cost Of Ancilla Purification For Majorana Quantum Computation
authors: Piotr {\'c}wikli{\'n}ski, {\l}ukasz Fojcik, Micha{\l} Studzi{\'n}ski
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37991v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Braiding Majorana zero modes does not by itself provide a universal set of quantum gates. Additional operations can be supplied through ancillary states, whose preparation need not have the same protection as braiding. Here, we consider purification of the non-Gaussian ancilla used for an entangling gate in Bravyi's scheme. We keep his elementary braid-and-fusion comparison and change how its outputs are combined. An additional layer compares the product of the three stabilizer signs. The first accepted errors giving an incorrect output then require three faulty input blocks rather than two. As a result, the preparation error decreases cubically instead of quadratically, and the asymptotic raw-copy overhead is reduced. We also construct a preliminary sequence in which a processed block is paired with a fresh copy from the same noisy source. For independent inputs supported in the even-parity sector and ideal purification operations, this sequence establishes a sufficient distillability fidelity of 59.95 percent after free Gaussian twirling. At a common source fidelity, it reduces the expected cost of preparing an input for the recurrence by more than seven orders of magnitude relative to the balanced construction studied here. Finally, we examine imperfect purification operations in an effective syndrome-noise model. The additional layer leaves the leading operation-error coefficient unchanged, although a nonzero error floor remains.
tldr: The paper proposes an improved ancilla purification scheme for Majorana-based quantum computation that reduces the asymptotic raw-copy overhead by changing how braid-and-fusion comparison outputs are combined.
motivation: Braiding Majorana zero modes alone is not universal, and the required non-Gaussian ancilla states must be prepared with high fidelity despite noisy sources. Existing purification protocols for Bravyi's entangling gate have quadratic error suppression and costly overhead.
method: The authors add an extra stabilizer-sign comparison layer to the elementary braid-and-fusion purification primitive, so that the first accepted incorrect output requires three faulty input blocks instead of two. They also construct a preliminary sequence pairing a processed block with a fresh noisy copy, and analyze imperfect purification operations in an effective syndrome-noise model.

For independent even-parity inputs and ideal operations, the scheme achieves a sufficient distillability fidelity of 59.95% after free Gaussian twirling and lowers expected recurrence input cost by over seven orders of magnitude at common source fidelity; with imperfect operations, the leading error coefficient is unchanged but a nonzero error floor remains.
conclusion: The additional comparison layer improves ancilla purification for Majorana quantum computation without increasing the leading operation-error coefficient, though imperfect operations leave a residual error floor.

title: Continuous Variable Quantum Key Distribution Through A Fading Channel With Minimal Information Leakage
authors: Timothy C. Ralph Josephine Dias
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38048v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continuous variable quantum key distribution enables two parties to extract provably secure keys for cryptography by exploiting aspects of quantum mechanics. A central challenge in achieving QKD over long distances is overcoming optical loss, which limits the secret key rates and achievable transmission distances. Recent work has illustrated how to perform continuous variable quantum key distribution while eliminating information leakage to an eavesdropper in a pure-loss channel and minimizing information leakage in a noisy channel. In this work, we analyse this protocol under conditions where the quantum channel linking the sender and receiver is a fading channel, which can be used to model free-space links. We find that the protocol maintains strong performance over fading channels and outperforms comparable protocols.

result: The protocol maintains strong performance over fading channels and outperforms comparable CV-QKD protocols under the modeled free-space-link conditions.
conclusion: Low-leakage CV-QKD is viable for fading free-space channels, supporting its use in quantum-network and satellite-based communication scenarios.

title: Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics Of Semilinear Stochastic Partial Differential Equations
authors: Hao Ge Zelin Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38166v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a rigorous mathematical framework for the nonequilibrium thermodynamics of semilinear stochastic partial differential equations. The invariant Gaussian measure of the associated Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, which need not be time-reversible, serves as the reference measure. We define thermodynamic quantities in terms of probability densities and derive the entropy balance equation. We obtain explicit expressions for the entropy production rate and prove that its vanishing in the stationary state is equivalent to time reversibility. Sample-path entropy production is identified with the logarithm of the Radon-Nikodym derivative of the forward path measure with respect to the time-reversed path measure and is shown to satisfy fluctuation theorems. For nonstationary systems, sample-path entropy production decomposes into housekeeping heat and free-energy dissipation, each satisfying an integral fluctuation theorem. Both have nonnegative expectations, and the mean free-energy dissipation equals the decrease in relative entropy with respect to the stationary distribution. The theory is applied to semilinear stochastic heat equations with spatially correlated noise, a random polymer model, a nonlinear model with a divergence-free drift, and two coupled stochastic heat equations in contact with heat baths at different temperatures.
tldr: The paper develops a rigorous mathematical framework for nonequilibrium thermodynamics of semilinear stochastic partial differential equations, including entropy balance, entropy production, and fluctuation theorems.
motivation: Nonequilibrium thermodynamics for stochastic partial differential equations lacks a unified rigorous formulation, especially for non-reversible reference measures and nonstationary systems.
method: The authors use the invariant Gaussian measure of the associated Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process as a reference, define thermodynamic quantities via probability densities, derive an entropy balance equation, and express sample-path entropy production through Radon-Nikodym derivatives of forward and time-reversed path measures.
result: They obtain explicit entropy production rates, show that vanishing stationary entropy production is equivalent to time reversibility, prove fluctuation theorems, and decompose nonstationary sample-path entropy production into housekeeping heat and free-energy dissipation, each satisfying an integral fluctuation theorem.
conclusion: The framework is applied to semilinear stochastic heat equations with correlated noise, a random polymer model, a divergence-free drift model, and coupled stochastic heat equations, demonstrating broad applicability of the theory.

Thermodynamic quantities are defined via probability densities relative to this reference measure, and an entropy balance equation is derived. The decomposition of entropy production into housekeeping and free-energy parts is achieved by considering the relative entropy with respect to the stationary distribution. The applications demonstrate the framework's versatility by treating specific SPDEs, including those with spatially correlated noise and divergence-free drifts, using explicit computations of the entropy production and verification of the fluctuation theorems.

Third, for nonstationary systems, the sample-path entropy production decomposes into housekeeping heat and free-energy dissipation, each satisfying an integral fluctuation theorem with nonnegative expectations. The mean free-energy dissipation equals the decrease in relative entropy with respect to the stationary distribution. These results are illustrated through applications: for the stochastic heat equation with spatially correlated noise, the entropy production rate is computed explicitly; for the random polymer model, the fluctuation theorems are verified; for the nonlinear model with divergence-free drift, the entropy production vanishes in the stationary state, indicating time reversibility; and for the two coupled stochastic heat equations in contact with heat baths at different temperatures, the housekeeping heat and free-energy dissipation are analyzed, demonstrating the framework's ability to handle nonequilibrium steady states.

title: Active Approach To Fast Quantum State Preparation And Reset In Atomic Arrays
authors: Ya-Tang Yu, Wei-Hsuan Chung, Tian-Shu Gou, Kuan-Ting Lin, H. H. Jen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38261v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rapid preparation of a target quantum state and reset to the many-body ground state are essential for quantum information processing. Here, we investigate both processes in a waveguide-coupled emitter array in the low-excitation regime. By decomposing the effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian into biorthogonal eigenmodes, we show that relaxation depends on the initial overlap with the more subradiant modes, providing a modal explanation of the Mpemba effect. Guided by this insight, we design a reset protocol in which a finite-duration local drive activelysuppresses the relatively slow-decaying components. For the parameters studied, this reduces the time to reach a fixed residual-excitation threshold by up to approximately 25% compared with free decay. To prepare a target Dicke state, we introduce a two-step protocol that initially leaves one emitter undriven before restoring the full drive that stabilizes the target. This local control redistributes spectral weight into the more subradiant modes, driving them closer to their target amplitudes, which reduces the preparation time by up to approximately 45% while consuming less driving energy than continuous driving. Finally, we show how directional waveguide coupling shifts collective modes toward a preferred boundary through the non-Hermitian skin effect, providing guidance for selecting the preferred site for local operations. We term this fundamental dependence of the relaxation dynamics on the system's chirality the ``non-Hermitian Skin-Mpemba effect.'' These results demonstrate how selective local control can accelerate state preparation and reset in open quantum systems.

motivation: Fast state preparation and reset are important for quantum information processing, but free decay in open emitter arrays can be slowed by subradiant modes. The authors seek modal control strategies that actively suppress slow-decaying components.
method: They model the low-excitation waveguide-coupled emitter array using an effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian diagonalized in a biorthogonal eigenmode basis. Guided by this modal decomposition, they design finite-duration local driving protocols for reset and Dicke-state preparation, and analyze directional waveguide coupling via the non-Hermitian skin effect.
result: The reset protocol reduces the time to reach a fixed residual-excitation threshold by up to about 25%, while the two-step Dicke-state preparation protocol reduces preparation time by up to about 45% with less driving energy than continuous driving. Directional coupling shifts collective modes toward a preferred boundary through the non-Hermitian skin effect.
conclusion: Selective local control can accelerate state preparation and reset in open quantum systems, and the chirality-dependent relaxation dynamics is termed the non-Hermitian skin-Mpemba effect, offering guidance for site selection in atomic-array experiments.

title: Schur$\unicode{x2013}$Weyl Reduction Of Finite-Copy Precision Bounds For Multiparameter Quantum Estimation
authors: Masahito Hayashi Jianchao Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38299v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In multiparameter quantum estimation, incompatible measurements can impose trade-offs among estimation errors. Understanding the precision attainable with a finite number of jointly measured copies is therefore important, but direct optimization becomes costly as the tensor product space grows exponentially. For independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) copies, the quantum statistical model is invariant under permutations of the copies. We exploit this symmetry through Schur--Weyl duality to remove permutation multiplicity spaces while using their dimensions as weights. This gives a reduced statistical model equivalent to the original under arbitrary collective measurements. On this reduced model, we derive an exact conic formulation of the tight Cram\'er--Rao bound and a semidefinite program for its Nagaoka--Hayashi (NH) relaxation. For fixed single-copy dimension, the reduced operator representation grows polynomially rather than exponentially with the number of copies. To approximate the tight bound, we use an exact quadratic identity to correct finite-ray dual solutions and obtain rigorous upper and lower bounds. For fixed copy number and parameter dimension, sufficiently fine meshes admit feasible primal points, and dual solutions with bounded objective gaps have uniformly bounded compact-search radii. These results yield quadratic convergence in the projective covering radius. Numerical examples illustrate the quadratic scaling of the mesh correction term and the computational reach of the reduced NH formulation.
tldr: The paper develops a Schur-Weyl-duality reduction for finite-copy multiparameter quantum estimation, yielding tractable exact and relaxed precision bounds under collective measurements.
motivation: Finite-copy multiparameter quantum estimation is computationally hard because the joint Hilbert space grows exponentially, yet incompatible measurements create important precision trade-offs that cannot be captured by simple asymptotic bounds.
method: The authors exploit permutation symmetry via Schur-Weyl duality to construct a reduced statistical model equivalent to the original for arbitrary collective measurements, then derive an exact conic Cramér-Rao formulation and a semidefinite program for its Nagaoka-Hayashi relaxation, with mesh-based rigorous upper and lower bounds.
result: For fixed single-copy dimension, the reduced representation grows polynomially with copy number, and numerical examples illustrate quadratic scaling of the mesh correction term and the computational reach of the reduced Nagaoka-Hayashi formulation.
conclusion: The reduction makes finite-copy multiparameter quantum precision bounds computationally accessible while retaining exactness for collective measurements, providing rigorous approximate bounds with controlled convergence.

By decomposing the tensor product space into irreducible representations of the symmetric and unitary groups, they eliminate permutation multiplicity spaces while retaining their dimensions as weights. This yields a reduced statistical model that is equivalent to the original under arbitrary collective measurements. On this reduced model, they formulate the tight CRB as an exact conic program and its Nagaoka-Hayashi (NH) relaxation as a semidefinite program (SDP). For fixed single-copy dimension, the reduced operator representation grows polynomially rather than exponentially with the number of copies, enabling practical computation. To approximate the tight bound, they introduce an exact quadratic identity to correct finite-ray dual solutions, yielding rigorous upper and lower bounds. They prove that for fixed copy number and parameter dimension, sufficiently fine meshes admit feasible primal points and dual solutions with bounded objective gaps, leading to quadratic convergence in the projective covering radius. Numerical examples demonstrate the quadratic scaling of the mesh correction term and illustrate the computational reach of the reduced NH formulation.

The authors construct a reduced statistical model by replacing the full density operator with a block-diagonal operator in the irreducible subspaces, weighted by the dimensions of the multiplicity spaces. To handle the continuous set of rays (rank-one projectors) in the dual problem, they discretize using a projective covering (a mesh) and apply an exact quadratic identity to correct the dual objective, yielding certified bounds. The analysis of convergence uses the geometry of the projective space and properties of the mesh to show that the gap between the upper and lower bounds scales quadratically with the covering radius.

title: Quantum Advantage By Designing Beneficial Dissipation From Lossless Dynamics
authors: Xiao Xue Zeng-Zhao Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38183v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Passive loss removes probability from a system and therefore seems unable to improve an unconditional target. This intuition is exact for classical population dynamics under sink-only removal: passive killing obeys a finite-strength monotonicity principle even after optimization over the remaining controls. Here we show that coherent quantum dynamics can violate this classical monotonicity because coherent contributions to the final target can interfere destructively. We derive a trajectory-level criterion that determines when such a detrimental contribution is physically accessible to passive loss and accumulates into a net unconditional benefit. The criterion is encoded in a response operator constructed entirely from the lossless dynamics: its spectrum determines whether weak passive loss can help, while its principal eigenvector identifies the optimal environmental mode. Applying this criterion to vibronically assisted transfer, we identify a beneficial mode formed by coherently combining two individually detrimental local loss directions. The predicted mode remains near-optimal at finite loss, producing an \(8.73\%\) enhancement over the independently optimized lossless benchmark, compared with \(9.52\%\) under full finite-loss optimization. Our results establish how coherent quantum dynamics can evade classical passive-loss monotonicity and provide a general task-dependent principle for designing beneficial passive environments from lossless dynamics.
tldr: The paper shows that coherent quantum dynamics can make passive loss beneficial by exploiting destructive interference, and derives a lossless-dynamics-based criterion for designing optimal dissipative environments.
motivation: Passive loss is usually expected to harm target probabilities, but quantum coherence may allow loss to enhance unconditioned target outcomes in ways impossible classically.
method: The authors derive a trajectory-level monotonicity criterion encoded in a response operator built from the lossless dynamics, whose spectrum and principal eigenvector predict beneficial weak loss and the optimal environmental mode.
result: Applied to vibronically assisted transfer, the criterion identifies a beneficial mode combining two individually detrimental local loss directions, yielding an 8.73% enhancement over the independently optimized lossless benchmark and nearing the 9.52% full finite-loss optimum.
conclusion: Coherent quantum dynamics can evade classical passive-loss monotonicity, providing a general task-dependent principle for designing beneficial passive environments from lossless dynamics.

title: Lower Bound For Region Of Non-Distillable Magic States
authors: Akul Sethi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37807v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Magic states are a leading proposal for realizing fault-tolerant and universal quantum computation. At the present moment, much of the theory of magic states is not understood. Even simple questions such as what single qubit states have magic remain open. In Campbell and Browne's seminal paper on bound magic states, they prove the existence of states outside of the stabilizer octahedron which cannot be used to achieve universal computation. In this paper we expand upon their proof and determine a lower-bound on this region.

result: A lower bound is obtained for the non-distillable region of magic states, providing a more refined characterization of states outside the stabilizer octahedron that cannot achieve universal computation.
conclusion: The work sharpens the known geometry of bound magic states and contributes to the resource theory of magic, though the contribution is an incremental theoretical advance rather than a broad new framework.

title: Stellar Representation Of Gottesman Kitaev Preskill States On The Double Discrete Cylinder
authors: Aidan Zlotak, Nicolas Fabre, Romain Murenzi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37831v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Covariant integral quantization is developed on the double discrete cylinder phase space, with the torus as configuration space, and yields the Wigner distribution and the stellar representation. This phase space is particularly well suited to translationally invariant states, such as the Gottesman Kitaev Preskill (GKP) states. These states are central to fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures, yet their quantum resources are still under investigation. The stellar representations of ideal GKP logical states, which behave as phase eigenstates of the double discrete cylinder, have no zeros on this phase space, whereas those of their superpositions have infinitely many. The vacuum, although Gaussian, has zeros on this phase space, and the zeros of finitely squeezed GKP states move with the widths of the peaks and of the envelope, and reach this phase space for fine-tuned widths. These features echo the role of the vacuum as the resource that makes GKP-based architectures hard to simulate.

motivation: GKP states are central to fault-tolerant quantum computing, but their quantum resources remain under investigation; phase-space representations may clarify non-Gaussian features relevant to simulability.
method: Covariant integral quantization is formulated on the double discrete cylinder with torus configuration space, yielding Wigner distributions and stellar representations for ideal and finitely squeezed GKP states and their superpositions.
result: Ideal GKP logical states have no zeros in this phase space, superpositions have infinitely many zeros, and finitely squeezed GKP zeros move with peak/envelope widths, with the vacuum also exhibiting zeros.
conclusion: The zero structure in the stellar representation echoes the role of the vacuum and non-Gaussian resources in making GKP-based architectures hard to simulate.

title: Noise Propagation And Effective Channels In Encrypted Quantum Cloning
authors: Yun-Fei Li, Fei-Hao Yang, Qing Chen, Liu-Jun Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38240v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate noise propagation in encrypted quantum cloning by formulating the protocol in terms of effective recovery channels. For local single-qubit completely positive trace-preserving noise, a Pauli-basis expansion of the Kraus operators reveals a strong dependence on the location of the physical channel. Noise on an auxiliary signal qubit leaves the reduced recovered state unchanged, whereas noise on an auxiliary key qubit induces a Pauli-diagonal effective channel on the recovered qubit. For the core qubits, the error propagation additionally depends on the parity of the number of entangled pairs. In particular, for noise on the core key qubit with odd parity, distinct physical Pauli sectors merge into the same effective sector, converting isotropic depolarizing noise into an anisotropic recovery channel. We also relate Werner-type resource imperfections to local depolarizing noise and distinguish distributed product depolarization from genuine global depolarization. The results demonstrate that the effective recovery noise is governed not only by noise strength, but also by its physical location and by the structure of the encryption-decryption protocol.

motivation: Encrypted quantum cloning involves encryption-decryption steps whose performance under realistic noise is not fully characterized, especially regarding how noise location affects the recovered state.
method: The authors formulate the protocol using effective recovery channels and expand Kraus operators in the Pauli basis for single-qubit CPTP noise on auxiliary and core qubits.
result: Noise on auxiliary signal qubits leaves the reduced recovered state unchanged, while noise on key or core qubits produces location- and parity-dependent effective channels, including conversion of isotropic depolarizing noise into anisotropic recovery channels.
conclusion: The effective recovery noise depends not only on noise strength but also on physical location and encryption-decryption structure, distinguishing distributed product depolarization from genuine global depolarization.

title: Approaching Landauer's Limit In A Single Superconducting Vortex Memory Bit
authors: Nofar Fridman, Itai Keren, Avia Noah, Yishay Zur, Martin E. Huber, Nadav Katz, Roland Willa, Hadar Steinberg, Yonathan Anahory
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37753v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work investigates the energy required to manipulate a memory bit using a superconducting vortex confined in a nanoscale double-well pinning potential. In the experiments, various double-well systems subjected to sinusoidal forces is explored, and the effects of both driving force and frequency is analyzed. Results reveal characteristic stochastic resonance behavior for weak drives and adiabatic manipulation at strong, low-frequency drives. Although our experimental method requires a steady sinusoidal drive incompatible with Landauer's erasure protocol, our numerical analysis demonstrates that the work required for such bit manipulation (erasure) is within an order of magnitude of Landauer's limit ([MATH]) at 4.2 K. These findings open possibilities for creating highly efficient memory elements that could be integrated with cryogenic quantum circuits or function as topological quantum computing qubits; thereby contributing to memory devices with lower energy consumption and mitigating the escalating global energy demand in the computing industry.
tldr: An experimental and numerical study of a superconducting vortex memory bit manipulated in a double-well pinning potential, showing work costs within an order of magnitude of Landauer's limit at 4.2 K.

method: They use a superconducting vortex confined in a nanoscale double-well potential, apply sinusoidal driving forces at varying amplitudes and frequencies, and analyze stochastic resonance and adiabatic manipulation regimes, supplemented by numerical modeling of bit-erasure work.
result: Weak drives produce stochastic resonance, while strong low-frequency drives yield adiabatic manipulation; numerical analysis shows the work required for bit manipulation is within an order of magnitude of Landauer's limit at 4.2 K.
conclusion: The system offers a promising route toward highly efficient cryogenic memory elements, though the experimental protocol is not directly compatible with Landauer erasure and the work remains above the fundamental bound.

title: Maximally-Matched Mixture Decoding For Correlated Atom Loss In Quantum Ldpc Codes
authors: Jacob W. Murri
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38283v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Heralded atom loss is a dominant noise channel in neutral atom quantum computing platforms, and losses at a two-qubit gate are strongly correlated: when one atom is lost, its gate partner is often lost too. This work shows how to exploit this correlation to construct a better decoder, focusing on [[144,12,12]] Gross code syndrome extraction circuits. Given a loss readout, the possible pairings of the lost qubits according to shared gates form a graph whose maximum matchings carry almost all of the conditional probability mass. Our maximal-matching-mixture (MMM) decoder builds a per-readout decoding hypergraph as a weighted mixture over exactly these loss scenarios. This decoding hypergraph can be used by an ordinary belief-propagation decoder. On the [[144,12,12]] Gross code, MMM lowers the logical error rate by as much as ~25x relative to a loss-unaware decoder and ~2x relative to a loss-aware uniform-mixture baseline from Baranes et al. (2026).
tldr: A maximal-matching-mixture (MMM) decoder that exploits correlated atom-loss events at two-qubit gates to build per-readout decoding hypergraphs for the [[144,12,12]] Gross code, substantially reducing logical error rates.
motivation: Heralded atom loss dominates noise in neutral-atom quantum computing, and losses at two-qubit gates are strongly correlated, so standard loss-aware decoders that treat lost qubits independently discard useful structure.
method: Given a loss readout, the authors construct a graph of possible pairings of lost qubits via shared gates, identify maximum matchings which carry nearly all conditional probability mass, and form a weighted mixture of these loss scenarios into a single decoding hypergraph for a standard belief-propagation decoder.
result: On the [[144,12,12]] Gross code syndrome extraction circuit, MMM lowers the logical error rate by up to ~25x versus a loss-unaware decoder and ~2x versus a loss-aware uniform-mixture baseline.
conclusion: Correlations in heralded loss are a useful and exploitable resource for decoding quantum LDPC codes on neutral-atom platforms, yielding tangible logical-error-rate gains with conventional decoders.

They introduce the maximal-matching-mixture (MMM) decoder, which constructs a per-readout decoding hypergraph as a weighted mixture over exactly these loss scenarios. This hypergraph can then be used by a standard belief-propagation decoder. On the Gross code, MMM reduces the logical error rate by up to ~25x compared to a loss-unaware decoder and ~2x compared to a loss-aware uniform-mixture baseline from Baranes et al. (2026). The work demonstrates that incorporating detailed correlation structure into the decoder yields substantial performance gains.

title: Exact Positive-P Simulation Of Open Quantum Spin Systems With Generalized Density Matrix Formalism
authors: Alex Ferrier, Yi Shi, Marzena H. Szyma\'nska, Piotr Deuar
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38059v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The positive-P representation for bosons allows scalable exact simulations of many-body open quantum systems, provided dissipation is strong enough to stabilise stochastic trajectories. Designing analogous methods for spin systems, relevant to quantum technologies, remains challenging, as previous spin positive-P formulations can exhibit systematic errors even when simulations are numerically stable. Here, we develop a phase-space representation that maps spin-[MATH] degrees of freedom onto parameters of a local generalized density matrix (GDM), rather than SU(2) coherent states. In all stable regimes, we observe no deviations from exact solutions, restoring the positive-P property: stable solutions are exact up to stochastic sampling noise. The GDM representation combines seamlessly with bosonic positive-P, enabling highly scalable treatment of coupled spin-boson systems. We map simulation stability versus spin and boson dissipation in the Jaynes-Cummings model and apply the method to a Jaynes-Cummings-Hubbard quasi-Lieb lattice, showing how spin dissipation and driving can destroy or restore excitation incompressibility.
tldr: The paper introduces a generalized density matrix phase-space representation for exact positive-P simulation of open quantum spin systems and coupled spin-boson models.
motivation: Positive-P methods enable scalable exact simulations of open bosonic systems, but analogous spin formulations can suffer systematic errors even in numerically stable regimes.
method: The authors map spin degrees of freedom onto local generalized density matrix parameters rather than SU(2) coherent states, and combine this with bosonic positive-P for coupled spin-boson dynamics.
result: In stable regimes the method reproduces exact solutions up to stochastic sampling noise, and is demonstrated on the Jaynes-Cummings model and a Jaynes-Cummings-Hubbard quasi-Lieb lattice.
conclusion: This restores the positive-P property for spin systems and provides a scalable simulation tool for open quantum spin-boson systems relevant to quantum technologies.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper introduces a new phase-space representation for spin-1/2 systems that maps spin degrees of freedom onto parameters of a local generalized density matrix (GDM), rather than SU(2) coherent states. This addresses a key limitation of previous spin positive-P formulations, which can produce systematic errors even when simulations are numerically stable. The GDM representation restores the positive-P property: in all stable regimes, the stochastic trajectories yield exact results up to sampling noise. The method combines naturally with bosonic positive-P, enabling scalable simulations of coupled spin-boson systems. The authors map the stability of the combined representation against spin and boson dissipation in the Jaynes-Cummings model, identifying regimes where the simulations are stable and exact. They then apply the method to a Jaynes-Cummings-Hubbard quasi-Lieb lattice, demonstrating how spin dissipation and driving can destroy or restore excitation incompressibility. The work provides a promising route for exact, scalable simulations of open quantum systems with spins and bosons, relevant to quantum technologies.

In the positive-P representation for bosons, the density matrix is expanded over coherent states, and the resulting Fokker-Planck equation is mapped to stochastic differential equations (SDEs) for complex variables. For spins, previous approaches used SU(2) coherent states, but the resulting SDEs could yield systematic deviations from exact results even when stable. The GDM approach instead represents each spin's density matrix by a set of parameters (e.g., three real numbers for a spin-1/2) that evolve stochastically. The authors derive the corresponding SDEs and show that in the stable regime, the stochastic averages reproduce exact quantum expectations. The method is then combined with bosonic positive-P by treating spins and bosons on equal footing, leading to a unified phase-space representation for coupled systems. The stability analysis is performed by examining the drift and diffusion terms of the SDEs, identifying conditions under which trajectories remain bounded. title: The Geometry Of Quantum Teleportation In Phase Space
authors: Jasel Berra-Montiel, Alberto Molgado, Mar S\'anchez-C\'ordova
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37861v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We formulate the standard quantum teleportation protocol within the framework of deformation quantization, employing the Stratonovich--Weyl (SW) correspondence and the associated star product on the coadjoint orbits of [MATH]. Each qubit is represented by a spherical phase space [MATH] endowed with the Kirillov--Kostant--Souriau (KKS) symplectic structure. Within this setting, we explicitly construct the phase space representations of the entangled Bell resource, the controlled-NOT and Hadamard operators, the projective measurements, and the conditional Pauli corrections. We demonstrate how the quantum information initially encoded in the Wigner function for the input qubit is redistributed through bipartite and tripartite phase space correlations. Upon consideration of a conditional unitary transformation, the measurement outcome produces a Wigner function on the receiver's coadjoint orbit that is related to the input by an outcome-dependent rotation, which can subsequently be inverted through the implementation of an appropriate Pauli correction. The covariance of the SW correspondence provides a geometric interpretation of this process, in which quantum information is redistributed and reconstructed without transferring the underlying symplectic geometry. Our formulation can also be extended to study quantum teleportation in more general phase space geometries equipped with suitable star products.
