title: Ontology Without States: Pbr As An Argument For Dynamics-first Realism
authors: Nick Ormrod
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37948v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Pusey--Barrett--Rudolph (PBR) theorem is commonly taken to establish that a pure quantum state represents a physical property of the system to which it is assigned, rather than merely encoding knowledge. In this work, I distinguish between state-first and dynamics-first physical theories, and argue that this reading presupposes the former. These two types of theories support different approaches to causal explanation, and one of PBR's stated assumptions depends on the state-first approach. Using a recent interpretation of quantum theory as a concrete example, I show how a dynamics-first theory can explain the PBR correlations while maintaining a broadly epistemic reading of quantum states. I conclude that the PBR theorem supports a dilemma: either the quantum state is part of reality, or reality is not fundamentally built out of states.
tldr: The paper reinterprets the Pusey–Barrett–Rudolph theorem by distinguishing 'state-first' from 'dynamics-first' physical theories, arguing that PBR only rules out epistemic readings of the quantum state if one presupposes that reality is fundamentally built out of states.
motivation: PBR is widely cited as settling the ontic-vs-epistemic debate about the quantum state, and the author aims to show that this conclusion depends on an unexamined assumption about the structure of physical theories rather than on the theorem alone.
method: Conceptual and interpretive analysis: a taxonomy of state-first versus dynamics-first theories is developed, the role of causal explanation in each is examined, and one of PBR's stated assumptions is shown to be state-first-dependent; a recent dynamics-first interpretation is used as a concrete case study.
result: A dynamics-first theory can reproduce the PBR correlations while retaining a broadly epistemic reading of quantum states, so PBR does not by itself force state ontology.
conclusion: PBR supports a dilemma: either the quantum state is part of reality, or reality is not fundamentally composed of states—making the theorem a constraint on ontology rather than a direct refutation of epistemic views.

title: Barren Plateaus In Quantum Linear Combinations: Interference And Lie-Algebraic Control
authors: Amir Koutahi, Pouya Kananian, Hans-Arno Jacobsen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38193v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A coherent sum of quantum circuits introduces interference that can alter the training signal. We distinguish a single linear combination of unitaries (LCU) from a circuit that repeatedly alternates branch operations and ancilla mixing. For a single-pass LCU, independent branches with zero matrix means cannot erase the differentiated branch's gradient variance: the total variance is at least the branch variance times the fourth power of its coefficient magnitude. This bound holds at any gate position and does not require the circuit unitaries to be Haar-random. Beyond this lower bound, we derive exact loss and gradient formulas that quantify the additional contributions from interference between branches. One of these terms depends on relative coefficient phases and vanishes when the branch ensemble is invariant under multiplication by [MATH]; a four-qubit matchgate example shows that it can be nonzero. For repeated interleaving with full special-unitary ancilla control, we determine the generated Lie algebra from the associative algebra of the branches, including the available central phase directions. This control result predicts concentration only with additional assumptions on circuit sampling. Matchgate examples exhibit polynomial single-pass LCU variances and exponential concentration under joint Haar-random sampling. We also derive coefficient-selection rules and bounds for postselection, measurement error, and approximate moments.
tldr: The paper analyzes barren plateaus in quantum circuits implementing linear combinations of unitaries, deriving gradient-variance bounds and Lie-algebraic controllability conditions that govern trainability.
motivation: Coherent sums of quantum circuits can introduce interference that changes the training signal in variational quantum algorithms, so it is important to understand when such LCU-based circuits avoid or exhibit barren plateaus.
method: The authors derive analytic loss and gradient formulas for single-pass LCU circuits, bound the gradient variance in terms of branch variances and coefficient magnitudes, identify phase-dependent interference contributions, and use Lie-algebraic control theory for repeated interleaving with ancilla mixing.
result: For a single-pass LCU, the total gradient variance is lower-bounded by the differentiated branch variance times the fourth power of its coefficient, independent of Haar randomness, while interference terms can be nonzero; matchgate examples show polynomial single-pass variance but exponential concentration under joint Haar-random sampling.
conclusion: Trainability of LCU-based quantum circuits depends on coherent interference structure, coefficient selection, and the generated Lie algebra, with barren plateaus predicted only under additional sampling assumptions.

title: A Coherent Neutron-Nucleus Hybrid System Mediated By The Strong Interaction
authors: Niels Geerits, Kylie A. Dickerson, Earl Babcock, Andreas Dvorak, Florian Engel, Konstantin Kholostov, Vladimir Ossovyi, Zahir Salhi, Clemens Trunner, Stephan Sponar
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38119v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A coherent ensemble of polarized helium-3 nuclei and free neutrons are coupled, forming a neutron-nucleus hybrid system. The nuclei are prepared in a spin superposition, while a magnetic field induces Zeeman splitting. The resulting nuclear energy phase is coherently transferred to the neutron, producing an intensity beat at the nuclear Zeeman frequency. Finally, the incident neutron is prepared in a spin-energy superposition state. The nuclear and neutron phases then heterodyne coherently, producing a signal at the sum or difference frequency depending on their relative helicity.
tldr: The authors demonstrate a coherent neutron–nucleus hybrid quantum system in which a polarized helium-3 spin ensemble coherently transfers its Zeeman phase to a free neutron, producing observable intensity beats and heterodyne signals.
motivation: Coherent coupling between distinct quantum systems is a prerequisite for hybrid quantum architectures, but neutron-based coherent interfaces to nuclear spin ensembles have remained largely unexplored.
method: Polarized 3He nuclei are prepared in a spin superposition under a magnetic field, and the resulting nuclear Zeeman phase is transferred to a neutron prepared in a spin-energy superposition; the relative helicity determines whether the coherent heterodyne signal appears at the sum or difference frequency.
result: The nuclear energy phase is coherently transferred to the neutron, yielding an intensity beat at the nuclear Zeeman frequency and a heterodyne signal at the sum or difference frequency depending on relative helicity.
conclusion: The work establishes a neutron–nucleus hybrid coherent system, suggesting neutron interferometry as a platform for coherent manipulation and readout of nuclear spin ensembles, though its connection to quantum information processing tasks remains to be established.

title: Ancilla-free Randomized Toffoli Gates And The T-count Of Boolean Oracles
authors: Arul Rhik Mazumder
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38189v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In fault-tolerant Clifford+T circuits, a Boolean oracle costs T gates and extra qubits, and on four or more qubits every exact Toffoli gate needs an extra qubit. Gosset, Kothari and Zhang showed that sampling a fresh random circuit for each call makes the T-count of the Toffoli gate independent of its size, but a direct implementation of their sampler uses about one extra qubit per bit of precision. We show that computing the sampled parities in place, on the gate's own controls, removes every extra qubit once the gate is large enough: each random circuit then uses about 8 T gates per bit of precision and borrows only the gate's own idle inputs. This is one T gate more per circuit than the best measurement-free variant that keeps one clean ancilla. The same holds for exclusive-ors of indicators of affine subspaces, such as equality tests and checks of linear equations. For randomized circuits that do not measure, this is within a factor of eight of optimal up to an additive constant, even with extra qubits, and when each random circuit computes a Boolean function exactly, closing the factor asymptotically is equivalent to determining the leading constant in the T-count of exact multi-controlled Toffoli gates. Finally, the oracle of the indicator of a random set of fixed density needs exponentially many T gates at constant error, while that of an affine subspace of the same density needs a constant number, and extra qubits reduce the exponential cost only quadratically.
tldr: The paper constructs ancilla-free randomized Toffoli gates and analyzes the T-count of Boolean oracles in fault-tolerant Clifford+T circuits.
motivation: Exact Toffoli gates on four or more qubits require extra qubits, and randomized implementations can make T-count independent of gate size but typically need ancillas.
method: The author computes sampled parities in place on the gate's own controls, eliminating extra qubits for sufficiently large gates, and extends the approach to exclusive-ors of affine-subspace indicators.
result: The construction uses about 8 T gates per bit of precision and only the gate's idle inputs, at the cost of one extra T gate per circuit compared with the best clean-ancilla measurement-free variant.
conclusion: The work improves ancilla requirements for randomized Toffoli circuits and gives T-count bounds for Boolean oracles, but it concerns circuit complexity and T-count, which are not prioritized in the stated research interests.

title: Dimension-free Exponential Entropy Quotients Over $\mathbb{F}_2$
authors: Josiah Park
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38525v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be a random vector in [MATH], and let [MATH] be an independent copy. We prove that, for every [MATH], there is a subspace [MATH] with [MATH] such that [MATH]. In particular, the quotient entropy is at most [MATH]. The structural result is a logarithmic rigidity estimate for finite weighted families of laws with averaged subspace entropy sparsity. A common variational quotient controls both a family and its convolution family without decreasing the original family's normalized mean entropy defect. Posterior families preserve averaged sparsity, and a fresh-index argument combines a local-to-global estimate with the entropic Marton theorem to increase the defect ratio at a fixed multiplicative sparsity cost. motivation: Entropy quotients—comparing a source's entropy to its entropy conditioned on a subspace—quantify how much randomness survives restriction to structured (subspace) constraints, a question relevant to randomness extraction, subspace-evasive sets, and entropic additive combinatorics.
method: The authors establish a logarithmic rigidity estimate for weighted families of laws with averaged subspace entropy sparsity, introduce a variational quotient controlling both a family and its convolution family, and combine a local-to-global estimate with the entropic Marton theorem via a fresh-index argument.

conclusion: The results give dimension-free, order-optimal entropy quotient bounds over F_2 and new structural tools (rigidity, variational quotients, entropic Marton-type arguments) for subspace-restricted entropy analysis, with constants left unoptimized.

title: Shor's Algorithm Compiled On Cat Qubits: 22 593 Qubits For Rsa-2048 In 3.14 Days
authors: Axel Pappalardo, Dahmun Goudarzi, Victor Hertz, Hugo Jacinto, Larissa Kroell, Andr\'e Schrottenloher, Peter Shanahan, \'elie Gouzien, R\'emi de la Vieuville, Vivien Londe
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37839v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present an end-to-end resource estimation of Shor's algorithm on superconducting cat qubits, from its mathematical description to the allocation and scheduling of physical qubits on a chip layout. We review modern versions of Shor's algorithm for RSA, ECDLP and FFDLP, and make their logical circuits and trade-offs explicit. We compile the dominant subroutines down to physical-qubit operations on two architectures: one based on repetition cat codes and one on LDPC cat codes. We design a parity-Cnot gate for cat qubits, extend a multi-target Cnot gate to the LDPC-cat architecture, and adapt an active injection procedure to cat qubits. Building on these primitives, we adapt to cat qubits the adder from Gidney's 2025 resource estimate for factoring RSA-2048. We combine our adder compilation and a coarser estimate for the phaseup with the factory designs and lookup compilation from the FeMoco resource estimation of Kroell et al. Together, these lead to chip layouts and schedules for factoring RSA-2048. Assuming a 1[MATH]s error-correction cycle time, a 10[MATH]s reaction time, circuit-level phase-flip noise with probability [MATH] and no bit-flips, factoring RSA-2048, the configuration we compile in full, requires about 23 000 cat qubits and 3.14 days. Reusing the compiled operations, solving ECDLP on secp256k1 requires at most 30 000 cat qubits and 1 hour, and FFDLP-512, which we propose as an intermediate benchmark, about 6 700 cat qubits and 21 minutes. Trading space for time, RSA-2048 runs in 1.25 hours on about 611 000 cat qubits. The no-bit-flip requirement (a bit-flip time of about 100 years) can be relaxed to a bit-flip time of about one hour by adding a concatenation layer with a distance-3 bit-flip code, in which case RSA-2048 needs about 45 000 cat qubits.
tldr: End-to-end resource estimation of Shor's algorithm compiled onto superconducting cat-qubit architectures, showing RSA-2048 factoring in ~3.14 days with ~23,000 cat qubits under idealized noise assumptions.
motivation: Bosonic cat qubits offer hardware-level bias against bit-flip errors, making them attractive for reducing the overhead of fault-tolerant factoring, but no full chip-level compilation and scheduling had been done for Shor's algorithm on this platform.
method: The authors review modern Shor variants for RSA, ECDLP and FFDLP, compile the dominant subroutines down to physical operations on repetition-code and LDPC-cat architectures, design a parity-CNOT gate, extend multi-target CNOTs, adapt active injection, and combine a Gidney-style adder with FeMoco-style magic-state factories and lookup compilation into chip layouts and schedules.
result: Assuming a 1 microsecond error-correction cycle, 10 microsecond reaction time and pure phase-flip noise, RSA-2048 requires ~23,000 cat qubits and 3.14 days (or 1.25 hours on ~611,000 qubits); ECDLP on secp256k1 needs ~30,000 qubits and 1 hour, FFDLP-512 ~6,700 qubits and 21 minutes, and a distance-3 concatenation layer relaxes the bit-flip requirement to ~1 hour at ~45,000 qubits.
conclusion: Cat-qubit architectures could substantially reduce qubit counts for cryptographically relevant quantum algorithms, though the estimates hinge on optimistic bias-preserving noise assumptions and error-correction hardware performance.

title: Exact Verification Of Givens Rotation Circuits For Efficient Quantum Phase Estimation Of Iron-sulfur Clusters
authors: Honghui Shang Lizhong Fu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37847v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Givens rotations with angles stored in quantum registers account for much of the cost of published quantum phase estimation algorithms based on double-factorized tensor hypercontraction and spectral amplification. These rotations create superpositions and cannot be verified directly by the basis-state evaluators used to optimize classical reversible circuits. We give an exact verification method that separates out a fixed Clifford change of basis and tracks basis states and phases in the remaining circuit. Integer conditions establish correctness of the full coherent action, including measurement-based uncomputation and restoration of the phase-gradient resource state. Under our interpretation of Low et al.'s angle grid and rotation convention, simplifying the adders lowers the rotation cost relative to the published accounting; fusing the two additions into one masked addition gives an additional saving. We verify both implementations exhaustively at every precision used in the published walks and prove the fused circuit correct for all widths. For benchmarks including FeMoco and other iron-sulfur clusters, replacing only the rotation term lowers total phase-estimation Toffoli counts by 9.5-14.3% under the published error budget, with the walk operator unchanged.
tldr: The paper presents an exact verification method for Givens rotation circuits used in quantum phase estimation of iron-sulfur clusters, reducing Toffoli counts by optimizing and verifying rotation subcircuits.
motivation: Givens rotations with register-stored angles dominate the cost of double-factorized tensor hypercontraction and spectral-amplification QPE algorithms, but they are difficult to verify because they create superpositions not handled by basis-state evaluators.
method: The authors separate a fixed Clifford basis change and track basis states and phases in the remaining circuit, using integer conditions to verify the full coherent action, including measurement-based uncomputation and phase-gradient state restoration; they also simplify adders and fuse two additions into one masked addition, verifying implementations exhaustively and proving the fused circuit correct for all widths.
result: For benchmarks including FeMoco and other iron-sulfur clusters, replacing only the rotation term lowers total QPE Toffoli counts by 9.5–14.3% under the published error budget while leaving the walk operator unchanged.
conclusion: The verified rotation-circuit optimizations provide a concrete cost reduction for chemistry-relevant QPE implementations, though the contribution is specialized to circuit verification and compilation rather than core quantum information theory.

title: Are Quantum Measurements Universal?
authors: Massimiliano Sassoli de Bianchi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37873v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With D. Aerts, we showed in 2014, within the extended Bloch representation of quantum mechanics, that the Born rule can be understood as resulting from a universal average over all the possible ways in which the measurement-interactions can be selected. The cellular construction used there was since questioned, in the context of Bertrand's paradox, by N. Shackel, who observed that the result depends on the discretization adopted, that the sequence of averages is constant, and that the sense in which the average is taken over "all" densities remains unclear. Taking these criticisms as a stimulus, we re-examine the notion. The key is to recognize that a universal measurement is a random way of selecting a measurement which does not privilege any portion of the structure describing the available interactions, a property we call indifference. We prove that every indifferent universal measurement, however constructed, produces exactly the Born probabilities: the universal average is unique, and the cellular construction of 2014 is one among infinitely many ways of obtaining it, exact at every finite resolution. Non-trivial indifferent universal measurements exist, but must involve deterministic measurements: Dirichlet processes are indifferent universal measurements reaching every way of selecting an interaction, whereas an indifferent universal measurement free of deterministic components necessarily selects the uniform density, so that the Born rule holds not only on average but with certainty. Deviations from the quantum statistics in sequences of measurements are governed by a single parameter, in principle accessible to experiment. The only geometric inputs are the Euclidean length of the membrane and the orthogonal landing of the point-particle on it; the latter is where the content of Gleason's theorem lies. Generalizations to N outcomes and to Bertrand's paradox are discussed.
tldr: The paper re-examines and defends the notion of universal quantum measurements, showing that any indifferent universal measurement yields exactly the Born probabilities and that the 2014 cellular construction is one of infinitely many such constructions.
motivation: The authors respond to criticisms by Shackel concerning the 2014 derivation of the Born rule via universal averaging in the extended Bloch representation, particularly issues related to discretization, Bertrand's paradox, and the meaning of averaging over all densities.
method: The paper formalizes the concept of an 'indifferent' universal measurement as a random selection of measurement interactions that does not privilege any part of the interaction structure, and proves that all such measurements reproduce the Born rule exactly at finite resolution.
result: The universal average is unique despite infinitely many indifferent constructions; non-trivial indifferent universal measurements must involve deterministic components, while those free of deterministic components select the uniform density, making the Born rule hold with certainty. Experimental deviations are governed by a single parameter.
conclusion: The work clarifies the foundations of the Born rule and its connection to Gleason's theorem, generalizing to N outcomes and Bertrand's paradox, but remains a foundational conceptual contribution rather than directly advancing the researcher's core interests.

title: Finite-step Statistical Mechanics Of Scale-invariant Learning: Spectral Equations Of State And Curvature Transport
authors: Alexander Itin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stationary learning admits an ideal-gas description under restrictive noise assumptions. In neural networks whose gradient noise departs from these assumptions, however, an entropy-scaling relation resembling a Maxwell relation remains approximately valid. We ask which thermodynamic-looking relations follow from scale symmetry rather than equilibrium, and how departures from the ideal-gas description can be quantified, for discrete stochastic gradient dynamics with memory. An exact rescaling of trajectories explains the entropy relation without assuming thermal equilibrium. Within a local harmonic approximation, self-adjusting weight norms yield a spectral equation of state whose virial coefficients are set by moments of the curvature spectrum, and coupled parameter groups can sustain stationary probability currents. Our central result beyond this approximation is an exact curvature-transport identity. Together with a finite-step loss balance, it decomposes corrections to the harmonic fluctuation relation into measurable curvature changes, finite-step remainders, gradient-memory correlations and finite-window drift terms. A related displacement-weighted curvature change provides a diagnostic of the arrow of time; its mean and second moment give a lower bound on the relative entropy between forward and reversed state pairs. We also calculate the activation-boundary contribution to curvature for rectified teacher-student networks with Gaussian inputs. Tests in sphere models, teacher-student networks and convolutional networks on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 support the transport description and identify limits of the harmonic and cubic-remainder approximations. These results separate symmetry-based relations from equilibrium assumptions and provide quantitative diagnostics of nonideal fluctuations in learning dynamics.
tldr: The paper develops a finite-step statistical-mechanical description of scale-invariant stochastic gradient learning, deriving spectral equations of state and an exact curvature-transport identity.
motivation: Stationary learning is often modeled as an ideal gas under restrictive noise assumptions, but realistic gradient noise violates these assumptions, motivating a symmetry-based rather than equilibrium-based thermodynamic description.
method: The author uses exact trajectory rescaling, a local harmonic approximation, and a curvature-transport identity to decompose corrections to harmonic fluctuation relations for discrete stochastic gradient dynamics with memory.
result: The framework yields spectral equations of state, stationary probability currents, and measurable correction terms involving curvature changes, finite-step remainders, gradient-memory correlations, and finite-window drift; tests on sphere models, teacher-student networks, and CNNs support the description.
conclusion: The work separates thermodynamic-looking relations derived from scale symmetry from those requiring equilibrium assumptions and provides quantitative diagnostics for nonideal fluctuations in learning dynamics, though it is not a quantum-information or quantum-thermodynamics result.

title: Ground-state Energy Estimation Compiled On Cat Qubits: 7 164 Qubits For FeMoco-54 In 23.5 Hours
authors: Larissa Kroell, Hugo Jacinto, Victor Hertz, Axel Pappalardo, Adel Ben Moussa, Manuel Rispler, Peter Shanahan, \'elie Gouzien, Christophe Vuillot, Vivien Londe
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37840v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We provide a detailed resource estimate of the state-of-the-art sum-of-squares block encoding algorithm for electronic structure Hamiltonians of Low et al. on superconducting cat qubits. To achieve this, we present compilations with closed-form costs of the dominant subroutines such as skew-tree Qrom, a Swap network and a Phaseup for both a repetition-cat and an LDPC-cat architecture. Our compilation represents algorithmic qubits in the [MATH] basis, taking advantage of the asymmetric cost of [MATH] and [MATH] access that the concatenation of cat qubits with phase-flip classical code brings. Additionally, we provide a protocol for [MATH]-state distillation and a two-level Toffoli-like [MATH] magic state distillation protocol, including three factory layouts. To minimize the cost of Clifford corrections induced by magic state injections we tailor injection gadgets to each subroutine. Combining our compilation work with the adder compilation from the companion work Pappalardo et al., we provide global layouts for the block encoding in both architectures which we use to obtain resource estimates for ground-state energy estimation for the benchmarks of FeMoco-54 and FeMoco-76. Assuming a cycle time of 1[MATH]s, a reaction time of 10[MATH]s, a phase estimation precision of 1 mHa and circuit-level phase-flip noise with probability [MATH] with negligible bit-flip error, FeMoco-54 requires fewer than [MATH] cat qubits with an expected runtime of under one day for a single phase estimation run using an LDPC-cat architecture. Relaxing the bit-flip requirement to [MATH] with an additional layer of elevator codes raises this to an estimated [MATH] cat qubits.
tldr: A detailed compilation and resource estimate showing that ground-state energy estimation for FeMoco-54 could be run on roughly 7,164 superconducting cat qubits in under a day using a sum-of-squares block encoding with LDPC-cat architecture.
motivation: Quantum chemistry benchmarks such as FeMoco are leading targets for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but concrete, architecture-aware resource counts are needed to judge feasibility; cat qubits with bias-preserving noise offer one plausible route.
method: The authors give closed-form compilations of dominant subroutines (skew-tree QROM, swap networks, Phaseup) in the Z-basis for repetition-cat and LDPC-cat architectures, plus T-state and two-level Toffoli-like CCZ magic-state distillation protocols and tailored injection gadgets, then combine these with a companion adder compilation into global layouts for block encoding.
result: Assuming 1 microsecond cycle times, 10 microsecond reaction times, 1 mHa phase-estimation precision, and circuit-level phase-flip noise with negligible bit-flip error, FeMoco-54 requires fewer than 10^4 cat qubits with sub-day runtime; relaxing the bit-flip requirement with an extra elevator-code layer raises the count substantially for FeMoco-76.
conclusion: Cat-qubit architectures with LDPC codes and magic-state factories make classically intractable chemistry benchmarks resource-plausible, though the estimates hinge on optimistic noise and timing assumptions.

title: Einstein Metrics And Quantum Control On Symmetric Tensor Product Quotients
authors: Honghuai Fang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38340v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be the space of projective [MATH]-qubit unitaries modulo local unitaries and permutations of the qubits. We prove that for all sufficiently large [MATH] the manifold [MATH] carries exactly two [MATH]-invariant Einstein metrics up to scaling. Both Einstein metrics have uniformly bounded diameter after normalizing two-qubit costs, although approximating a Haar-random unitary requires exponentially many two-qubit gates. In contrast, we construct non-Einstein metrics with nonnegative Ricci curvature and exponentially growing typical control distances, and determine the sharp curvature threshold for this family.
tldr: The paper proves that the manifold of projective n-qubit unitaries modulo local unitaries and qubit permutations admits exactly two invariant Einstein metrics for large n, and contrasts these with non-Einstein nonnegative-Ricci-curvature metrics exhibiting exponentially growing control distances.
motivation: The geometry of the space of quantum gates modulo local operations bears on the complexity of compiling unitaries, so understanding its canonical Riemannian (Einstein) structures and curvature/cost-distances could inform quantum control.
method: Riemannian/differential-geometric analysis: classification of G-invariant Einstein metrics on a symmetric space quotient of SU(2^n) by local unitaries and permutations, plus explicit construction of alternative metrics with controlled Ricci curvature and diameter bounds under a two-qubit cost normalization.
result: Exactly two invariant Einstein metrics exist for sufficiently large n, both with uniformly bounded diameter despite Haar-random unitaries requiring exponentially many two-qubit gates; a sharp curvature threshold separates metrics with exponential typical control distance.
conclusion: Canonical Einstein structures do not capture circuit complexity, whereas curvature-thresholded non-Einstein metrics do, linking Ricci geometry to control distance growth.

title: A Photonic-integrated Optomechanical Mid-infrared Detector
authors: Guillermo Arregui, Amirali Arabmoheghi, Alessio Zicoschi, Xinru Ji, Scott E. Kenning, Marco Golino, Shivaprasad U. Hulyal, Yi Xia, Sunil A. Bhave, Tobias J. Kippenberg
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37771v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tracking the resonance frequency of a mechanical oscillator is the basis of atomic force microscopy, mass sensing and thermometry. Nanomechanical thermal detectors exploit this principle to sense absorbed radiation, most effectively with tensile-stressed resonators, whose tension converts thermal expansion into a large frequency shift and dilutes dissipation. Approaching their fundamental sensitivity limit, however, has required free-space or fibre-coupled interferometers, hindering compact deployment and scaling to arrays. Here we remove this bottleneck by monolithically integrating a high-Q nanomechanical resonator with a silicon nitride photonic integrated circuit. A tensile-stressed silicon nitride trampoline with an impedance-matched platinum absorber is dispersively coupled to a photonic integrated microresonator beneath it. At room temperature and with microwatt-level optical power, the detector reaches a noise-equivalent power of 3.4 pW/[MATH] for broadband thermal radiation (3-12 [MATH]m), referred to incident power. Referred to absorbed power, this is within a factor of 1.5 of its fundamental thermal fluctuation limit. Using our detector in a state-of-the-art commercial Fourier-transform infrared spectrometer, we resolve the vibrational fingerprint of a polymer film across 2-20 [MATH]m and reach the precision of the built-in pyroelectric detector with about an order of magnitude lower incident power. This architecture opens a route to multiplexed optomechanical focal-plane arrays.
tldr: The authors monolithically integrate a high-Q tensile-stressed silicon nitride nanomechanical trampoline resonator with a silicon nitride photonic integrated circuit microresonator to realize a compact, scalable optomechanical mid-infrared thermal detector.
motivation: Nanomechanical thermal detectors based on resonance-frequency tracking approach their fundamental sensitivity limit only with free-space or fibre-coupled interferometers, which prevents compact deployment and scaling to focal-plane arrays; an integrated photonic readout is needed.
method: A tensile-stressed Si3N4 trampoline with an impedance-matched platinum absorber is dispersively coupled to a photonic-integrated microresonator beneath it, and the mechanical resonance frequency is tracked optically at room temperature with microwatt-level power.
result: The detector achieves a noise-equivalent power of 3.4 pW/√Hz for broadband 3–12 µm radiation (within a factor of 1.5 of the thermal fluctuation limit referred to absorbed power), and resolves a polymer's vibrational fingerprint from 2–20 µm in a commercial FTIR spectrometer at roughly an order of magnitude lower incident power than the built-in pyroelectric detector.
conclusion: The integrated optomechanical architecture removes the free-space/fibre bottleneck and opens a route toward multiplexed optomechanical focal-plane arrays for mid-infrared sensing.

title: Homogenization Theory Of Topological Anderson Insulators: Genuine Gaps And Pseudo-gaps
authors: Guillaume Bal
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38150v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A topological Anderson insulator is an insulator whose non-trivial topological phase is induced by disorder. We develop a homogenization theory of this phenomenon for constant-coefficient elliptic systems perturbed by fluctuations oscillating at scale [MATH]. Periodic fluctuations of every order below that of the operator, with appropriate amplitudes, do not average out: they produce an order-one correction [MATH] given by a second-order (Born) formula, and the operator converges in the norm-resolvent sense to its homogenized limit. In particular, electric potentials and magnetic fields of zero mean, usually regarded as topologically trivial perturbations, generate corrections [MATH] that change the topological phase. Fluctuations confined to a half-plane create an interface that carries the bulk-difference invariant of the homogenized operator for all [MATH] sufficiently small, a property that is stable under local defects. For random fluctuations, rare regions typically fill the homogenized gap, which becomes a pseudo-gap, and the standard interface index need no longer be defined. We define an index along cuts deformed so as to avoid the rare regions, and prove that it equals almost surely the bulk-difference invariant of the operator homogenized in the Born approximation, for first-order alloys with vanishing low moments and for a class of second-order systems with scalar disorder at criticality that includes the BHZ model.
tldr: The paper develops a homogenization theory for topological Anderson insulators, showing how disorder-induced fluctuations can modify topological phases and defining an index in the presence of pseudo-gaps.
motivation: Topological Anderson insulators are materials whose nontrivial topological phase is induced by disorder, but a rigorous homogenization framework for such systems is lacking.
method: The author analyzes constant-coefficient elliptic systems perturbed by multiscale fluctuations using Born approximation, norm-resolvent convergence, and interface invariants.
result: Periodic fluctuations produce order-one corrections that can change the topological phase, half-plane fluctuations create topological interfaces, and random fluctuations turn genuine gaps into pseudo-gaps requiring deformed-cut indices.
conclusion: The work provides a mathematical homogenization theory for disorder-induced topological phases, including almost-sure index results for first-order alloys and critical second-order systems such as the BHZ model.

title: A Poisson Transition And Bias Law For Ksg Mutual-Information Estimation
authors: Tsachy Weissman Abhiram Gorle
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37941v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We quantify the error of the strict-radius Kraskov--St\"ogbauer--Grassberger (KSG-1) mutual-information estimator on a Gaussian channel as the sample size \(n\) grows and the channel becomes nearly deterministic. For fixed dimension \(p\) and neighbor index \(k\), we define the resolution parameter \(u_n=ne^{-I_n}\), where \(I_n\) is the true mutual information in nats. When \(u_n\to u\in(0,\infty)\), we prove that the estimation error converges in mean square to a computable deterministic bias \(B_{p,k}(u)\). Sampling fluctuations therefore vanish, while an additive bias can persist. We derive this bias from an explicit marked-Poisson law for the neighborhood counts, characterize its small-\(u\) asymptotics, and show that it tends to zero as \(u\to\infty\). The same law describes how often neighborhoods saturate, meaning that they make the largest possible contribution to the estimate. The limiting saturation probability decreases continuously and strictly from one to zero, allowing a Gaussian-model bias correction on fixed critical intervals. Finite-sample experiments show substantial bias even when the true information lies below the estimator's logarithmic ceiling and saturated neighborhoods are rare. Saturation-based correction reduces estimation error in these experiments, though recovering the resolution parameter from the observed saturation fraction can remain difficult when saturation is rare.
tldr: The paper analyzes the finite-sample bias of the KSG-1 mutual-information estimator on a Gaussian channel in the nearly deterministic regime via a marked-Poisson law for neighborhood counts.
motivation: KSG estimators are widely used to estimate mutual information, but their behavior when the channel becomes nearly deterministic and sample size scales with information is not fully understood.
method: For fixed dimension and neighbor index, the authors study the resolution parameter u_n = n e^{-I_n} and prove mean-square convergence of the estimation error to a deterministic bias derived from an explicit marked-Poisson law.
result: They characterize the limiting bias B_{p,k}(u), its small-u asymptotics, and its vanishing as u→∞, and propose a saturation-based Gaussian-model bias correction that reduces error in experiments.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical characterization and practical correction for persistent KSG mutual-information estimation bias in the near-deterministic Gaussian setting, though recovering the resolution parameter can be difficult when saturation is rare.

title: MacKay-Neal Codes For Dna Channels Under Block-MAP Decoding
authors: Kenta Kasai
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38440v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove achievability below the symmetric information rate (SIR) under block maximum a posteriori (MAP) decoding for a fixed-degree MacKay-Neal (MN) socket ensemble on the quaternary insertion-deletion-substitution channel used to model DNA reads. For every integer [MATH], the [MATH] socket ensemble, with one transmitted bit fixed and an independent uniform known offset, has limiting rate [MATH] bits per stored nucleotide. If the joint SIR [MATH] of a fixed number [MATH] of reads under independent, uniformly distributed input nucleotides exceeds [MATH], the ensemble-average full extended-word block error is [MATH], and deterministic graph-offset sequences attain the same limiting rate and message-average error bound. This result concerns the discrete rate family [MATH], not arbitrary rates approaching a given SIR. The channel permits arbitrarily many insertions and unbounded drift, with no alignment supplied to the receiver. The proof combines established MN parity and distance estimates with a strict arbitrary-candidate-list bound and a list construction that accounts for hidden output boundaries.
tldr: The paper proves achievability below the symmetric information rate for fixed-degree MacKay-Neal socket ensembles on a quaternary DNA insertion-deletion-substitution channel under block-MAP decoding.
motivation: DNA data storage requires reliable coding schemes for channels with insertions, deletions, and substitutions, where synchronization is challenging.
method: The analysis combines existing MacKay-Neal parity-check and distance estimates with a strict arbitrary-candidate-list bound and a list construction handling hidden output boundaries.
result: For the fixed-degree socket ensemble, ensemble-average block error probability vanishes below the joint symmetric information rate for a fixed number of reads, and deterministic graph-offset sequences attain the same limiting rate and error bound.
conclusion: The work establishes achievable rates for a discrete family of MacKay-Neal codes on DNA channels without receiver-side alignment, but does not address arbitrary rates approaching a given SIR.

title: A $\pi / 4$ Lower Bound For Random Access In Symmetric Linear Ensembles Under Optimal Decoding
authors: Daniella Bar-Lev, Ohad Elishco, Ryan Gabrys
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38446v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the expected number of random linear observations required to recover a prescribed information symbol. For ensembles with uniformly random supports, independently sampled nonzero coefficients, and uniformly bounded column weights, we prove that the asymptotic normalized expected recovery time is at least [MATH] under optimal decoding. The result holds over finite or infinite fields and extends the lower bound previously established for binary fully symmetric codes under peeling decoding. For singleton - pair observations, we determine the exact limiting expectation and show that optimal and peeling decoding have the same limit, independently of the field and coefficient distribution. The minimum within this family is approximately [MATH], which explicit constructions attain asymptotically over every fixed finite field.
tldr: The paper proves a π/4 asymptotic lower bound on the expected number of random linear observations needed to recover an information symbol in symmetric linear ensembles under optimal decoding, extending earlier peeling-decoding bounds and giving exact limits for singleton-pair observations.
motivation: Random access / locally recoverable coding schemes in which a symbol is recovered from a small number of random linear measurements are of interest for storage and distributed systems; prior lower bounds existed only for binary fully symmetric codes under the restricted peeling decoder.
method: Probabilistic analysis of random linear ensembles with uniformly random supports, independent nonzero coefficients, and uniformly bounded column weights, using information-theoretic/optimal decoding arguments over finite or infinite fields; exact limiting expectations computed for singleton-pair observation structures.
result: The asymptotic normalized expected recovery time is at least π/4 under optimal decoding; for singleton-pair observations the exact limiting expectation matches the peeling-decoding limit, with minimum ≈ π/4 attained asymptotically by explicit constructions over any fixed finite field.
conclusion: Optimal decoding provides no asymptotic advantage over peeling for this family, and π/4 is a sharp threshold for symmetric linear random-access ensembles.

title: Rydberg Atomic Quantum Receiver Empowered Hybrid Non-orthogonal Multiple Access
authors: Xinya Shen, Zheng Chu, David Chieng, Chiew Foong Kwong, Qihao Peng, Pei Xiao, Theodoros Tsiftsis, Jianyue Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38451v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel uplink Hybrid Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (NOMA) architecture assisted by Rydberg Atomic Quantum Receivers (RAQRs) to improve energy efficiency by addressing the physical constraints of atomic sensing. We formulate a joint optimization problem encompassing phase measurements and multi-user power allocation to minimize the total transmit power. This problem is particularly challenging due to the non-linear amplitude-only observations of atomic vapor cells. To decomposes the resulting non-convexity, we develop a hierarchical three-layer decomposition optimization framework that systematically decouples the global problem. The inner layer employs a customized Expectation Maximization-Gerchberg-Saxton (EM-GS) algorithm to resolve phase ambiguity and estimate equivalent channel gains. The middle layer derives closed-form optimal power allocation solutions via Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions. The outer layer utilizes linear Minimum Mean Square Error (MMSE) detection for high-reliability signal recovery. Simulation results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed framework over conventional RF-based Hybrid NOMA. Notably, the atomic architecture achieves approximately a 93% reduction in total power consumption compared to Orthogonal Multiple Access (OMA) baselines while maintaining strict backward compatibility, thereby laying a solid foundation for practical deployment in next-generation green communication networks.
tldr: The paper proposes an uplink hybrid NOMA architecture assisted by Rydberg atomic quantum receivers, jointly optimizing phase measurements and multi-user power allocation to minimize total transmit power.
motivation: Rydberg atomic receivers offer high sensitivity for next-generation green communications, but their amplitude-only nonlinear observations impose physical constraints that complicate multi-user power allocation and channel estimation.
method: A three-layer decomposition framework is developed: an inner EM-Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm resolves phase ambiguity and estimates equivalent channel gains, a middle layer derives closed-form KKT-based power allocation, and an outer layer applies linear MMSE detection.
result: Simulations show the atomic architecture achieves roughly 93% reduction in total power consumption versus OMA baselines while outperforming conventional RF-based hybrid NOMA and retaining backward compatibility.
conclusion: Rydberg atomic receivers can enable energy-efficient hybrid NOMA for green communication networks, though the contribution is a communication-theoretic optimization rather than a quantum information or thermodynamic result.

title: Recurrent Bipartite Graph Neural Networks For Qc-mdpc Error Decoding In McEliece Cryptosystems
authors: Elisabeth Fink Parth Rajeshkumar Tandel
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38479v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As the advent of large-scale quantum computing threatens classical encryption, Quasi-Cyclic Moderate Density Parity-Check (QC-MDPC) codes have emerged as a foundational element of Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). However, decoding these relatively dense codes using classical Belief Propagation algorithms often leads to failures caused by short graph cycles that stall the decoder. In cryptographic applications, these failures are severe security vulnerabilities that leak secret key information. To address this, this paper proposes a Recurrent Bipartite Graph Neural Network (R-BGNN) as proof of concept. By integrating Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) into the message-passing framework and employing a multi-topology curriculum training strategy, the R-BGNN actively learns to break limit-cycle oscillations. Evaluated across 20 unseen matrix topologies, the proposed architecture significantly outperforms classical Bit-Flipping and Min-Sum baselines, reducing the Decoding Failure Rate (DFR) by 63.7\% at moderate noise levels ([MATH]) while converging in fewer iterations.
tldr: The paper proposes a recurrent bipartite graph neural network decoder for QC-MDPC codes used in McEliece post-quantum cryptosystems, reducing decoding failure rates versus classical baselines.
motivation: QC-MDPC codes are important for post-quantum cryptography, but classical belief-propagation decoding suffers from short-cycle-induced failures that can leak key information.
method: The authors integrate gated recurrent units into a message-passing graph neural network and train with a multi-topology curriculum to break limit-cycle oscillations during decoding.
result: Across 20 unseen matrix topologies, the R-BGNN reduces the decoding failure rate by 63.7% at moderate noise levels compared with bit-flipping and min-sum baselines, while converging in fewer iterations.
conclusion: The work demonstrates a proof-of-concept learned decoder for QC-MDPC codes, but it is an applied post-quantum cryptography and coding-theory contribution rather than a quantum information theory advance.

title: Exact Second-Order Asymptotics For The Gaussian Gray--Wyner Problem
authors: Lei Yu Lin Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38306v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We revisit the Gray-Wyner problem of lossy compression of bivariate Gaussian sources under the quadratic distortion measure and derive the exact second-order asymptotics. Specifically, we first identify the boundary rate tuples using the explicit first-order asymptotics by Yu (TIT 2023) and then characterize the tradeoff among three second-order coding rates subject to a constraint on the joint excess-distortion probability. Our main contribution is the achievability proof, where we derive a covariance shell covering lemma that is analogous to the type covering lemma for the discrete case. In particular, our covering lemma classifies the source sequences into power shell types via their empirical covariance matrix. For each such power shell type, we derive sufficient conditions on the compression rates so that covering within distortion levels are achievable. Finally, asymptotical analysis via the Berry-Esseen theorem yields the desired result.
tldr: The paper derives exact second-order asymptotics for the Gaussian Gray-Wyner lossy compression problem, characterizing the tradeoff among three second-order coding rates under a joint excess-distortion constraint.
motivation: First-order asymptotics for the Gaussian Gray-Wyner problem were recently established, but the finite-blocklength second-order behavior, which governs practical code design, remained open.
method: The authors build on explicit first-order rate regions and prove achievability via a new covariance shell covering lemma that classifies source sequences into power shell types by empirical covariance matrix, then apply Berry-Esseen-type asymptotic analysis.
result: Sufficient conditions on the compression rates for covering within distortion levels are obtained for each power shell type, yielding an exact second-order rate tradeoff among the three Gray-Wyner rates.
conclusion: The work completes the second-order asymptotic theory for Gaussian Gray-Wyner compression and provides a continuous-alphabet analogue of the type covering lemma.

title: An Improved Johnson Bound For List-Decoding With Hints
authors: Harry Sha Swastik Kopparty
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38022v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies when list-decodability guarantees for error-correcting codes of good distance can go beyond the classical Johnson radius and gives a corresponding efficient list-decoding algorithm for Reed-Solomon codes up to this new radius. The Johnson bound shows that any error-correcting code with distance [MATH] is automatically list-decodable with small list size up to a certain radius [MATH] around any received word [MATH]. We show that if the received word [MATH] is known to have some codewords that are somewhat close to it (we call these ``hints"), then [MATH] is list-decodable with small list size up to an even larger radius around [MATH]. We determine the optimal list-decoding radius in this setting for single and multiple hints over both large and small alphabets and show that this radius is the optimum of a natural convex program. Remarkably, even a single hint that is [MATH]-close to [MATH] improves the list-decoding radius around [MATH] to [MATH]. Finally, we give an efficient algorithm, based on the weighted Guruswami-Sudan decoder, that list-decodes Reed-Solomon codes up to this optimal radius.
tldr: The paper derives an optimal list-decoding radius for codes of good distance when hints (codewords partially close to the received word) are available, and gives an efficient weighted Guruswami–Sudan algorithm for Reed–Solomon codes achieving it.
motivation: The classical Johnson bound limits list-decodability of codes with good distance to a fixed radius; the authors ask whether side information in the form of one or more nearby codewords can push this radius beyond the Johnson bound.
method: They characterize the optimal list-decoding radius with single and multiple hints over large and small alphabets, showing it equals the optimum of a natural convex program, and construct an efficient decoder based on a weighted version of the Guruswami–Sudan algorithm.
result: Even a single hint that is sufficiently close to the received word strictly improves the achievable list-decoding radius, and the new radius is provably optimal in the hinted setting; Reed–Solomon codes are list-decodable up to this radius in polynomial time.
conclusion: Hints provably beat the Johnson bound, yielding an optimal radius characterized by a convex program together with a practical decoding algorithm for Reed–Solomon codes.

title: On The $b$-Symbol Weight Distribution Of Dual Melas Codes And A Poisson Randomness Postulate
authors: Moshe Schwartz Gabriel Sac Himelfarb
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38017v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove a new lower bound on the [MATH]-symbol weight of codewords in dual Melas codes, which is strictly better than known results. We employ a new strategy that translates a pattern counting problem in linear-feedback shift register sequences to a problem on orbits of binary polynomials under a certain action. We use the same techniques to provide an improved lower bound on the burst-covering radius of Melas codes and a new upper bound on the critical exponent of dual Melas codes. We then define a new randomness postulate on (families of) binary sequences, based on the definition of infinite Poisson generic sequences. We conjecture that codewords in the dual Melas code satisfy this postulate, and we show partial progress in establishing this conjecture. We also show how a relaxed version of the problem can be completely resolved, and relate the conjecture to the first part of the paper, giving a justification of why the improved bounds on the [MATH]-symbol weight were somewhat to be expected.
tldr: The paper derives improved bounds on b-symbol weight distributions, burst-covering radii, and critical exponents of dual Melas codes, and proposes a Poisson-type randomness postulate for binary sequences generated by such codes.
motivation: Melas codes are classical algebraic codes whose generalized weight and covering properties are incompletely understood; the authors aim to sharpen known bounds and to connect codeword randomness to pseudorandomness notions from Poisson genericity.
method: They reduce a pattern-counting problem for linear-feedback shift register sequences to the study of orbits of binary polynomials under a group action, then formalize a randomness postulate for families of binary sequences inspired by infinite Poisson generic sequences.
result: New lower bounds on b-symbol weight and burst-covering radius, an improved upper bound on the critical exponent of dual Melas codes, and partial progress toward the conjectured Poisson randomness property, with a relaxed version fully resolved.
conclusion: The work strengthens the quantitative theory of Melas codes and offers a link between algebraic coding bounds and pseudorandomness heuristics, but remains entirely classical with no quantum information-theoretic content.

title: Drift-induced Nonreciprocity In Image-polariton-mediated Dipole Emission
authors: Christian Nicolaisen Hansen, Eduardo J. C. Dias, Christos Tserkezis, Joel D. Cox
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38348v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electrical current bias offers a magnet-free route to nonreciprocal light propagation at the nanoscale. Here, we theoretically explore drift-induced nonreciprocity in graphene heterostructures containing hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), where graphene plasmons interact with hBN phonon polaritons in the infrared. Both the random-phase approximation and the Boltzmann transport equation are used to characterize the nonlocal optical response of drift-biased graphene. We compare graphene on hBN with an image-polaritonic structure comprising graphene, a thin hBN spacer, and a gold substrate. Carrier drift produces pronounced directional shifts of the polariton dispersion, while coupling to hBN phonon polaritons strongly modifies the nonreciprocal response. In the image-polaritonic structure, the graphene polaritons become up to twice as confined while retaining a comparable Fizeau shift. The nonreciprocal polariton dispersion produces directional near-field emission and nonreciprocal dipole-dipole interactions, the latter quantified through the cross density of optical states, reaching a left-right dissymmetry of up to ~40%. Our results identify image polaritons in drift-biased graphene as a compact, electrically tunable platform for directional coupling between quantum emitters at the nanoscale.
tldr: A theoretical study of drift-biased graphene/hBN image-polariton heterostructures showing that carrier drift produces nonreciprocal polariton dispersion and directional dipole emission with up to ~40% left-right dissymmetry.
motivation: Electrical current bias offers a magnet-free route to nanoscale nonreciprocal light propagation, and the authors aim to understand how coupling to hBN phonon polaritons and image-polariton geometries modifies this drift-induced nonreciprocity.
method: Random-phase approximation and Boltzmann transport equation are used to model the nonlocal optical response of drift-biased graphene, comparing graphene-on-hBN with an image-polaritonic graphene/thin-hBN/gold stack; nonreciprocity is quantified via polariton dispersion shifts and the cross density of optical states.
result: Carrier drift gives pronounced directional shifts of the polariton dispersion, hBN phonon-polariton coupling strongly alters the nonreciprocal response, and image polaritons become up to twice as confined while retaining a comparable Fizeau shift, yielding directional near-field emission and nonreciprocal dipole-dipole interactions with ~40% dissymmetry.
conclusion: Image polaritons in drift-biased graphene are identified as a compact, electrically tunable platform for directional coupling between quantum emitters at the nanoscale.

title: An Eigenmode Expansion Framework For Bi-Directional Multimode Nonlinear Mixing Processes
authors: Salvador Poveda-Hospital, Vincent Girouard, Yves-Alain Peter
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37846v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An approach to simulating complex photonic systems is the eigenmode expansion method, in which scattering matrices are used to model and track the electric field in layered media. In this work, we formulate parametric nonlinear processes within the eigenmode expansion framework, enabling the simulation of nonlinear generation in varying photonic systems. This new simulation method includes both classical nonlinear processes and their quantum counterparts, including spontaneous parametric down-conversion and spontaneous four-wave mixing.
tldr: The authors extend the eigenmode expansion method to model bi-directional multimode nonlinear mixing processes, including their quantum counterparts such as SPDC and spontaneous four-wave mixing.
motivation: Simulating complex layered photonic devices with nonlinear and quantum-optical generation requires a unified scattering-matrix framework that can handle both classical and quantum nonlinear processes.
method: Parametric nonlinear interactions are formulated within the eigenmode expansion / scattering-matrix formalism, tracking the field in layered media and including multimode, bi-directional propagation for processes like SPDC and SFWM.
result: The framework enables simulation of nonlinear generation in a variety of structured photonic systems, covering both classical mixing and quantum spontaneous processes within a single numerical approach.
conclusion: The eigenmode expansion framework offers a practical design and simulation tool for nonlinear and quantum photonic devices, though it is primarily a numerical/device-modeling contribution.

title: Algebraic Quantum Field Theory
authors: Kasia Rejzner
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37904v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Algebraic quantum field theory describes a quantum system through its observables, their localisation in spacetime, and the states that assign them expectation values. The separation of the specification of observables from the choice of a state makes it possible to compare vacuum, thermal and charged representations without assuming that they share a preferred Hilbert space. We develop the framework from familiar quantum mechanics, construct the free scalar field, and explain how causality and positive energy constrain local measurements. The Reeh--Schlieder theorem, the structure of local von Neumann algebras and the split property reveal key differences between quantum theory in the continuum (i.e. QFT) and ordinary quantum mechanics with finitely many degrees of freedom. Superselection theory relates observable charges to statistics and internal symmetries. Finally, local covariance and perturbative and homological methods extend the discussion to curved spacetime, interactions and gauge theories. We also discuss measurement theory and quantum information aspects of AQFT.
tldr: A pedagogical overview of algebraic quantum field theory, covering observables, states, local algebras, superselection, and extensions to curved spacetime and interactions.
motivation: AQFT separates the specification of observables from the choice of state, allowing vacuum, thermal, and charged representations to be compared without a preferred Hilbert space.
method: The paper develops the framework from ordinary quantum mechanics, constructs the free scalar field, and uses causality, positive energy, local von Neumann algebras, the split property, superselection theory, local covariance, and perturbative/homological methods.
result: It explains key structural differences between continuum QFT and finite-dimensional quantum mechanics, including the Reeh--Schlieder theorem and local von Neumann algebra structure, and extends the discussion to curved spacetime, interactions, gauge theories, measurement theory, and quantum information aspects.
conclusion: The work is a broad introduction/review of AQFT rather than a focused contribution to the researcher's listed quantum-information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid-systems directions; its quantum-information content is peripheral.

title: Strict Frequency Bandwidths From Causal Light Cones Enable Scalable Exact Gradient Evaluation In Quantum Optimization
authors: Zhaoyang Song, Wei Zhang, Ji Cao, Xuexi Yi, Hong-Fu Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38322v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamical locality is often regarded as a limitation of shallow quantum circuits, yet we show that it can reduce the number of circuit settings required for exact evaluation of gradients with respect to shared parameters. For layered ansatze generated by commuting local terms, strict Heisenberg light cones confine energy slices obtained by varying one shared layer parameter to finite Fourier bandwidths dictated by local causal geometry. This bandlimit recasts exact gradient evaluation as a local signal recovery problem and, when the relevant frequencies lie on a known frequency lattice, yields an exact multipoint parameter-shift rule based on the discrete sine transform. The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) provides a canonical realization in which this mechanism is governed by the local structure of the graph. Specifically, when a cost angle is varied, the relevant geometry is encoded by the contact region in the interaction line graph. At fixed circuit depth on graphs of bounded degree, the number of distinct circuit settings required for the corresponding derivative collapses from [MATH] to [MATH]. This shows that dynamical locality is not merely a constraint on correlation propagation, but also a computational resource that enables exact gradient evaluation with fewer circuit settings in quantum optimization.
tldr: The paper shows that causal light cones in shallow layered quantum circuits impose strict Fourier bandwidth limits, enabling exact gradient evaluation with fewer circuit settings for QAOA-style optimization.
motivation: Exact gradient evaluation in variational quantum algorithms can be costly because many circuit settings are required; the authors ask whether dynamical locality can be exploited as a computational resource rather than only as a limitation.
method: For layered ansatze generated by commuting local terms, they analyze energy slices as functions of a shared layer parameter, use Heisenberg light cones to bound Fourier support, and derive an exact multipoint parameter-shift rule via a discrete sine transform when frequencies lie on a known lattice.
result: In QAOA on bounded-degree graphs at fixed depth, the number of distinct circuit settings needed for a derivative is reduced from a scaling linear in the number of terms to one determined by local graph contact geometry.
conclusion: Dynamical locality can enable scalable exact gradient evaluation in quantum optimization, suggesting light-cone structure as a practical resource for variational algorithm design.

title: Quantum Change Point Metrology
authors: Xue Ma Xu Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38345v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We quantify the extra Bayes risk of locating a quantum change point and estimating its amplitude with one measurement. The joint and marginal optimizations use the full record and the same joint prior, with both parameters unknown. For product records on a known pure state curve, position has clipped absolute loss in resolution units, and amplitude offset has squared loss in fixed calibrated units. Ideal steps exhibit certified conflict at finite signal strength, including in phase records of sixteen qubits, and recover both informative marginal optima at strong signal. For finite offset prior width, a retained quantum boundary region serves position, and the remaining suffix serves amplitude. Physical recovery holds when strength grows more slowly than the square root of record length. Known smooth rises also admit leading recovery in the coherent experiment as strength grows and width shrinks. For the quintic profile, we establish two residual cost scaling laws. The residual cost is [MATH] as [MATH]. Taking the strong signal limit at fixed [MATH] yields a limiting cost of [MATH] as [MATH].
