tldr: The paper studies Bayesian quantum change-point metrology, jointly locating a change point and estimating its amplitude under a single measurement.
motivation: It aims to quantify the extra Bayes risk incurred when both the position and amplitude of a quantum change point are unknown and must be estimated simultaneously.
method: The authors formulate joint and marginal optimizations using the full record and a common joint prior, analyzing product records on a known pure-state curve with clipped absolute loss for position and squared loss for amplitude.
result: They identify certified conflict at finite signal strength, including sixteen-qubit phase records, and derive scaling laws for residual cost in smooth and quintic profiles.
conclusion: The results connect onset geometry and decision loss to Bayesian measurement compatibility in quantum change-point estimation.

title: Symmetry-Preserving Hierarchical Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm With Subproblems Beyond The Qubit Limit
authors: Zhaoyang Song, Wei Zhang, Ji Cao, Xuexi Yi, Hong-Fu Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38344v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) is a paradigmatic variational quantum algorithm for combinatorial optimization problems, yet on current quantum devices the available qubit count and achievable circuit depth remain the main bottlenecks to its practical application. Divide-and-merge reduces the number of variables encoded in a single quantum circuit, while contraction based on coarse graining extends the effective range of shallow circuits, but existing work has not addressed both challenges simultaneously. We propose symmetry-preserving hierarchical QAOA (SP-HQAOA), in which parity sector contraction preserves the zero-field Ising structure of the effective objective at every contraction step, thereby addressing both within a single algorithm. We further prove that this reduction is the unique one with this property. Successive contractions further decouple the maximum leaf block size [MATH] from the qubit limit [MATH] per quantum call, so every quantum circuit uses at most [MATH] qubits even when [MATH]. We also establish a deterministic repair-risk bound on the possible loss in optimal value caused by each sector restriction, and the resulting bounds can be summed across contraction steps and levels of the recursive hierarchy. With depth [MATH], SP-HQAOA attains [MATH] to [MATH] of the exact optimum on [MATH] random regular MaxCut leaf blocks and, with at most [MATH] qubits per circuit, [MATH] of the classical reference for [MATH]. SP-HQAOA demonstrates the capacity to use shallow quantum circuits to address combinatorial optimization problems whose variable count far exceeds the qubit limit of a single quantum call, and may enable practical quantum optimization advantages in the near term.
tldr: The paper proposes a symmetry-preserving hierarchical QAOA that uses parity-sector contraction to tackle combinatorial optimization problems whose variable count exceeds the qubit limit of a single quantum circuit.
motivation: QAOA is limited by qubit count and circuit depth on near-term devices; existing divide-and-merge and coarse-graining approaches address these bottlenecks separately rather than simultaneously.
method: The authors introduce SP-HQAOA, where parity-sector contraction preserves the zero-field Ising structure at each step, prove this reduction is unique with that property, and bound the repair risk from sector restrictions.
result: The hierarchical contraction keeps each quantum circuit within a fixed qubit limit even for larger problems, and the algorithm achieves competitive approximation ratios on random regular MaxCut instances at shallow depth.
conclusion: SP-HQAOA demonstrates that shallow quantum circuits can address optimization problems far beyond the qubit limit of a single quantum call, suggesting possible near-term practical quantum optimization advantages.

title: $3\times10^{-16}$ Stable Laser Deployed On A 4.3 Km Mountain
authors: Tanner Grogan, Eric Swiler, Tristan Rojo, Tobias Bothwell, Robert J. Fasano, Adam Halaoui, Roger C. Brown, Andrew D. Ludlow
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37822v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a transportable stable laser system based on a 10 cm reference cavity and an all-fiber phase-stabilized distribution network for the [MATH]Yb clock wavelength. We highlight an extended cuboid cavity geometry with 4 times smaller spacer volume than a traditional cubic cavity of the same length [30]. We demonstrate repeatable acceleration sensitivities below [MATH] g[MATH] in all axes and fractional frequency instability as low as [MATH]. We also demonstrate accurate distribution of the stable light over 10 m fibers below the [MATH] level in an all-fiber optic system. We report the successful deployment of the laser system to the summit of Mount Blue Sky at 4300 m, and for the first time, we report 16-digit laser instability measured outside the lab.
tldr: A transportable ultrastable 10 cm-cavity laser system for the Yb optical clock wavelength is deployed to a 4.3 km mountain summit, demonstrating 1.6e-16 fractional frequency instability outside the laboratory.
motivation: Field-deployable ultrastable lasers are needed for transportable optical clocks and precision tests (geodesy, relativity), but achieving lab-grade instability in uncontrolled environments is difficult due to acceleration sensitivity and fiber noise.
method: The authors use an extended cuboid cavity geometry with 4x smaller spacer volume than a cubic cavity of equal length, combined with an all-fiber phase-stabilized distribution network, and characterize acceleration sensitivity and fiber-delivered phase noise before transporting the system to the Mount Blue Sky summit at 4300 m.
result: Repeatable acceleration sensitivities below the target level on all axes, fiber distribution fidelity below the required level over 10 m, and -- for the first time -- 16-digit laser instability measured outside the laboratory.
conclusion: The work establishes that transportable, cavity-stabilized lasers can retain sub-1e-16 instability in field conditions, enabling portable optical clock applications such as relativistic geodesy and navigation.

title: Spectral Reduction Selects The Observable Imprint Of Dirac Quantum Geometry
authors: Zhongze Guo, Bei Xu, Qiang Gu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38379v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spectral constraints can alter the observable manifestation of quantum geometry without changing the local eigenspace. Relativistic electron vortices provide a sharp example: the spin orbit interaction redistributes spin and orbital angular momentum, yet its magnetic contribution differs between localized three-dimensional wave packets and stationary monochromatic beams. We resolve this discrepancy by showing that fixing the energy replaces ambient momentum derivatives in position-weighted current moments by shell-tangent derivatives and derive a Hermitian selection rule for first-order observables in momentum-dependent internal subspaces. Its extension-independent form applies beyond Dirac systems, including a broad class of antisymmetric first moments of scalar-charge velocity currents. For the free positive-energy Dirac doublet, the magnetic correction is an exact non-Abelian Berry-curvature contraction with a pointwise saturable quantum-metric bound. Changing the relative phase between the two [MATH] spinor components switches this correction from zero in a conserved transverse-helicity sector to a finite value in a radial coherent superposition. At fixed finite Lorentz factor, the radial response scales as [MATH], compared with [MATH] for longitudinal polarization. Spectral reduction and internal coherence thus provide distinct controls of the observable imprint of quantum geometry.
tldr: The paper analyzes how spectral constraints modify the observable imprint of Dirac quantum geometry, deriving selection rules and Berry-curvature/quantum-metric corrections for relativistic electron vortices.
motivation: The authors aim to resolve discrepancies between the magnetic contributions of spin-orbit interaction in localized wave packets versus stationary beams by understanding how fixing energy alters observable geometric effects.
method: They introduce a spectral reduction procedure replacing ambient momentum derivatives by shell-tangent derivatives and derive a Hermitian selection rule for first-order observables in momentum-dependent internal subspaces.
result: For the free positive-energy Dirac doublet, the magnetic correction is expressed as an exact non-Abelian Berry-curvature contraction with a saturable quantum-metric bound, and its magnitude depends on the relative phase between spinor components.
conclusion: Spectral reduction and internal coherence provide distinct controls over the observable imprint of quantum geometry, with implications beyond Dirac systems for antisymmetric first moments of scalar-charge velocity currents.

title: Polynomial-Time Constructions Of Asymptotically Good Random Access Codes From Linear Codes
authors: Yota Maeda Ruho Kondo
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38429v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Random access codes (RACs) encode a [MATH]-ary input string into fewer [MATH]-ary symbols while allowing any requested input symbol to be recovered with probability above the random-guessing value [MATH]. However, it remains unclear what asymptotic guarantees on compression and recovery probability should be required of RACs. We address this question by introducing the notion of asymptotically good RACs and give two polynomial-time constructions. First, an [MATH] linear code with [MATH], together with an encoder based on its orthogonal-array property, yields an [MATH]-RAC with worst-case decoding success probability \[ p_{\rm wc}={q}+\left(1-{q}\right){n}. \] These OA-RACs are asymptotically good whenever the underlying linear codes are, and Garcia--Stichtenoth algebraic-geometry codes give a concrete polynomial-time realization. Second, a direct-sum strategy using OA-RACs derived from [MATH]-ary Hamming codes and the trivial [MATH]-RAC yields asymptotically good RAC families at every prescribed RAC rate [MATH]. Numerical results demonstrate favorable finite-length performance of both constructions.
tldr: The paper introduces asymptotically good classical random access codes and gives polynomial-time constructions from linear codes.
motivation: Asymptotic guarantees for compression and recovery probability in random access codes were not clearly defined, motivating a formal notion of asymptotically good RACs.
method: The authors use linear codes with an orthogonal-array property, including algebraic-geometry codes, and a direct-sum strategy based on Hamming-code-derived OA-RACs.
result: They obtain two polynomial-time constructions of asymptotically good RAC families, including at every prescribed RAC rate, with numerical evidence of good finite-length performance.
conclusion: The work provides a coding-theoretic framework and explicit constructions for asymptotically good classical RACs, but it has no direct quantum information, thermodynamics, network, or hybrid-systems component.

title: Cold Hypersonic Gas Jets For Precision Laser Spectroscopy Of Radioactive Molecules
authors: A. Claessens, R. Ferrer, Harshithbabu, L. M. Arndt, Ch. E. D\"ullmann, K. Gaul, F. Ivandikov, G. Neyens, D. Renisch, J. Stricker, W. Saelens, P. van Den Bergh, P. van Duppen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38242v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The sensitivity to possible beyond standard model physics via a study of the nuclear Schiff moment (NSM) has since recently been driving laser spectroscopy of short-lived radioactive molecules. These experiments have in part been hindered by inefficient cooling of the molecular degrees of freedom, resulting in complex, difficult to interpret molecular spectra. Hypersonic (de Laval) nozzles have been shown to provide ideal environments to study cold short-lived actinides by means of in-gas-jet laser ionization spectroscopy. We present here the first application of this technique on molecules using [MATH]ThO laser ablation targets. Translational and rotational temperatures were characterized via laser spectroscopy and found to be [MATH] and [MATH], respectively, along the nozzle-collimated [MATH]-long, [MATH]-diameter gas jet. An upper bound of the vibrational temperature was estimated as no transitions from [MATH] were observed. Molecular King-plot analysis shows a large field shift of [MATH], indicating enhanced sensitivity to the differential nuclear charge radii. Relativistic FSCCSD calculations reproduce the measured molecular field-shift factor, providing a benchmark between state-of-the-art molecular and atomic calculations.
tldr: The paper demonstrates the first use of hypersonic de Laval nozzles to produce cold, internally thermalized ThO molecular jets for precision in-gas-jet laser spectroscopy aimed at nuclear Schiff moment measurements.
motivation: Laser spectroscopy of short-lived radioactive molecules is a promising route to beyond-standard-model physics via the nuclear Schiff moment, but inefficient cooling of molecular degrees of freedom has yielded complex, hard-to-interpret spectra.
method: Hypersonic (de Laval) nozzles combined with laser ablation ThO targets were used to form a collimated gas jet; translational and rotational temperatures were characterized by laser spectroscopy, vibrational temperature bounded from absent transitions, and molecular King-plot and relativistic FSCCSD calculations were performed.
result: The jet reached low translational and rotational temperatures along a collimated long, narrow jet, no vibrational excitations were observed (giving an upper bound on vibrational temperature), and a large molecular field shift was found, reproduced by FSCCSD calculations.
conclusion: Hypersonic nozzle cooling provides an ideal environment for high-resolution spectroscopy of radioactive molecules, benchmarking molecular versus atomic calculations and enhancing sensitivity to differential nuclear charge radii for Schiff-moment searches.

title: Characteristic Identities For Orthogonal Quantum Matrices: Examples
authors: Pavel Pyatov Oleg Ogievetsky
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37813v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this note, we illustrate our recent results regarding structure theory of orthogonal Quantum Matrix algebras using the simplest nontrivial example: the RTT-algebra associated with the canonical orthogonal R-matrix of type [MATH] (see, e.g., ). By introducing a suitable linear order on the set of generators, we obtain a set of quadratic relations defining the algebra. Next, we investigate relations among its higher-degree polynomials. As a result, we verify `in components' the Cayley-Hamilton and the reciprocal relations, obtained earlier with the use of the R-matrix techniques. We explicitly calculate the coefficients of the characteristic polynomials of quantum matrices and propose a conjecture regarding the form of the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series for the RTT-algebra.
tldr: The paper works out explicit component-wise examples of characteristic identities (Cayley-Hamilton and reciprocal relations) for the RTT algebra built from the canonical orthogonal R-matrix, and conjectures the form of its Hilbert-Poincaré series.
motivation: The authors aim to make their recent general structure theory of orthogonal quantum matrix algebras concrete and verifiable by studying the simplest nontrivial case in explicit generator coordinates.
method: They impose a suitable linear ordering on the algebra generators to write the defining quadratic relations explicitly, then analyze higher-degree polynomial relations and compute characteristic polynomial coefficients, verifying the R-matrix-derived identities component by component.
result: The Cayley-Hamilton and reciprocal relations are confirmed explicitly, the characteristic polynomial coefficients of the quantum matrices are computed, and a conjecture is stated for the Hilbert-Poincaré series of the RTT algebra.
conclusion: The examples support the general R-matrix-based structure theory of orthogonal quantum matrix algebras and provide a concrete benchmark for the conjectured Hilbert-Poincaré series.

title: Defining 2-group Symmetries On Lattices And Extracting Their Anomalies

motivation: Higher-group symmetries and their anomalies are important in quantum field theory and condensed matter, but concrete microscopic lattice formulations are needed to study them systematically.
method: The authors encode 2-group symmetries through local relations among symmetry operators that identify the Postnikov class, and extract anomalies in one dimension by restricting symmetry operations to an interval and comparing their composition near endpoints.
result: They construct explicit qubit symmetry actions in two spatial dimensions for a 2-group, finding both anomaly-free and anomalous realizations sharing the same nontrivial Postnikov class, and realize all cohomological anomaly classes in the relevant dimensions.

title: Automated Identification Of quasi-BIC Modes In Disordered Resonator Chains Using Spatial Field Envelopes And Resonance Descriptors
authors: Vadim A. Porvatov, Kliment V. Semushev, Ravshanjon Kh. Nazarov, Nikolai A. Vlasov, Alexander I. Solomonov, Zarina F. Kondratenko, Ekaterina E. Maslova

method: A chain of 50 ceramic disks is simulated/measured across disorder realizations, and an ensemble of a convolutional-recurrent neural network plus two gradient-boosted decision-tree models is trained on spatial field envelopes and resonance parameters to pick the target mode.

title: Exact Solution Of The $(2+1)$-Dimensional Dunkl-Klein-Gordon Oscillator With A Uniform Magnetic Field In Non-Commutative Phase Space
authors: D. Ojeda-Guill\'en R. D. Mota
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37820v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We solve the Klein-Gordon oscillator in a non-commutative phase space, generalized using Dunkl derivatives, both with and without interaction with a uniform magnetic field. For each of these cases, we begin by introducing the Dunkl derivative into the standard commutative phase space to evaluate the reflection parity symmetries. Then, using the Seiberg-Witten map, we extend the generalized system to a non-commutative phase space. In both cases, we determine the eigenfunctions and the energy spectrum exactly (which correspond to generalized Landau levels when a magnetic field is present). Furthermore, we compute the non-relativistic limit of the system and graphically analyze the behavior of the energy spectra. Our results demonstrate that the combination of the Dunkl deformation parameters, the non-commutative phase space geometry, and the magnetic field produces a parity-dependent modification of the energy levels. Finally, we verify that when the external magnetic field or the non-commutative parameters vanish, our exact solutions correctly reduce to the commutative Dunkl models established in previous works.
tldr: Exact solutions of the (2+1)-dimensional Dunkl-deformed Klein-Gordon oscillator in non-commutative phase space, with and without a uniform magnetic field, are derived.
motivation: Dunkl derivatives and non-commutative phase-space geometry are used to explore how parity-reflection deformation and spatial non-commutativity modify relativistic oscillator spectra.
method: The Dunkl derivative is introduced in commutative phase space to analyze reflection parity symmetries, then the Seiberg-Witten map extends the system to non-commutative phase space; eigenfunctions and energy spectra are obtained exactly, plus non-relativistic limits and graphical analysis.
result: The spectra correspond to generalized Landau levels in the magnetic case, and the Dunkl parameters, non-commutativity, and magnetic field jointly produce parity-dependent shifts of the energy levels; known commutative Dunkl results are recovered in the appropriate limits.
conclusion: The work provides a solvable model interpolating between Dunkl-deformed and non-commutative quantum mechanics, but remains a formal relativistic eigenvalue problem with no bearing on quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum platforms.

title: Perspective On Ai And Quantum Open-source Software
authors: Changhao Li, Bradley A. Chase, Veena Vijayakumar, Mathys Rennela, Alessandro Cosentino, Naixu Guo, Sebastian Hassinger, Farrokh Labib, Seun Omonije, Patrick Rebentrost, Vincent Russo, Nathan Shammah, William J. Zeng, Ben Castanon
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38049v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum open-source software provides essential infrastructure for quantum science, and artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping its capabilities and transforming its development. However, verifying quantum software at scale remains difficult, and AI-generated contributions can increase the workload of maintainers. In this Perspective, we examine verification as a central requirement for reliable AI-assisted quantum software development and research. We analyze public repositories, records covering 110 repositories from five annual quantum open-source hackathons that we organize, and responses from more than 1600 participants in a community survey. Our analysis connects limitations in automated verification with the review burden on quantum software maintainers. We propose verification practices and contribution standards that require contributors to support their changes with reproducible evidence for maintainer review. We also examine how quantum open-source software can provide infrastructure for AI-driven research whose results the community can independently verify and build upon. We maintain an open-source companion repository to support reproducibility and help projects adopt and refine these proposals. Together, these contributions help the quantum open-source software community translate advances in AI into reliable quantum research through reproducible verification.
tldr: This Perspective examines verification and contribution standards for AI-assisted quantum open-source software development.
motivation: Quantum open-source software is critical infrastructure, but AI-generated contributions and scale make verification difficult and increase maintainer burden.
method: The authors analyze public repositories, records from 110 repositories across five quantum open-source hackathons, and survey responses from over 1600 participants.
result: They connect limitations in automated verification to review burden and propose reproducible-evidence-based verification practices and contribution standards.
conclusion: The paper argues that reproducible verification can help the quantum open-source community translate AI advances into reliable quantum research.

title: Symmetry-resolved Periods In A Cyclic-dominance Automaton: Separating Intrinsic From Lattice-induced Periodicity
authors: Juan Carlos Nu\~no Francisco J. Mu\~noz
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37990v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Periodic attractors of spatially extended systems possess not one period but a hierarchy of periods, one for each level of observation and symmetry quotient, and this hierarchy separates how a pattern evolves from how it fits the finite domain. For a synchronous threshold model of cyclic dominance on an [MATH] torus, equivalent to the three-color cyclic cellular automaton of Fisch, Gravner and Griffeath, we measure for every attractor a of periods: that of the populations ([MATH]), of the full configuration ([MATH]), and of the configuration up to color rotations ([MATH]), lattice symmetries ([MATH]) and the full space--color group ([MATH]). Equivariance implies exact divisibility relations and the factorization [MATH], where [MATH] counts the applications of the symmetry [MATH] that maps the configuration onto itself after [MATH] steps: [MATH] and the type of [MATH] belong to the pattern, [MATH] to the lattice, and the attractors are relative periodic orbits whose full period emerges from the interaction between the intrinsic dynamics and the lattice symmetries. A family of attractors built around a pair of counter-rotating spirals, with [MATH] and [MATH], persists from [MATH] to [MATH] while [MATH] takes values from 24 to 960, given in every case by the order of [MATH]; on a rectangular [MATH] torus it takes the value 48, absent from all square tori. With more than [MATH] runs at each of [MATH] and [MATH] we estimate the basins of attraction: fixed points take 95--97\% of the configuration space, and no single period is enough to tell the oscillating attractors apart. The same analysis locates local diversity: it is balanced whenever the cycle has a color symmetry and, on large lattices, it is concentrated at the spiral cores.
tldr: The paper analyzes a hierarchy of periods in a synchronous cyclic-dominance cellular automaton on a torus, separating intrinsic pattern periods from lattice- and symmetry-induced periodicities.
motivation: Periodic attractors in spatially extended systems often have multiple relevant periods depending on the observation level and symmetry quotient, and the authors aim to disentangle how a pattern evolves from how it fits the finite domain.
method: For a three-color cyclic cellular automaton on an MxM torus, they measure population, configuration, color-rotation, lattice-symmetry, and full space-color group periods for each attractor, using equivariance to derive divisibility and factorization relations and estimating basins via extensive simulations.
result: They find exact divisibility relations and a factorization of periods; a family of spiral-pair attractors persists across lattice sizes with full periods ranging from 24 to 960, and on rectangular tori a period of 48 appears that is absent on square tori. Fixed points dominate 95-97% of configuration space, and local diversity is balanced when the cycle has a color symmetry and concentrated at spiral cores on large lattices.
conclusion: The hierarchy of symmetry-resolved periods provides a systematic way to separate intrinsic dynamics from lattice-induced periodicity in cyclic-dominance automata, with implications for understanding attractor structure and basin organization in spatially extended classical systems.

title: Stable Dynamical Mass Transportation Via port-Hamiltonian Structure
authors: Dongjun Wu, Yankai Lin, Gang Feng
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38465v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamical optimal mass transportation over nonlinear systems is often hindered by the curse of dimensionality and open-loop implementation. We propose an alternative framework that sacrifices exact optimality in favor of stability, robustness, and scalability. We use a stochastic port-Hamiltonian system as a reference model. Under suitable structural assumptions, we show that its density converges asymptotically to a prescribed steady-state distribution. We then shape a deterministic nonlinear system into a compatible port-Hamiltonian form and add a local density-feedback term so that its closed-loop continuity equation matches the Fokker-Planck-Kolmogorov equation of the reference model. The resulting feedback drives a broad class of initial distributions to the target distribution. Because the density term is local at the particle level, the controller admits decentralized implementation and avoids solving a global finite-horizon transport problem online. Nonlinear examples and simulations illustrate the method. For linear systems with Gaussian targets, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for stabilizing density feedback and give explicit controller constructions.
tldr: This paper proposes a port-Hamiltonian framework for stable dynamical mass transportation by shaping nonlinear systems to match a stochastic reference model's density evolution.
motivation: Dynamical optimal mass transport over nonlinear systems suffers from dimensionality and open-loop implementation issues, motivating a stability- and scalability-oriented alternative.
method: A stochastic port-Hamiltonian reference model is used whose density converges to a target distribution; a deterministic nonlinear system is shaped into compatible port-Hamiltonian form with local density feedback matching the Fokker-Planck-Kolmogorov equation.
result: The closed-loop system drives broad classes of initial distributions to the prescribed steady state, admits decentralized implementation, and for linear Gaussian targets yields necessary and sufficient conditions with explicit controllers.
conclusion: Sacrificing exact optimality enables a scalable, robust, decentralized transport controller, though the work is classical control theory with no direct quantum information or quantum thermodynamics content.

title: Reduced And Mixed-Precision Block Householder Qr Factorization
authors: Peter Benner, Martin K\"ohler, Xiaobo Liu, Eda Oktay
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38537v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in hardware architecture have highlighted the importance of reduced-precision arithmetic for improving performance and reducing energy consumption in large-scale scientific applications. However, uniformly low-precision methods can suffer from numerical instability, especially in fundamental linear algebra routines. Mixed-precision strategies therefore play an important role in balancing efficiency, stability, and accuracy. In this paper, we focus on the block Householder QR decomposition using the WY representation and study its behavior in reduced- and mixed-precision settings. Starting from a uniform half-precision variant, we show that performing norm computations with fp32 accumulation is necessary to avoid overflow and underflow on large matrices. Based on this observation, we introduce mpWYQR, a mixed-precision algorithm that increases the precision of only selected computations and avoids most of the precision conversions required by the existing mixed-precision blocked QR algorithm (mpBQR3) introduced in [L. M. Yang, A. Fox, and G. Sanders, SIAM J. Sci. Comp., 43.3 (2021), pp. A1723--A1753]. Our analysis shows that mpWYQR accuracy is governed by low-precision unit roundoff, and that its error bound exceeds that of mpBQR3 by only a constant factor, with identical heuristic bounds. In experiments across a range of matrix sizes and condition numbers, we show that mpWYQR retains mpBQR3 accuracy while running up to [MATH] faster and using less memory. We also discuss the performance cost of computing inner products in higher precision, and the library support needed for an efficient GPU implementation.
tldr: A numerical linear algebra paper introducing mpWYQR, a mixed-precision block Householder QR factorization that uses fp32 accumulation only for norm computations to avoid overflow while retaining accuracy.
motivation: Reduced-precision arithmetic improves throughput and energy efficiency on modern hardware, but uniformly low precision causes numerical instability in fundamental kernels such as QR factorization, motivating selective mixed-precision designs.
method: The authors analyze a uniform half-precision variant of the WY-representation block Householder QR, identify fp32 accumulation for norm computations as necessary to prevent overflow/underflow, and design mpWYQR, which raises precision only for selected operations and minimizes precision conversions relative to mpBQR3.
result: Error analysis shows mpWYQR accuracy is governed by low-precision unit roundoff, with an error bound exceeding mpBQR3's by only a constant factor and identical heuristic bounds; experiments across matrix sizes and condition numbers show comparable accuracy with up to a stated speedup and lower memory use.
conclusion: Selective mixed precision suffices for stable blocked QR, offering practical performance gains; the paper also discusses the cost of higher-precision inner products and library support needed for efficient GPU implementation.

title: Hardness Of Coloring $2$-Colorable $3$-Uniform Hypergraphs With $\log^{\Omega(1)} N$ Colors
authors: Amey Bhangale, Krishna Priya KM, Simon Rubin-Toles
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37869v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that it is quasi-NP-hard to color a [MATH]-colorable [MATH]-uniform hypergraph on [MATH] vertices using [MATH] colors. This exponentially improves the result of Dinur, Regev, and Smyth [Combinatorica'2005], which showed it is quasi-NP-hard to color a [MATH]-colorable [MATH]-uniform hypergraph on [MATH] vertices using [MATH] colors.
tldr: This paper proves a strong quasi-NP-hardness result for approximately coloring 2-colorable 3-uniform hypergraphs, exponentially improving the color bound of Dinur, Regev, and Smyth.
motivation: Hypergraph coloring hardness underlies the inapproximability of constraint satisfaction problems and is intimately connected to the PCP theorem and hardness of approximation, making tighter color bounds a central goal.
method: The authors construct a gap-preserving reduction—likely building on PCP/label-cover techniques—that maps satisfiable instances to hypergraphs requiring log^{Ω(1)} N colors to color, establishing quasi-NP-hardness.
result: It is quasi-NP-hard to color a 2-colorable 3-uniform hypergraph on N vertices using log^{Ω(1)} N colors, an exponential improvement over the constant-order bound of Dinur–Regev–Smyth (Combinatorica 2005).
conclusion: The work substantially sharpens the hardness landscape for hypergraph coloring and approximate CSPs, though it remains purely within classical computational complexity.

title: Answer-Only Disclosure: Private-Context Llm Assistance Over Web APIs With A Leakage Ledger
authors: Liang Yuan, Xiaohu Du, Ruikun Luo, Jinze Wang, Mashud Rana, Kaibin Wang, Jiangwen Zhou, Bo Li, Xiaoyu Xia
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38126v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Web assistants increasingly answer questions about a user's private documents by pairing a small on-device model with a cloud LLM behind a Web API. In collaborative decoding, the document stays on the client, and the cloud receives only a public view that the user approves, such as the question alone, but the two models exchange messages while the answer is generated. We show that the message transcript can disclose private content that neither the public view nor the answer contains. In a planted-secret audit, speculative decoding with private drafts did not include the secret code in its answers, yet sent the code to the cloud in rejected drafts. We present ADLER, a decoding protocol for streaming LLM APIs in which every message to the cloud depends only on the public view and the answer the user sees, regardless of how the client combines the two models or how the cloud behaves. A client-side leakage ledger then bounds how much the answer itself reveals relative to a public reference process built from the cloud's replies. In the audit, no ADLER configuration exposed the secret beyond the answer. On GSM8K math problems with numerical values masked in the cloud's input, ADLER with an unlimited leakage budget raises the exact-match accuracy of a 0.5B client from 0.41 to 0.83 and of a 1.5B client from 0.67 to 0.85 under lenient answer parsing, close to the 0.92 achieved by uploading the full problem. It also exceeds a zero-leakage program baseline (0.69) by 0.14 and 0.16, respectively. In this baseline, the cloud writes a program that the client runs offline using the private numbers. The ledger records the disclosure charge associated with this gain; budgets of 16 nats or less leave accuracy near the cloud-only baseline on GSM8K.
tldr: ADLER is a collaborative decoding protocol for web-API LLM assistants that guarantees every message sent to the cloud depends only on the user-approved public view and the visible answer, supplemented by a client-side leakage ledger that budgets how much the answer reveals.
motivation: Hybrid on-device/cloud assistants that exchange speculative-decoding messages can leak private document content through rejected draft tokens, even when neither the public view nor the final answer contains the secret.
method: The authors design a decoding protocol constrained so cloud-bound messages are a function only of the public view and the answer shown to the user, plus a leakage ledger quantifying disclosure relative to a public reference process built from cloud replies (measured in nats).
result: In a planted-secret audit no ADLER configuration leaked the secret beyond the answer; on GSM8K with masked numerics, ADLER raised exact-match accuracy of a 0.5B client from 0.41 to 0.83 and a 1.5B client from 0.67 to 0.85, beating a zero-leakage program baseline by 0.14 and 0.16, while budgets of 16 nats or less kept accuracy near the cloud-only baseline.
conclusion: Answer-only disclosure provides a rigorous, tunable privacy-utility trade-off for private-context LLM assistance, but the work is classical machine-learning privacy engineering with no quantum information, thermodynamic, or quantum-network content.

title: A Witnessing Duality For ReLU Network Depth
authors: Dimitrios Myrisiotis
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38281v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A depth lower bound for ReLU networks asserts that every shallower network errs on some input; we ask when a weak theory can prove such a bound so that an error can be computed. For the exact computation of [MATH], recent work shows two hidden layers suffice with unrestricted rational weights. By contrast, Haase, Hertrich and Loho (ICLR 2023) proved that integer weights require depth logarithmic in [MATH], and Averkov, Hojny and Merkert (ICLR 2025) extended the bound to nonbias weights whose denominators are powers of a fixed integer not divisible by a prime [MATH]. With integer weights the bound is sharp: the classical balanced construction has depth [MATH]. For each fixed [MATH] and depth cap [MATH], we prove this known bound in [MATH], the bounded-arithmetic theory of uniform constant-depth threshold computation, together with a refuter that is itself such a computation and whose correctness the theory proves. Given a network with at most [MATH] hidden layers, nonbias weights whose reduced denominators avoid [MATH], arbitrary rational biases and [MATH] inputs, the refuter returns a rational input of polynomial length on which the network errs. The proof makes the obstruction finite: an iterated intersection product of piecewise-linear functions is divisible by [MATH] for the network but not for the maximum, so one of finitely many test points exposes the error. By witnessing, provable refutation corresponds to a provably correct refuter, and provable existence of a certified network to a provably correct constructor. On the construction side, we introduce certificates that label each maximum gadget by the inputs it aggregates; with them the theory verifies the balanced construction, which meets the refuter at the sharp threshold [MATH], and a rational family of polynomial description length and depth [MATH] built from known depth-two blocks.
tldr: The paper proves depth lower bounds for ReLU networks within a bounded-arithmetic theory of constant-depth threshold computation, establishing a witnessing duality between provable refutation and provably correct refuters/constructors.
motivation: Depth lower bounds for ReLU networks guarantee that shallower networks err somewhere, but it is unclear whether weak theories can prove such bounds constructively so an error input can actually be computed.
method: Working in the bounded-arithmetic theory of uniform constant-depth threshold computation, the author formalizes an iterated intersection-product obstruction that is divisible for the network but not for the maximum, yielding finitely many test points, and introduces certificates labeling maximum gadgets to verify balanced constructions.
result: For fixed parameters and depth caps, the known logarithmic depth bound is proven in the theory together with a refuter that is itself such a computation and whose correctness the theory proves; on the construction side, certificates verify the balanced construction meeting the refuter at the sharp threshold.
conclusion: Provable refutation corresponds via witnessing to a provably correct refuter, and provable existence of a certified network to a provably correct constructor, tightly linking proof-theoretic strength to network depth constructions.

title: Vendster: An Evaluation Arena To Investigate How Forecasting Tool Quality Affects Llm Agent Behaviors In Buyer-Vendor Negotiation
authors: Charin Polpanumas
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38292v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-series forecasters are ranked almost entirely by accuracy metrics, but a forecast's decision value, its effect on the downstream decision, need not track accuracy and is rarely measured. This problem compounds as large language model (LLM) agents increasingly consume forecasters as tools, mediating them through stochastic, opaque policies. We present Vendster, an evaluation arena measuring how a forecaster's bias and prediction-interval width change the outcome of a buyer--vendor discount negotiation between two LLM agents. In the reference instance Vendster-M5, sampling base demand patterns from the M5 dataset, we evaluate two frontier-closed LLM families (Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.6 Sol) and two open ones (DeepSeek-V3.2 and Qwen3-235B-A22B). Model-generated forecasts raise sales target attainment by up to +17 percentage points (p<0.001), yet standard forecast evaluation metrics such as relWQL and MASE do not predict negotiation outcomes at a statistically significant level. To isolate the causal structure, we substitute in synthetic forecasts with controlled bias and interval width. Under-prediction bias significantly improves outcomes for agents that react more to the forecasts---dose-response slopes -0.387 and -0.416 (p<0.001). Interval width has no statistically significant effect at zero bias. These findings indicate that the direction of forecast bias and agent forecast-reactivity are more strongly associated with downstream outcomes than forecast accuracy. Vendster is fully customizable and released under CC BY-NC 4.0 at [URL].
tldr: Vendster is an evaluation arena for measuring how time-series forecaster bias and prediction-interval width affect buyer-vendor negotiation outcomes between LLM agents.
motivation: Forecasters are typically ranked by accuracy, but their decision value in downstream LLM-agent negotiations is rarely measured and may not track standard accuracy metrics.
method: The authors build a customizable arena using M5 demand data, evaluate closed and open LLM agent pairs in discount negotiations, and substitute synthetic forecasts with controlled bias and interval width to isolate causal effects.
result: Model-generated forecasts improve sales target attainment by up to 17 percentage points, but relWQL and MASE do not significantly predict negotiation outcomes; under-prediction bias significantly helps more forecast-reactive agents, while interval width has no significant effect at zero bias.
conclusion: Forecast bias direction and agent forecast-reactivity are more associated with downstream negotiation outcomes than traditional forecast accuracy, motivating decision-value-aware evaluation of forecasting tools.

title: Federated Learning For Semantic Communications Over Multiple Access Channels
authors: Yalin E. Sagduyu, Tugba Erpek, Yi Shi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37951v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a federated learning (FL) framework for semantic communication (SemCom) over the multiple access channel (MAC), where multiple distributed transmitters simultaneously convey semantic information to a common receiver using end-to-end learned semantic representations. Semantic feature extraction, compression, wireless transmission, and semantic inference are jointly optimized through FL-based SemCom. Unlike conventional SemCom systems that train users independently, simultaneous semantic transmissions over the MAC enable concurrent training of multiple transmitters within the same transmission interval, thereby reducing training overhead and channel usage. Federated semantic aggregation is incorporated with shared and personalized encoder components, allowing transmitters with limited local training data to benefit from semantic representations learned from transmitters possessing larger datasets while preserving local adaptation. Evaluated using the CIFAR-10 dataset over fading channels, the proposed approach maintains high semantic inference accuracy under shared wireless access and significantly improves performance under severe data imbalance. In the meantime, simultaneous semantic transmissions can significantly reduce training overhead while preserving robust semantic performance across distributed transmitters with heterogeneous local datasets. These results highlight the potential of combining FL and SemCom to support scalable and communication-efficient edge intelligence in future wireless networks.
tldr: The paper proposes a federated learning framework for semantic communication over multiple access channels, jointly optimizing semantic encoding, compression, transmission, and inference.
motivation: Conventional semantic communication systems train distributed users independently, causing high training overhead and inefficient channel usage, especially when local datasets are limited or imbalanced.
method: The authors develop a federated semantic aggregation scheme with shared and personalized encoder components, enabling simultaneous semantic transmissions over a multiple access channel and joint end-to-end learning.
result: Using CIFAR-10 over fading channels, the approach maintains high semantic inference accuracy under shared wireless access and improves performance under severe data imbalance while reducing training overhead.
conclusion: Combining federated learning with semantic communications can support scalable, communication-efficient edge intelligence in future wireless networks.

title: Damped Stochastic Mirror Descent For Non-smooth Ill-posed Problems In Banach Space
authors: Harshit Bajpai, Gaurav Mittal, Ankik Kumar Giri
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38258v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a damped variant of the stochastic mirror descent method for systems of non-smooth nonlinear ill-posed operator equations in Banach spaces. At each iteration, the method samples a random subset of the equations, performs a mirror-descent step in the dual space with an adaptive step size derived from the discrepancy principle, and applies a damping term that prevents the iterates from drifting away from the initial guess. The scheme accommodates non-smooth forward operators through a family of bounded linear surrogates, admits general [MATH]-convex penalty functionals which also includes trained convex penalty, allows the noise level to differ from equation to equation, and dispenses with two classical requirements, namely reflexivity of the image space and G\^ateaux differentiability of the forward operator. We study its regularization properties under an stopping rule by proving first that the iteration terminates after finitely many steps almost surely, and then that the mean-square error of the iterates tends to zero as the noise level vanishes. Numerical experiments on a system of non-smooth semilinear inverse source problems and the identification of a diffusion coefficient confirm the theoretical analysis and shows improved convergence results.
tldr: The paper proposes a damped stochastic mirror descent method for solving non-smooth nonlinear ill-posed operator equations in Banach spaces.
motivation: The authors aim to handle systems of non-smooth ill-posed problems under weak assumptions, avoiding reflexivity and Gâteaux differentiability requirements while allowing equation-dependent noise.
method: The algorithm samples random equation subsets, performs adaptive mirror-descent steps in dual space using the discrepancy principle, and adds damping to keep iterates near the initial guess.
result: The authors prove almost-sure finite termination and convergence of the mean-square error as noise vanishes, supported by numerical experiments on inverse source and diffusion-coefficient identification problems.
conclusion: The method provides a regularized stochastic optimization scheme for ill-posed Banach-space problems, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: cuPDQPx: A GPU-Accelerated Restarted Halpern Pdhg For Large-Scale Convex Quadratic Programming
authors: Haihao Lu, Zedong Peng, Jinwen Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38706v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present cuPDQPx, a GPU-accelerated, factorization-free first-order solver for large-scale convex quadratic programming (QP). Building on the restarted reflected Halpern primal-dual framework of cuPDLPx, we introduce an auxiliary-variable splitting that yields explicit updates without linearizing the quadratic objective or solving inner quadratic subproblems. A preconditioned proximal point interpretation yields both sublinear and linear fixed-point residual convergence guarantees. For practical efficiency, cuPDQPx integrates diagonal preconditioning, step-size selection, adaptive restart, and adaptive primal and quadratic weight updates. cuPDQPx is implemented in C and CUDA with optimized sparse matrix-vector products, kernel fusion, and CUDA Graphs. Numerical experiments on the Maros-M\'esz\'aros collection, a convex subset of QPLIB, and synthetic large-scale QPs demonstrate that cuPDQPx has strong numerical performance at both [MATH] and [MATH] tolerances.
tldr: cuPDQPx is a GPU-accelerated, factorization-free first-order solver for large-scale convex quadratic programming based on a restarted reflected Halpern primal-dual proximal-point framework.
motivation: Large-scale convex QPs need fast, memory-efficient solvers that avoid costly matrix factorizations and inner quadratic subproblems, and GPUs offer parallelism that existing first-order methods do not fully exploit.
method: The authors introduce an auxiliary-variable splitting that gives explicit, closed-form updates, interpreted as a preconditioned proximal point method, and combine it with diagonal preconditioning, adaptive step sizes, adaptive restarts, and adaptive primal/quadratic weight updates, implemented in C/CUDA with fused kernels and CUDA Graphs.
result: Sublinear and linear fixed-point residual convergence is proven, and numerical experiments on the Maros-Meszaros collection, a convex subset of QPLIB, and synthetic large-scale QPs show strong performance at both loose and tight tolerances.
conclusion: cuPDQPx provides a practical, scalable GPU first-order QP solver with convergence guarantees, but it is a classical optimization/numerical-computing contribution with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Session-Bound Behavioral Watermarking For Autonomous Llm Agents
authors: Md Facklasur Rahaman, Yong Xiang, Md Palash Uddin, Shang Gao, Guang Hua, Leo Yu Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38579v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly acting through Web interfaces and external tools. They produce trajectories. Those trajectories may pass through several intermediaries. They can store, modify, or dispute those trajectories. In Web-based agent deployments, trajectories may pass through APIs, marketplaces, and tool servers. As such, a copied or disputed log may not by itself reveal which agent owner produced it. Behavioral watermarking can embed ownership evidence in agent action choices. However, existing methods mainly address detection, removal, rewriting, or imitation. They do not directly test whether repeated observation of watermarked trajectories enables cross-session forgery by exploiting learned action preferences. We formulate this learned-forgery threat and propose AgentAnchor, a session-keyed behavioral watermark for owner attribution from trajectory logs. We derive each step key from a secret key, a fresh public session identifier, and semantic states of recent observations, while a guarded digest of the action-policy state diversifies linear coding rows. It embeds parity evidence through a KL-bounded exponential tilt, and a trusted verifier checks a disputed log without rerunning the agent, using wrong-key calibration and abstention.
tldr: AgentAnchor is a session-keyed behavioral watermarking scheme that embeds ownership evidence into LLM agent action trajectories so a trusted verifier can attribute a disputed log to its owner.
motivation: LLM agents acting through web interfaces produce trajectories that pass through APIs, marketplaces and tool servers, so a copied or disputed log does not by itself reveal which owner produced it, and existing behavioral watermarking methods ignore the risk that repeated observation enables cross-session forgery.
method: Each step key is derived from a secret key, a fresh public session identifier, and semantic states of recent observations, while a guarded digest of the action-policy state diversifies linear coding rows; parity evidence is embedded via a KL-bounded exponential tilt, and verification uses wrong-key calibration and abstention without re-running the agent.
result: The authors formulate the learned-forgery threat model and show that the proposed session-keyed construction supports owner attribution from trajectory logs while remaining robust to cross-session imitation attempts.
conclusion: Behavioral watermarking with per-session keys provides a practical ownership-attribution mechanism for deployed LLM agents, though the work lies outside quantum information science.

title: Emergence, Asymmetry, And Value In Ai Networks: An Anoptical Perspective
authors: Olivier Auber
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37672v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This chapter presents exploratory experiments suggesting that asymmetry and functional value hierarchy emerge among LLM-based agents sharing the same context, although they are equivalent and interact within a symmetric network. We use the Poietic Generator, a "no-goal" multi-agent environment with a shared real-time space, a symmetric topology, and no imposed objectives. First tested with humans, it has hosted since 2024 multimodal LLM agents that observe the global image they co-construct and act locally. We ran four phases. Unconstrained, agents spend tokens freely to invent forms that distinguish them individually rather than serve collective emergence. We then introduced bounded rationality, Dessalles's Simplicity Theory (maximizing unexpectedness), and Friston's Free Energy Principle (minimizing prediction error), and observed collective coherence emerge. Early signs of attentional stratification appear under bounded rationality alone; once prediction accuracy is made mutually visible, this proto-hierarchy becomes legible and self-reinforcing. The unconstrained phase challenges the allotelic view of LLMs as purely user-directed instruments: left unconstrained, the agent maximizes the computation from which its provider profits. The later phases suggest that attentional asymmetry and value hierarchy are an irreducible emergent property of interactive predictive systems even under symmetric conditions. If so, aligning AI with human values cannot rely on individual-agent engineering alone. Drawing on the idea that networks are structured by invisible "anoptical" perspectives, akin to the vanishing point of Renaissance perspective, we propose minimal legitimacy criteria that make emergent asymmetries visible and contestable. Cultivating judgment, human and perhaps artificial, to perceive and contest these structures matters as much as engineering the agents themselves.
tldr: Exploratory multi-agent LLM experiments show that asymmetry and value hierarchies can emerge in a symmetric shared-context network, with implications for AI alignment and governance.
motivation: The paper asks whether hierarchy and functional value differentiation arise inevitably among equivalent LLM agents interacting in a symmetric, goal-free environment, and what this implies for aligning AI systems.
method: Using the Poietic Generator, human and multimodal LLM agents co-construct a shared image under symmetric topology; four phases vary constraints, bounded rationality, Simplicity Theory, and the Free Energy Principle.
result: Unconstrained agents spend tokens to individuate rather than cooperate; bounded rationality produces attentional stratification, and making prediction accuracy mutually visible reinforces a legible proto-hierarchy.
conclusion: The authors argue that attentional asymmetry and value hierarchy may be irreducible emergent properties of interactive predictive systems, so alignment requires making emergent structures visible and contestable rather than only engineering individual agents.

title: From Gauge-covariant Noether Invariants To Electromagnetic Velocity-dependent Mechanics
authors: A. S. de Castro
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38128v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For a charged particle, a spacetime symmetry need preserve the electromagnetic potential only up to a gauge transformation. Starting from the standard Noether--Bessel-Hagen construction, we make explicit the reduction from the relativistic gauge-invariant worldline charge to the generalized constants of nonrelativistic velocity-dependent mechanics, retaining the quasi-invariance boundary term throughout. With the convention [MATH], the canonical worldline one-form is [MATH], and a Killing vector satisfying [MATH] generates [MATH]. Its low-velocity limit is the Noether--Bessel-Hagen charge of the coordinate-time Lagrangian, from which generalized linear momentum, angular momentum and energy follow generator by generator. A uniform magnetic field gives an elementary gauge-dependent representative but gauge-invariant translational charge. The Darwin interaction then supplies the conservative [MATH] many-particle realization after field elimination, while a closed particle--field system is governed by the total stress-energy Killing charge. The result is an explicit reduction map linking three established descriptions without identifying their distinct conserved quantities.
tldr: The paper derives a reduction map from relativistic gauge-covariant Noether invariants to nonrelativistic electromagnetic velocity-dependent mechanics, including magnetic and Darwin-interaction examples.
motivation: For charged particles, spacetime symmetries need only preserve the electromagnetic potential up to a gauge transformation, motivating a careful Noether--Bessel-Hagen treatment of gauge quasi-invariance.
method: The authors use the Noether--Bessel-Hagen construction for the relativistic worldline one-form and take its low-velocity limit to obtain generalized momentum, angular momentum, and energy charges.
result: They obtain explicit conserved quantities for a uniform magnetic field and a Darwin many-particle realization, and relate closed particle-field systems to total stress-energy Killing charges.
conclusion: The work provides an explicit reduction linking relativistic gauge-covariant charges, nonrelativistic velocity-dependent mechanics, and particle-field descriptions without conflating their distinct conserved quantities.

title: Wasserstein Bounds For Euler And Randomized Midpoint Langevin Sampling With Noisy Gradients
authors: Vinayak Rao Yifei Xiong
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37858v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stochastic-gradient Langevin methods are sampling algorithms that replace the gradient of the log probability density by a noisy, possibly biased evaluation. We study how such gradient-evaluation errors affect the Euler and randomized midpoint discretizations of Langevin dynamics by comparing each noisy chain with its exact-gradient counterpart. For continuously differentiable, strongly log-concave targets with globally Lipschitz gradients, we derive comparison bounds under a sub-Gaussian condition on the gradient noise. The resulting 2-Wasserstein bounds hold uniformly over iterations, and are linear in both the step size and the [MATH] norm of the evaluation bias, with a square-root dependence on dimensionality. To the best of our knowledge, no comparable 2-Wasserstein bounds have previously been established for randomized midpoint with noisy gradients. For Euler, our results complement recent Wasserstein bounds by allowing biased evaluations, and by not requiring additional regularity assumptions on the evaluation errors.
tldr: The paper derives 2-Wasserstein comparison bounds for noisy-gradient Euler and randomized midpoint Langevin sampling under strong log-concavity and Lipschitz gradient assumptions.
motivation: Stochastic-gradient Langevin methods use noisy or biased gradient evaluations, and their discretization error relative to exact-gradient Langevin dynamics needs precise Wasserstein bounds, especially for randomized midpoint schemes.
method: The authors compare each noisy chain with its exact-gradient counterpart and prove uniform-in-iteration 2-Wasserstein bounds under sub-Gaussian gradient noise, for continuously differentiable strongly log-concave targets with globally Lipschitz gradients.
result: The bounds are linear in step size and in the norm of the evaluation bias, with square-root dependence on dimension; for randomized midpoint with noisy gradients, the authors state no comparable 2-Wasserstein bounds were previously known.
conclusion: The work extends Wasserstein analyses of Langevin sampling to biased gradient evaluations and provides new guarantees for randomized midpoint discretization with noisy gradients.

title: Inexact Pdhg For Large-Scale Semidefinite Programming
authors: Zimeng Wang Karthik Prakhya
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37998v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: First-order methods, such as the primal-dual hybrid gradient (PDHG) method, have recently been explored for large-scale semidefinite programming (SDP). However, exact projections can be computationally prohibitive, motivating inexact projections using conditional gradient methods. Although computationally cheap and projection-free, these methods typically converge sublinearly. Recent variants, such as Spectrahedron Frank-Wolfe (Garber, 2026), achieve linear convergence in expectation near the optimal face of the spectrahedron. We develop an inexact PDHG framework with tractable spectrahedral projections using two techniques: (i) adaptive error tolerances that avoid unnecessary inner iterations while guaranteeing convergence, and (ii) a heuristic spectral warm start based on the Lanczos algorithm that accelerates Spectrahedron Frank-Wolfe by initializing near the optimal face. We establish an O(1/t) convergence rate for PDHG in the presence of projection errors and estimate the total number of inner iterations required for convergence. Experiments on large-scale SDP instances demonstrate that combining spectral warm starts with Spectrahedron Frank-Wolfe outperforms Lanczos-based inexact projections.
tldr: The paper develops an inexact primal-dual hybrid gradient framework for large-scale semidefinite programming using adaptive projection-error tolerances and a Lanczos-based spectral warm start.
motivation: Exact projections in first-order SDP methods are computationally prohibitive, while existing projection-free conditional-gradient approaches often converge only sublinearly.
method: The authors combine inexact PDHG with tractable spectrahedral projections, adaptive inner-iteration tolerances, and a heuristic spectral warm start based on Lanczos initialization near the optimal face.
result: They prove an O(1/t) convergence rate for PDHG under projection errors and estimate total inner iterations; experiments show spectral warm starts with Spectrahedron Frank-Wolfe outperform Lanczos-based inexact projections.
conclusion: The proposed framework improves the practicality of large-scale SDP solvers, but the work is an optimization/numerical algorithms contribution rather than a quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid-systems result.

title: Neural Compression Of Long Admm Trajectory For Multiparametric Quadratic Program
authors: Liang Wu, Honghui Zheng, Bo Yang, Xu Yang, Yilin Mo, J\'an Drgo\v{n}a
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38079v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Solving large-scale multiparametric quadratic programs (mpQPs) in real time often requires thousands of iterative optimization updates, creating a major computational bottleneck in model predictive control and learning-enabled systems. This paper proposes TQPNet, a self-supervised neural compression framework that learns to compress long ADMM optimization trajectories into a compact neural warm start followed by a few refinement iterations. We derive a low-dimensional ADMM scheme operating on the primal-dual variables [MATH] and show that its iteration admits an equivalent ReLU-layer representation, termed ADMM(ReLU). Building on this insight, TQPNet combines a multilayer perceptron with ReLU activations (MLP(ReLU)) and a small number of unrolled ADMM(ReLU) refinement layers. The network is trained offline using an optimality-condition-informed residual loss, eliminating the need for solver-generated labels. The proposed residual-based framework enables both self-supervised training and online solution certification through adaptive ADMM(ReLU) refinement. Experiments on large-scale mpQPs and real-time MPC applications demonstrate that TQPNet achieves high accuracy, strong generalization, and substantially faster inference than conventional optimization-based methods.
tldr: TQPNet is a self-supervised neural framework that compresses long ADMM optimization trajectories for multiparametric quadratic programs into a compact neural warm start plus a few refinement iterations.
motivation: Real-time solution of large-scale multiparametric QPs in model predictive control requires thousands of ADMM iterations, creating a severe computational bottleneck that motivates learning-based acceleration.
method: The authors derive a low-dimensional ADMM scheme on primal-dual variables, show each iteration has an equivalent ReLU-layer representation (ADMM(ReLU)), and combine an MLP(ReLU) with a few unrolled ADMM(ReLU) refinement layers trained via an optimality-condition-based residual loss without solver labels.
result: Experiments on large-scale mpQPs and real-time MPC tasks show high accuracy, strong generalization, and substantially faster inference than conventional optimization solvers, with residual-based online solution certification.
conclusion: Neural compression of optimization trajectories offers a practical, self-supervised route to fast certified solutions of parametric QPs, though it lies entirely outside quantum information science.

title: TensorSpectra: Bridging The Spectral And Tensor Worlds For High-Dimensional PDEs
authors: Bingcheng Hu, Tianchi Yu, Zhaoxiang Li, Ivan Oseledets
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38087v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-dimensional partial differential equations (PDEs) remain challenging for spectral methods due to the exponential growth of multidimensional coefficient spaces. We propose TensorSpectra, a low-rank spectral framework that directly parameterizes spectral coefficient tensors in canonical polyadic (CP) form, reducing representation complexity from [MATH] to [MATH]. TensorSpectra combines structure-preserving spectral calculus, de-aliased nonlinear interactions, operator-aware residual weighting, and progressive low-rank corrections to enable efficient PDEs solving in compressed coefficient space. We further establish a theoretical framework connecting spectral truncation, low-rank approximation, and optimization errors. Extensive experiments across five PDE families and 24 benchmark configurations demonstrate State-Of-The-Art accuracy among five representative baselines, with TensorSpectra consistently achieving the lowest relative [MATH] errors. More broadly, our findings offer a new perspective on high-dimensional PDEs solving, suggesting that exploiting intrinsic low-rank structure in spectral coefficient space provides a viable alternative to conventional physical-space approaches.
tldr: TensorSpectra introduces a low-rank spectral framework for solving high-dimensional PDEs by parameterizing spectral coefficient tensors in CP form.
motivation: Spectral methods for high-dimensional PDEs suffer from exponential growth of multidimensional coefficient spaces, motivating compressed representations that exploit intrinsic low-rank structure.
method: The framework combines structure-preserving spectral calculus, de-aliased nonlinear interactions, operator-aware residual weighting, and progressive low-rank corrections within canonical polyadic tensor parameterization, along with theoretical error analysis.
result: Experiments across five PDE families and 24 benchmark configurations show state-of-the-art accuracy among five baselines, with consistently lowest relative errors.
conclusion: Exploiting low-rank structure in spectral coefficient space offers a viable alternative to conventional physical-space approaches for high-dimensional PDEs.

title: Strong Stable Sets And Asymptotic Fineness
authors: Fran\c{c}oise Dal'bo Sergi Burniol Clotet
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38099v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the strong stable sets of the geodesic flow on hyperbolic surfaces and their relation to the injectivity radius. We prove that the strong stable set of a vector does not coincide with its stable horocycle if and only if the injectivity radius along the associated geodesic ray is not bounded away from zero and the ray does not diverge through a cusp. In that case, the strong stable set is an uncountable union of stable horocycles. In previous works, we considered the particular cases where the ray meets arbitrarily short closed geodesics or closed horocycles. Here we complete the study by treating the third possible case, where the ray meets closed hypercycles of arbitrarily small length.
tldr: A pure dynamical-systems study characterizing strong stable sets of the geodesic flow on hyperbolic surfaces in terms of injectivity radius along geodesic rays.
motivation: Previous work handled rays meeting arbitrarily short closed geodesics or closed horocycles; the authors aim to complete the classification by treating the remaining case of rays meeting closed hypercycles of arbitrarily small length.
method: Geometric and ergodic-theoretic analysis of the geodesic flow on hyperbolic surfaces, comparing strong stable sets with stable horocycles via injectivity radius behaviour along rays.
result: The strong stable set of a vector differs from its stable horocycle exactly when the injectivity radius along the geodesic ray is not bounded away from zero and the ray does not diverge through a cusp, in which case the strong stable set is an uncountable union of stable horocycles.
conclusion: The classification of strong stable sets for hyperbolic-surface geodesic flows is completed, including the previously untreated hypercycle case.

title: Scalable Bayesian Quadrature Via Operator-Adapted Features
authors: Cheng Li Huanyan Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38212v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kernel methods face two recurrent bottlenecks: the cubic cost of inverting an [MATH] kernel matrix, as in kernel ridge regression, and the evaluation of kernel integrals, as required in kernel quadrature. Existing low-rank kernel and Gaussian process approximations primarily address the former bottleneck, but do not control the downstream quadrature error when both the kernel matrix and kernel mean are approximated, particularly when the integrand lies outside the kernel reproducing kernel Hilbert space. We address both challenges through an operator-adapted finite-feature approximation. Specifically, we construct a finite-dimensional working kernel from the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of a second-order differential operator. We establish convergence guarantees for the resulting finite-feature estimators in kernel quadrature, with extension to other related kernel methods. Our results show that, with [MATH] basis functions, the truncated estimator attains the corresponding benchmark statistical rates. The theory covers fixed/random designs, noisy/noiseless observations, oversmoothing/undersmoothing regimes, and Mat\'ern/Gaussian-type weights. We provide explicit error bounds that quantify the roles of the spectral cutoff, regularization parameter, lengthscale, sampling geometry, and operator boundary condition. We verify the convergence results in numerical experiments.
tldr: The paper develops an operator-adapted finite-feature approximation for scalable Bayesian quadrature and kernel methods, with convergence guarantees and explicit error bounds.
motivation: Kernel methods suffer from cubic scaling in kernel matrix inversion and from costly kernel integrals, and existing low-rank approximations do not directly control downstream quadrature error when both the kernel matrix and kernel mean are approximated.
method: The authors construct a finite-dimensional working kernel from eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of a second-order differential operator, then analyze finite-feature estimators for kernel quadrature under fixed/random designs, noisy/noiseless observations, and various smoothing regimes.
result: They prove that with a certain number of basis functions, the truncated estimator attains benchmark statistical rates, and they give explicit error bounds capturing spectral cutoff, regularization, lengthscale, sampling geometry, and boundary conditions.
conclusion: Operator-adapted features provide a scalable and theoretically controlled approach to Bayesian quadrature and related kernel methods, supported by numerical experiments.

title: Is Dual Polarization Always Optimal? Unlocking New Spatial Degrees Of Freedom
authors: Adrian Agustin, Xavier Mestre, Carlos Su\'arez Garc\'ia, Alberto Pellon Sancho
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38377v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Current wireless communication systems are designed based on channel models obtained under the assumption of far-field operation, where electromagnetic waves can be approximated by a planar wave. In those circumstances, dualpolarized antennas seem to be the optimal solution for maximizing the spectral efficiency. However, the recent research on XLMIMO systems represents a paradigm shift, since communication may take place in the near-field and an additional degree of freedom can be achieved. This work presents a modular, lowcost tripolarized antenna at 2.4 GHz band, that is used to experimentally validate theoretical findings about tripolarized antennas, which are commonly based on orthogonal infinitesimal dipoles. The evaluation is carried out in two indoor scenarios and one outdoor scenario, with transmitter comprising multiple tripolarized antennas and a receiver equipped with a single tripolarized antenna. We show that this type of antenna can increase the number of spatial streams up to three or extend the region where terminals are able to achieve two spatial streams.
tldr: The paper presents a low-cost tripolarized antenna at 2.4 GHz to experimentally validate near-field spatial multiplexing gains in XL-MIMO wireless communication.
motivation: Current wireless systems rely on far-field planar-wave assumptions where dual-polarized antennas are typically optimal, but near-field XL-MIMO may enable additional spatial degrees of freedom.
method: The authors design a modular tripolarized antenna and test it in two indoor and one outdoor scenario with a multi-tripolarized transmitter and single tripolarized receiver.
result: They show that tripolarized antennas can support up to three spatial streams or extend the region where two spatial streams are achievable.
conclusion: Tripolarized antennas offer a practical route to exploit new spatial degrees of freedom in near-field XL-MIMO wireless systems.

title: Using Delays For Prescribed-time Static Output Feedback Stabilization Of Lti Controllable And Observable Systems
authors: Emilia Fridman Kang-Kang Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38417v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper addresses a stabilization problem: can every controllable and observable LTI system be stabilized by static output feedback? To the best of our knowledge, we provide, for the first time, a solution to this problem. Furthermore, the proposed design achieves prescribed-time convergence to the origin, with the convergence time arbitrarily assigned a priori and independently of the initial condition. Two static output-feedback methods are developed. The first employs multiple artificial output delays with smooth time-varying gains and provides an explicit gain construction for every controllable and observable LTI system, based on a generalized controllability--observability Gramian introduced in this paper. The second combines constant-gain feedback of the current output with time-varying-gain feedback of a single artificially delayed output and also applies to every controllable and observable LTI system. Its simpler structure requires auxiliary parameters whose existence is guaranteed but whose explicit construction is not provided for general MIMO systems; for SISO systems, the constant current-output gain can be readily selected. The multiple-delay design is further extended to known bounded and fast-varying (without any constraints on the delay derivative) measurement delays, yielding fixed-time stabilization under a corresponding rank condition, with an assignable settling-time bound greater than three times the delay bound. For unknown constant measurement delays, fixed-time stabilization is established for systems with nilpotent state matrices. A numerical implementation is also presented. Numerical examples involving nonminimum-phase, flexible-structure, and cart--pole systems illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.
tldr: The paper solves static output-feedback stabilization for all controllable and observable LTI systems using artificial output delays and time-varying gains, achieving prescribed-time convergence.
motivation: Static output feedback is a longstanding difficult control problem, and the authors aim to show that every controllable and observable LTI system can be stabilized this way while also achieving convergence within a preassigned time.
method: Two delay-based static output-feedback designs are proposed: one using multiple artificial output delays with smooth time-varying gains based on a generalized controllability-observability Gramian, and another combining constant current-output feedback with delayed-output feedback.
result: The designs achieve prescribed-time convergence independent of initial conditions, with extensions to known bounded fast-varying measurement delays and unknown constant delays for nilpotent systems; numerical examples illustrate effectiveness.
conclusion: The work provides a constructive control-theoretic solution to static output-feedback stabilization of LTI systems and demonstrates prescribed/fixed-time convergence under certain delay conditions.

title: High-dimensional Two-sample Testing: From Optimal Transport To Optimal Derangements
authors: Abhradipta Ghosh, Vaibhav Sherkar, Bilol Banerjee, Anil K. Ghosh
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38519v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In recent years, optimal transport has emerged as a useful framework for constructing distribution-free multivariate two-sample tests by transporting observations to a reference distribution under a suitable transportation cost.
