However, existing optimal transport-based tests can perform poorly in high dimension, low sample size (HDLSS) settings, and their performance depends critically on the choice of the reference distribution and transportation cost. We investigate this phenomenon and show that suitable choices can substantially improve their performance. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce a class of two-sample tests based on optimal derangements that do not require an external reference distribution. The minimum distance pairing test of Rosenbaum arises as a special case when the optimization is restricted to a subclass of derangements, thereby revealing a connection between this method and optimal transport. We propose the optimal derangement (ODER) test and its distribution-free variant, the ODER-SHC test, obtained by restricting the minimization to derangements consisting of a single Hamiltonian cycle. We establish their consistency under both HDLSS and classical large-sample asymptotic regimes. We also develop corresponding procedures based on the [MATH] distance and establish their high-dimensional consistency under conditions involving coordinate-wise energy distances. These [MATH] distance based tests can also discriminate between two high-dimensional distributions with identical first two moments but different marginal distributions. Analyses of benchmark datasets and extensive simulation studies demonstrate the performance of the proposed methods across a variety of alternatives and data settings.
tldr: The paper develops high-dimensional two-sample tests using optimal transport and optimal derangements, with distribution-free variants and asymptotic consistency results.
motivation: Existing optimal-transport-based two-sample tests often perform poorly in high-dimensional, low-sample-size settings and depend strongly on the reference distribution and transportation cost.
method: The authors analyze reference-distribution and cost choices, then introduce optimal derangement (ODER) tests and ODER-SHC variants based on minimizing pairing distances without an external reference distribution, including L2-distance procedures.
result: They establish consistency in HDLSS and classical large-sample regimes, show high-dimensional consistency under coordinate-wise energy-distance conditions, and demonstrate strong performance on benchmark datasets and simulations.
conclusion: Optimal derangement testing provides a flexible, distribution-free framework for high-dimensional two-sample testing and reveals connections to Rosenbaum's minimum-distance pairing and optimal transport.

title: Optimality Conditions And Solution Set Characterisations Of Convex Minimal Time Optimisation Problems
authors: Nguyen Duy Cuong Doan Huu Hieu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38553v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The paper studies convex minimisation problems involving a composition of a coordinatewise nondecreasing convex function with a finite family of nonnegative, locally Lipschitz continuous and convex functions. We establish complete dual optimality conditions and characterise the entire solution set using multipliers and subgradients associated with a given solution. The results are applied to norm optimisation problems involving minimal time functions with different convex dynamics sets and convex target sets. The sum, maximum and p-norms yield minimal time versions of the Fermat--Torricelli, Chebyshev centre and p-Fermat--Torricelli problems, respectively. Examples in finite and infinite dimensional spaces are provided to illustrate the solution set characterisations.
tldr: A convex analysis paper deriving complete dual optimality conditions and full solution-set characterizations for composite convex minimization problems, applied to minimal-time norm optimization.
motivation: The authors aim to go beyond single optimal solutions and characterize the entire solution set of structured convex programs built from nondecreasing convex compositions of locally Lipschitz convex functions.
method: They use multipliers and subgradients at a known solution to establish dual optimality conditions, then apply the framework to minimal time functions with various convex dynamics and target sets (sum, max, p-norms).
result: Complete optimality conditions and solution-set characterizations are obtained, yielding minimal-time variants of the Fermat-Torricelli, Chebyshev centre, and p-Fermat-Torricelli problems, illustrated with finite- and infinite-dimensional examples.
conclusion: The framework provides a unified route to describing full solution sets of convex minimal-time problems, but is purely mathematical optimization with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or quantum hardware.

title: Revision-Bound Evidence Cuts: Authenticated Queries And Contextual Witness Capacity
authors: Taylan Alpay Faruk Alpay
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37982v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Authentic records can support unauthorized narratives when their qualifications, query scope, or counterevidence are silently dropped. We present revision-bound evidence cuts, a framework for authenticating both supporting and opposing inference obligations across changing source versions. Signed complete-update frontiers permit transport of unaffected certificates, alternative-cut recovery, and an exact certified-reuse radius given by a frontier-hypergraph transversal number. Their source obligations induce an integral model of context-bound authorization. To secure database-derived claims, we introduce an authenticated relational query contract that binds original source records, complete selected bags, counting units, parameters, and aggregates independently of execution strategy. A full-source verifier checks 16,824 Chogha Mish records across SQLite scans, indexes, and materialized views; three valid strategies agree and eight contract/view mutations are rejected. A separate 340-row NISP cohort shows that changing the admitted weighting rule can reverse a comparison while preserving every source record. A frozen English text-to-frame compiler produces qualified evidence receipts, with linguistic accuracy evaluated separately from cryptographic integrity. We also separate logical-source from transport commitments so lossless re-encoding need not invalidate unchanged scientific evidence. The SCENE prototype evaluates signed revisions, authenticated queries, scoped disclosures, and adversarial mutations at scales reaching one million source records. These guarantees rely on declared policies and independently pinned trust roots; they authenticate specified computations and obligations, not historical truth, complete counterevidence, or institutional endorsement.
tldr: The paper introduces 'revision-bound evidence cuts', a cryptographic and database-provenance framework for authenticating both supporting and opposing inference obligations across changing source versions.
motivation: Authentic records can be misused to support unauthorized narratives when qualifications, query scope, or counterevidence are silently dropped, so there is a need to bind claims to the exact source revision and query that produced them.
method: The authors define signed complete-update frontiers enabling certificate transport and a certified-reuse radius given by a frontier-hypergraph transversal number, plus an authenticated relational query contract binding source records, selected bags, counting units, parameters, and aggregates; a verifier is validated on Chogha Mish SQLite data and a 340-row NISP cohort with a text-to-frame compiler producing qualified evidence receipts.
result: Three valid query strategies agree on 16,824 records while eight contract/view mutations are rejected; changing the admitted weighting rule reverses a comparison without altering source records, and the SCENE prototype scales to one million records separating logical-source from transport commitments.
conclusion: The framework authenticates specified computations and inference obligations rather than historical truth or institutional endorsement, relying on declared policies and pinned trust roots.

title: Zero Trust-Enabled Adaptive Incident Response Using Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
authors: Jisoo Lee, Bhagath Singh Bondili, Harshith Doppalapudi, Gwynith Godin, Nathaniel D. Bastian, Ankit Shah
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38146v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern enterprises increasingly operate through complex information systems (IS) enabled by cloud computing, remote and hybrid work practices, and digitally integrated supply chains. These structural shifts have expanded organizational attack surfaces and weakened traditional perimeter-based trust assumptions, giving rise to new and persistent forms of cyber threats. In response, adversaries have shifted toward identity-centric, trust-based intrusion techniques that exploit legitimate access within organizational systems. This evolution has created a pronounced speed asymmetry, whereby attackers can adapt and act at machine speed while defenders remain constrained by reactive or rule-based incident response (IR) processes. Drawing on design science research, we propose ZT-AIR, an adaptive IR artifact that uses zero trust architecture as its design theory and hierarchical reinforcement learning as its kernel theory. ZT-AIR learns context-aware trust decisions, separates strategic prioritization from tactical execution, encodes zero-trust controls as actions, and jointly optimizes security effectiveness and operational continuity. Experimental results across diverse adversarial strategies, network scales, and defense environments show that ZT-AIR achieves a strong balance between security and continuity through frequent, minimally disruptive interventions. Practitioner validation further confirms the design's practical viability. This study contributes to IS research by extending computational design science from threat identification to response execution, theorizing zero trust architecture for adaptive IR, and deriving reusable design principles for adaptive decision support artifacts.
tldr: The paper proposes ZT-AIR, an adaptive incident-response artifact combining zero trust architecture with hierarchical reinforcement learning to make context-aware trust decisions in enterprise networks.
motivation: Expanding attack surfaces, identity-centric intrusions, and the speed asymmetry between machine-speed attackers and reactive rule-based defenders motivate a more adaptive response paradigm.
method: Using design science research, the authors build a hierarchical RL agent that separates strategic prioritization from tactical execution and encodes zero-trust controls as actions, jointly optimizing security effectiveness and operational continuity.
result: Experiments across adversarial strategies, network scales, and defense environments show ZT-AIR balances security and continuity via frequent, minimally disruptive interventions, with practitioner validation supporting practical viability.
conclusion: The work extends computational design science from threat identification to response execution and derives reusable design principles for adaptive decision-support artifacts.

title: A Minimally Informed Black-Box Fake-Report Attack On Drl Traffic-Signal Control
authors: Amro Saleh, Loukas Lazos, Mohammad J. Abdel-Rahman
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38557v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) traffic-signal controllers may use vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) reports, exposing their perception layer to false-data injection. Existing demonstrations typically assume either white-box access to the controller's weights or full observability of the traffic state. We study the impact of a weaker and more realistic adversary who has no access to the RL model and whose traffic observations are limited to her own approach. This black-box, minimally informed attacker trains an imitation surrogate of the controller. She then crafts bounded fake reports, restricted to inflating vehicle counts on her own approach, that transfer to the real controller. We demonstrate that despite the loss of accuracy relative to an attacker who can observe the entire state and action space, this limited attacker can significantly increase the average waiting time for other approaches while barely changing the waiting time on her own approach, i.e. externalizing the added delay onto the other approaches. Because the only realizable move is to inflate one's own reported queue, we find that a zero-knowledge attacker that simply reports the maximum feasible queue is as damaging as the surrogate-based one, while an unstructured random inflation is not: the surrogate is not required to reproduce the degradation, and the exposed vulnerability is the V2I sensing channel itself. The surrogate's role is directional control, selecting a disruptive or a selfish objective at the same budget. The attack persists under +/-20% uniform demand variation. Finally, on a common per-lane budget we place the attacker on a knowledge ladder against white-box adversaries, and find the black-box surrogate matches a realizable white-box attacker that uses the victim's own gradients; only abandoning realizability raises the damage further.
tldr: A black-box, minimally informed attacker can degrade DRL traffic-signal control by inflating self-reported vehicle counts over V2I, externalizing delay onto other approaches.
motivation: DRL traffic controllers may rely on V2I reports, creating a false-data injection risk even for adversaries without model access or full traffic observability.
method: The attacker trains an imitation surrogate of the controller and crafts bounded fake queue reports on her own approach; the study compares this against zero-knowledge, random, and white-box attacks under demand variation.
result: The limited black-box attacker significantly increases average waiting time on other approaches while barely affecting her own; simple maximum feasible queue inflation is as damaging as the surrogate-based attack.
conclusion: The core vulnerability is the V2I sensing/reporting channel rather than the DRL model itself, and the surrogate mainly provides directional control of the attack objective.

title: Extending Higher-Order Critical Pairs
authors: Aart Middeldorp Johannes Niederhauser
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38576v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Confluence is a fundamental property of computation which implies that the nondeterminism of a system does not affect its outcomes. A key concept of confluence research in rewriting theory is the notion of critical pairs which captures the potential local sources of non-confluence. In this paper, we lift the definition of higher-order critical pairs to a more expressive class of higher-order rewrite systems. Thereby, we facilitate confluence analysis of rewrite systems which can express complex one-step computations as well as program transformations from functional programming.
tldr: The paper extends the notion of higher-order critical pairs to a broader class of higher-order rewrite systems to enable confluence analysis.
motivation: Confluence guarantees that nondeterminism in a computational system does not affect outcomes, and critical pairs capture local sources of non-confluence; existing definitions of higher-order critical pairs were limited to a restricted class of rewrite systems.
method: The authors lift the definition of higher-order critical pairs so it applies to a more expressive class of higher-order rewrite systems, then use these pairs to analyse confluence.
result: The generalized definition allows confluence analysis for rewrite systems expressing complex one-step computations and program transformations from functional programming.
conclusion: The extended framework broadens the applicability of critical-pair-based confluence checking in higher-order rewriting theory.

title: Data-driven Stochastic Asymptotic Regularization For Ill-posed Inverse Problems With A Posteriori And Heuristic Stopping
authors: Simran Soni, Harshit Bajpai, Ankik Kumar Giri
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38279v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A novel Data-driven STochastic Asymptotic Regularization () method is proposed for solving linear and nonlinear ill-posed inverse problems, which incorporates a data-driven drift and a stochastic diffusion mechanism. Both known and unknown noise level cases are accommodated by the method, thereby making the framework applicable to a broader range of practical inverse problems. For known noise level, a modified discrepancy principle is employed, whereas for unknown noise level, a heuristic stopping rule based solely on noisy data is developed. For each stopping rule, an appropriate diffusion term is defined and the well-posedness of the associated stochastic differential equation is demonstrated. The finite termination of method under both stopping rules is established and its convergence to the exact solution in the noise-free setting is proved. For the noisy data, stability and the regularization property in the mean-square sense are further established. In addition, the uncertainty quantification of the proposed method and its comparison with the Stochastic Asymptotic Regularization () method under both rules are provided. Furthermore, it is shown that local minima arising in the Data-Driven Iteratively Regularized Landweber () method may be escaped. Finally, detailed numerical experiments, including comparisons with existing and methods, are presented on X-ray computed tomography and nonlinear schlieren tomography for both stopping rules, thereby demonstrating the performance of .
tldr: The paper proposes a data-driven stochastic asymptotic regularization method for linear and nonlinear ill-posed inverse problems with known or unknown noise levels.
motivation: Ill-posed inverse problems require robust regularization, especially when noise levels are unknown, and the authors aim to combine data-driven drift with stochastic diffusion to broaden practical applicability.
method: The method uses a modified discrepancy principle for known noise levels and a heuristic stopping rule for unknown noise levels, with diffusion terms chosen to ensure well-posedness of the associated stochastic differential equations.
result: Finite termination, convergence in the noise-free setting, mean-square stability and regularization under noisy data are proved, and numerical experiments on X-ray computed tomography and nonlinear schlieren tomography demonstrate performance.
conclusion: The proposed framework provides a stochastic regularization approach for inverse problems and can escape local minima arising in data-driven iteratively regularized Landweber methods.

title: Optimal Approximation Error Approach In Bayesian Inverse Problems
authors: Tapio Helin Fabian Schneider
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38434v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In many inverse problems, evaluating the forward operator is computationally expensive, making it common practice to accelerate inference with a less costly approximate model. However, such approximations introduce unwanted bias and must be carefully accounted for to ensure the reliability of the solution. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced in Bayesian inference, where accurate posterior characterisation typically requires a large number of forward model evaluations. In this paper, we focus on the approximation error model (AEM), which compensates for the modelling error by adjusting the likelihood density. More precisely, AEM incorporates the model error into the additive Gaussian noise distribution. A central challenge in this approach is how to choose the modified noise mean and covariance in a principled way. To address this, we propose a new framework, optimal approximation error (OAE) which determines the noise model by minimising the expected information loss, measured via the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the true and approximate posterior distributions. We show that the standard enhanced error approach (EEA) is recovered as the minimiser of the expected divergence between likelihoods rather than posteriors and develop OAE as a direct alternative targeting posterior accuracy. We establish bi-convexity of the OAE objective, introduce a regularised, provably convergent proximal alternating minimisation scheme, and derive closed-form expressions in the Gaussian linear setting. We further show that OAE estimates computed from empirical training data are statistically consistent. Numerical experiments on a linear CT problem and a nonlinear Darcy-flow problem show that OAE improves posterior accuracy relative to both the uncorrected and EEA-corrected likelihoods.
tldr: The paper introduces an optimal approximation error (OAE) framework for Bayesian inverse problems that selects the modified noise mean and covariance in the likelihood by minimising the expected KL divergence between true and approximate posteriors.
motivation: Expensive forward operators are often replaced by cheap approximate models in Bayesian inference, which introduces model bias; the standard enhanced error approach (EEA) corrects the likelihood but does not directly target posterior accuracy.
method: OAE minimises expected information loss (KL divergence between true and approximate posteriors) over the additive Gaussian noise model, yielding a bi-convex objective solved by a regularised, provably convergent proximal alternating minimisation scheme, with closed-form solutions in the Gaussian linear case.
result: EEA is recovered as the minimiser of expected likelihood divergence, empirical OAE estimates are shown to be statistically consistent, and numerical experiments on linear CT and nonlinear Darcy-flow problems show improved posterior accuracy over uncorrected and EEA-corrected likelihoods.
conclusion: Targeting posterior-level divergence rather than likelihood-level divergence gives a principled and computable correction for approximate forward models, improving Bayesian inversion reliability.

title: Conformal Predictive Distributions For Contextual Order Fulfillment Optimization
authors: Tinghan Ye, Amira Hijazi, Pascal van Hentenryck
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38046v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ship-to-home fulfillment requires a retailer to select a fulfillment location and carrier before the delivery time is known. These decisions often rely on static transit-time estimates, which cannot represent how delivery-time uncertainty varies across orders and fulfillment options. This paper constructs conformal predictive distributions (CPDs) using Conformal Predictive Systems (CPS) for regression and the cross Venn-Abers predictor (CVAP) for multiclass classification, and uses them in a contextual optimization model for fulfillment decisions. The model is solved by contextual sample-average approximation (C-SAA). The regret of each fulfillment decision, its expected cost above that of the best decision, is bounded by forecast error, scenario-evaluation error, and the candidate-generation gap. The forecast term depends on how well calibration residuals or class probabilities represent the current order. On more than five million proprietary order records, CVAP raises exact-day accuracy from 49.5% for the rule-based estimate to 64.1%. Paired with a decision rule that selects a quantile weighting late errors more heavily, the split CPS (SCPS) gives a point estimate that raises late-delivery detection from 3.8% to 79.4%. Residual-based CPS distributions also meet or slightly exceed nominal interval-coverage targets. In decision experiments with a JD.com simulator over six test dates, C-SAA with CVAP lowers mean total cost by 7.1% and C-SAA with the Mondrian CPS (MCPS) lowers it by 6.7%, relative to C-SAA with the original nonconformal forecast. Both cut the late-delivery rate from 5.7% to below 4.0%.
tldr: The paper applies conformal predictive distributions and contextual sample-average approximation to optimize ship-to-home fulfillment decisions under delivery-time uncertainty.
motivation: Retail fulfillment decisions typically rely on static transit-time estimates that fail to capture order- and option-specific delivery uncertainty.
method: It constructs conformal predictive distributions using Conformal Predictive Systems, cross Venn-Abers predictors, and Mondrian CPS, then embeds them in a contextual optimization model solved by contextual sample-average approximation.
result: On over five million proprietary orders, CVAP improves exact-day accuracy from 49.5% to 64.1%, and decision experiments with a JD.com simulator show 7.1% lower mean total cost and late-delivery rates below 4.0%.
conclusion: Conformal predictive distributions can improve contextual fulfillment optimization by better representing delivery-time uncertainty and reducing cost and late deliveries.

title: An Energy-based Discontinuous Galerkin Method For The Westervelt Equation With Absorbing Boundary Conditions
authors: Lu Zhang Yiwei Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38058v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper develops and analyzes an energy-based discontinuous Galerkin method for the Westervelt equation in the acoustic-velocity-potential formulation with spatially varying material parameters and nonlinear absorbing boundary conditions. The semi-discrete scheme is constructed from the underlying energy balance and incorporates an additional consistent term to accommodate the strong damping operator within the discrete energy framework. Numerical fluxes are designed at both interelement and physical boundaries to provide a unified treatment of interior and boundary dissipation. For the nonlinear analysis, we study an auxiliary variable-coefficient linearized problem and establish stability and a priori error estimates, including the additional terms induced by the solution-dependent absorbing boundary flux. These estimates are combined with a fixed-point argument to prove existence, uniqueness, and convergence of the nonlinear semi-discrete approximation under suitable regularity, smallness, and nondegeneracy assumptions. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical convergence results and illustrate the performance of the proposed method.
tldr: This paper develops and analyzes an energy-based discontinuous Galerkin scheme for the nonlinear Westervelt acoustic wave equation with spatially varying coefficients and absorbing boundary conditions.
motivation: The Westervelt equation models nonlinear acoustic propagation with absorption, and robust, provably stable numerical schemes are needed for such nonlinear damped wave problems with solution-dependent boundary fluxes.
method: The semi-discrete scheme is derived from an underlying energy balance with an added consistent term for the strong damping operator; numerical fluxes handle interelement and physical boundary dissipation, and stability plus a priori error estimates are proved via an auxiliary variable-coefficient linearized problem and a fixed-point argument.
result: Existence, uniqueness, and convergence of the nonlinear semi-discrete approximation are established under regularity, smallness, and nondegeneracy assumptions, and numerical experiments confirm the predicted convergence rates.
conclusion: The energy-based DG approach provides a unified, provably convergent framework for nonlinear acoustic propagation with absorbing boundaries, though it is a purely classical numerical analysis contribution.

title: In-Context Learning For Multi-Fidelity Multiscale Model Closure And Cross-Operator Out-Of-Distribution Generalization
authors: Xinyuan Li, Matthew Zahr, Panos Stinis, Zecheng Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-fidelity learning uses low-fidelity information (coarse-scale PDE models) together with limited high-fidelity data (fine-scale solutions) to obtain high-accuracy PDE solutions. It is a data-driven approach to downscale reduced-order models to solve PDEs efficiently and accurately. Standard multi-fidelity learning focuses on one operator or PDE; given a new PDE, retraining using additional coarse-fine solution pairs may be required, which is costly. In this work, we propose an in-context multi-fidelity learning framework for learning multiple multi-fidelity operators with one shared model. The model is trained using paired low- and high-fidelity examples as demonstrations from multiple operators, together with a new coarse-scale solution query, to predict the corresponding fine-scale solution. Once trained, given a new PDE operator, a few (fewer than five) coarse-fine demonstration pairs, and a low-cost coarse query, the model predicts the corresponding fine-scale solution without fine-tuning. When the target operator appears in the training dataset but has a different prediction goal, such as predicting beyond the training time interval, no additional demonstrations are needed. Instead, the model uses training coarse-fine pairs from that PDE and information from other training operators. Testing then only requires generating a low-cost coarse-scale solution query, without fine-tuning. Notably, our smallest model contains only 255,364 trainable parameters, corresponding to approximately 456 parameters per training operator for 560 operators.
tldr: The paper proposes an in-context multi-fidelity learning framework that trains a single shared model to map coarse-scale PDE solutions to fine-scale solutions across many operators, enabling few-shot generalization to new PDE operators without fine-tuning.
motivation: Standard multi-fidelity learning is restricted to a single PDE operator, requiring costly retraining with new coarse-fine solution pairs whenever a new operator is encountered.
method: A shared model is trained on paired low- and high-fidelity demonstrations drawn from many operators, and at inference it uses fewer than five coarse-fine demonstration pairs plus a cheap coarse query to predict the fine-scale solution, with no gradient updates.
result: The approach generalizes in-context to unseen PDE operators and to out-of-distribution targets such as extrapolation beyond the training time interval, using a model with only 255,364 trainable parameters (about 456 per operator across 560 operators).
conclusion: In-context learning provides an efficient route to multi-fidelity, multiscale PDE closure with strong cross-operator generalization and very small parameter budgets.

title: Tight Stationarity Transfer And Repeatability For Inexact Proximal-Gradient Methods
authors: Shenghan Mei
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38310v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Proximal-gradient methods are widely used for composite optimization, but inexact proximal updates introduce a residual in the proximal optimality condition, complicating the analysis of how stationarity changes across a step. We study this question for composite objectives consisting of a smooth convex term and a possibly nonsmooth weakly convex term, focusing on the relationship between the directional-stationarity measures at the input and output points of an inexact proximal-gradient step. We first establish separate input and output bounds, but their combination can yield a conservative estimate because their worst-case residual directions may differ. By exploiting the magnitude and orientation of this shared residual, we establish tight joint bounds and derive an exact one-step stationarity-transfer factor that strictly improves the estimate from separate bounds in the short-step regime. We also identify the precise residual-tolerance threshold for finite uniform stationarity transfer. A further distinction emerges over multiple steps: endpoint worst cases can repeat over arbitrarily many iterations, whereas interior worst cases cannot persist across two consecutive steps, yielding strict two-step submultiplicativity. These results also provide principled tolerance-selection rules, descent estimates, and stationarity-complexity guarantees for inexact proximal-gradient methods.
tldr: The paper derives tight one-step stationarity-transfer factors and residual-tolerance thresholds for inexact proximal-gradient methods on composite convex/weakly convex objectives.
motivation: Inexact proximal updates leave a residual in the proximal optimality condition, making it hard to characterize how stationarity degrades across a step, and naive combinations of separate input and output bounds are overly conservative.
method: The authors analyze the shared residual's magnitude and orientation to derive joint stationarity bounds, an exact one-step transfer factor, residual-tolerance thresholds for uniform transfer, and a two-step submultiplicativity property.
result: The joint bound strictly improves on separate bounds in the short-step regime, an exact tolerance threshold for finite uniform stationarity transfer is identified, and endpoint worst cases are shown to repeat while interior worst cases cannot persist across consecutive steps.
conclusion: The results yield principled tolerance-selection rules, descent estimates, and stationarity-complexity guarantees, but pertain entirely to classical convex optimization with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Five-species Counterexample To The Hofbauer--Kon--Saito Conjecture On Qualitative Permanence
authors: Halanay Andrei-Dan Beldiman Miruna-Mihaela
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38374v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hofbauer, Kon and Saito (J. Math. Biol. 2008) showed that a Lotka-Volterra interaction matrix [MATH] with negative diagonal can be qualitatively permanent only if (C1) every cycle of length [MATH] of [MATH] is nonpositive and (C2) every negative cycle contains exactly one negative entry. They conjectured that these conditions are also sufficient, and proved this for [MATH]. We give a [MATH] integer matrix with seven nonzero off-diagonal entries that satisfies (C1) and (C2) but is not qualitatively permanent. For an explicit integer growth vector the system has an interior equilibrium, and an asymptotically stable heteroclinic cycle on the boundary of the orthant attracts an open set of interior orbits. Adding non-interacting species gives counterexamples for every [MATH]. The interactions form a one-way feedback loop (two one-sided benefits and one one-sided harm) together with a predator of two prey. The verification is elementary except for one heteroclinic connection, which lies in a face that is not Volterra-Lyapunov stable. For it we prove a connection lemma based on invasion graphs.
tldr: The authors construct a five-species Lotka–Volterra counterexample disproving the Hofbauer–Kon–Saito conjecture that conditions (C1) and (C2) are sufficient for qualitative permanence.
motivation: Hofbauer, Kon and Saito (2008) proved that negative-diagonal Lotka–Volterra matrices must satisfy two cycle conditions to be qualitatively permanent, conjectured sufficiency, and verified it only for three species; this work tests that conjecture beyond three species.
method: An explicit integer interaction matrix with seven nonzero off-diagonal entries satisfying (C1) and (C2) is exhibited, forming a one-way feedback loop plus a predator of two prey; permanence failure is shown via an asymptotically stable boundary heteroclinic cycle, with the one nontrivial connection proved by an invasion-graph-based connection lemma.
result: For an explicit growth vector the system has an interior equilibrium, yet an open set of interior orbits is attracted to a heteroclinic cycle on the boundary; adding non-interacting species extends the counterexample to every higher dimension.
conclusion: Conditions (C1) and (C2) are not sufficient for qualitative permanence in five or more species, refuting the conjecture and showing that Volterra–Lyapunov stability of boundary faces matters.

title: Beyond Reachability: When Edit Order Preserves Couplings In Graph Flow Matching
authors: Zixing Song Zilin Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38486v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Shortest-path optimality does not guarantee that a memoryless graph generator preserves a prescribed source-target correspondence. We study whether reordering legal shortest edits can retain this correspondence without changing the pairing, mandatory edits, or sampling budget. Under a common Poisson clock, we establish an exact criterion for endpoint coupling recoverability: the source-blind Markov projection attains the unavoidable clock-error floor if and only if routes to distinct targets do not share graph states. Routes to the same target may merge without sacrificing endpoint fidelity. This characterization leads to an exact finite-state routing formulation and a legality-preserving scheduling procedure with recovery certificates. A marker-free construction demonstrates how shared edge structure can retain source distinctions, while a capacity-constrained family exhibits a sharp separation in paired error between edit orders with identical marginal error. Finally, a target-conditioned aliasing bound connects structural route design to the terminal fidelity of a learned graph-only generator. These results characterize when legal edit ordering can preserve a prescribed coupling under fixed operational costs.
tldr: The paper derives an exact criterion for when reordering legal shortest-path graph edits preserves a prescribed source-target coupling, framed as a finite-state routing and scheduling problem.
motivation: Shortest-path optimality alone does not guarantee that a memoryless graph generator maintains a prescribed source-target correspondence, so the authors ask when reordering legal edits can preserve that coupling under fixed operational costs.
method: Under a common Poisson clock they characterize endpoint coupling recoverability via a source-blind Markov projection, formulate an exact finite-state routing problem, and design a legality-preserving scheduling procedure with recovery certificates.
result: They show recoverability holds exactly when routes to distinct targets do not share graph states, give a marker-free construction retaining source distinctions, and exhibit a capacity-constrained family with sharp separation in paired error between edit orders having identical marginal error.
conclusion: Legal edit ordering can preserve a prescribed coupling if and only if route structures avoid shared states across distinct targets, linking structural route design to the terminal fidelity of a learned graph-only generator.

title: Proof Theory Of Quantifier Shifts - An Overview
authors: Mariami Gamsakhurdia Matthias Baaz
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37887v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantifier shifts are one of the oldest proof methods, but they are orthogonal to the cut free format: They can shorten proofs non-elementarily. (The proof is based on the sequence of proofs exhibiting a non-elementary difference between proofs with cuts and cut-free proofs by Orevkov). The cost is, however, that those proofs are globally sound but locally unsound. (Their subderivations might be unsound in contrast to the Hilbert concept of proof). In non-classical logics these calculi are only sound when all quantifier shifts are added. This characterizes all intermediate logics where Skolemization and the epsilon calculus is conservative (in contrast to the epsilon theorem which holds only for finite-valued Goedel logics).
tldr: An overview of quantifier-shift proof methods in classical and non-classical logics, focusing on their non-elementary proof compression and local unsoundness relative to cut-free calculi.
motivation: Quantifier shifts are among the oldest proof techniques but are orthogonal to cut-free formalisms, and their soundness behavior in intermediate logics is not well characterized.
method: Survey and proof-theoretic analysis building on Orevkov's sequence of proofs demonstrating non-elementary speedups of proofs with cuts over cut-free proofs, examining global versus local soundness of subderivations.
result: Quantifier-shift calculi are globally sound but locally unsound, and in non-classical logics they are sound only when all quantifier shifts are included, which characterizes intermediate logics where Skolemization and the epsilon calculus are conservative.
conclusion: The overview clarifies the proof-theoretic status of quantifier shifts and delineates the class of intermediate logics admitting conservative Skolemization and epsilon-calculus extensions, in contrast to the epsilon theorem valid only for finite-valued Gödel logics.

title: What Can Firms Do In The Face Of Model Distillation?
authors: Diptangshu Sen, Jibang Wu, Juba Ziani
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38088v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model distillation has become a major concern in the rapidly growing generative AI discourse. In its simplest form, distillation is the phenomenon where smaller firms can use data distilled from transcripts of conversations with powerful proprietary closed-weight models to train their own models, thus achieving reasonably high model quality but at much lower costs. Besides the legitimate safety and security concerns associated with distillation, another major issue is how it can also distort marketplace outcomes. This motivates us to initiate an exploration of the problem from an economic theory lens. We consider a setting with two players: an incumbent and a distilling competitor and characterize how the incumbent's model characteristics drive the incentives around how much the competitor should distill. We also consider the impact of distillation on key market outcomes like user-side surplus and the incumbent's utility. Our key contribution, however, is to study interventions for preventing or limiting distillation attacks. In this context, we study two settings: i) when it is possible, with a certain probability (which grows in the extent of distillation conducted), to detect an attack on the incumbent's model; and ii) when a distillation attack cannot be reliably detected. In the first setting, we show that penalty-based regulations can be very effective in completely deterring distillation, although it can have potentially adverse effects on market competition and user surplus. In the latter setting, we show that the incumbent can use self-distillation as a mitigation strategy. Importantly, the effectiveness of self-distillation depends on how cost-efficiently the incumbent can deploy a new self-distilled model on the market. On the positive side, self-distillation can preserve market competition thus protecting user surplus to some extent.
tldr: An economic-theory analysis of model distillation in generative AI markets, examining when incumbents can deter or mitigate competitors who train on distilled outputs.
motivation: Distillation of proprietary closed-weight models raises safety concerns but also distorts market outcomes, motivating a formal economic treatment of incumbent–competitor incentives.
method: A two-player game-theoretic model (incumbent vs. distilling competitor) analyzing detection-probability-dependent penalties and a no-detection regime where self-distillation serves as mitigation.
result: Penalty-based regulation can fully deter distillation but may harm competition and user surplus; absent reliable detection, self-distillation can preserve competition and partially protect user surplus depending on deployment cost efficiency.
conclusion: Regulatory and self-distillation interventions trade off deterrence against market competition and consumer welfare, with effectiveness hinging on detection reliability and cost efficiency.

title: Rosemary: Efficient And Adaptable In-Storage Acceleration For Fully Homomorphic Encryption
authors: Xuan Wang, Tianqi Zhang, Gabrielle de Micheli, Yujin Nam, Keming Fan, Augusto Vega, Minxuan Zhou, Tajana Rosing
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38262v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) enables computation on encrypted data and is promising for privacy-preserving computing. However, FHE deployment remains constrained due to massive computational, memory, and data-movement overheads. Existing acceleration strategies often overlook the storage I/O bottleneck caused by the enormous size of FHE data in large-scale applications, as most prior works focus on small benchmarks that fit in main memory. Our studies show that state-of-the-art FHE systems spend 71\% to 85\% of their execution time moving data between storage and compute units rather than performing useful computation. To address the I/O bottleneck, we present Rosemary, a heterogeneous FHE acceleration system that incorporates a novel in-storage processing (ISP) architecture with compiler-level and algorithmic optimizations. Our key innovations include 1) an adaptable hardware-aware FHE engine inside a NAND flash-based solid-state drive (SSD) for efficient and cost-effective in-storage FHE processing, 2) a Throughput-Data-Aware Program Allocator (TDAP) that partitions FHE workloads into heterogeneous programs, and 3) a Compiler-Level Ciphertext-Aware Optimizer (CLCAO) that exploits ISP-friendly FHE kernels for low-cost ISP execution. Across a diverse set of FHE workloads, including encrypted deep learning inference and cloud database queries, Rosemary achieves geometric-mean speedups of [MATH] over state-of-the-art CPU/GPU implementations and [MATH] over prior FHE accelerators, while improving energy efficiency by up to [MATH] and Energy-Delay-Area-Product (EDAP) by up to [MATH].
tldr: Rosemary is an in-storage acceleration system for fully homomorphic encryption that addresses storage I/O bottlenecks using SSD-integrated FHE engines and compiler-level optimizations.
motivation: FHE enables privacy-preserving computation but suffers from severe computational, memory, and data-movement overheads; existing accelerators overlook the storage I/O bottleneck in large-scale workloads.
method: The authors propose a heterogeneous FHE acceleration architecture with an in-storage processing engine inside a NAND flash SSD, a Throughput-Data-Aware Program Allocator, and a Compiler-Level Ciphertext-Aware Optimizer.
result: Rosemary achieves geometric-mean speedups over state-of-the-art CPU/GPU implementations and prior FHE accelerators, with improved energy efficiency and EDAP across encrypted deep learning inference and cloud database query workloads.
conclusion: In-storage acceleration with hardware-aware FHE kernels and compiler optimizations can substantially mitigate the I/O bottleneck in large-scale FHE applications.

title: Simultaneous Gradient Learning In First-Price Auctions
authors: Janik B\"urgermeister, Julius Durmann, Martin Bichler, Mete \c{s}eref Ahunbay, Bary Pradelski, Marco Scarsini
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38487v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study equilibrium learning in discretized Bayesian games, focusing on first-price auctions as a testbed for gradient-based learning dynamics under private information. While the symmetric independent private values model admits a unique Bayesian correlated equilibrium (BCE) in the continuous limit, standard convergence guarantees for gradient-based learners do not apply: classical no-regret theory predicts convergence only to Bayesian coarse correlated equilibria (BCCE), which can remain large and far from the competitive equilibrium even under fine discretizations. To bridge this gap, we introduce the notion of Bayesian semicoarse correlated equilibrium (BSCCE), an equilibrium concept that refines BCCE by restricting deviations to probability-preserving transformations consistent with projected gradient dynamics. We provide a linear programming characterization of BSCCE with polynomially many variables and constraints and establish the inclusion hierarchy [MATH]. Our main finding is that the BSCCE set contracts in many cases as the discretization of the Bayesian game is refined. Even with priors for which BCCE fails to concentrate, the diameter of the BSCCE polytope shrinks toward zero, indicating convergence to the unique continuous-game Bayes-Nash equilibrium. These results provide a principled explanation for the observed robustness of gradient-based learning in discretized Bayesian games, showing that these dynamics select a smaller equilibrium set than standard no-regret theory predicts.
tldr: The paper introduces Bayesian semicoarse correlated equilibrium (BSCCE) to explain why projected gradient learning in discretized first-price auctions converges toward the unique Bayes-Nash equilibrium rather than merely to large sets of Bayesian coarse correlated equilibria.
motivation: Standard no-regret guarantees only ensure convergence to Bayesian coarse correlated equilibria, which can be far from the competitive equilibrium even under fine discretization, leaving the observed robustness of gradient-based learning unexplained.
method: The authors define BSCCE by restricting deviations to probability-preserving transformations consistent with projected gradient dynamics, give a polynomial-size linear programming characterization, establish an inclusion hierarchy among equilibrium notions, and study how the BSCCE polytope contracts under refinement of the discretization.
result: The BSCCE set contracts in many cases as discretization is refined, with the polytope diameter shrinking toward zero even for priors where BCCE fails to concentrate, indicating convergence to the unique continuous-game Bayes-Nash equilibrium.
conclusion: Gradient-based learning in discretized Bayesian games selects a strictly smaller equilibrium set than standard no-regret theory predicts, providing a principled explanation for its empirical robustness in first-price auctions.

title: Order Maintenance In Worst-Case Constant Time, Verified
authors: Denis Firsov
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38616v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Order maintenance asks for a data structure that keeps a sequence of elements under insertions and deletions and tells which of two elements comes first. We give an algorithm, assembled from published components, that performs each operation in worst-case constant time, and verify it in Lean 4. The algorithm is a program for a random-access machine deeply embedded in Lean, whose interpreter counts every instruction. We prove that the program answers every query as a simple reference specification does, that each operation takes at most a fixed number of steps, independent of the number of elements and of the history, and that after [MATH] operations no value it has computed has more than [MATH] bits, so it runs unchanged on a machine with words of that size. A verified translation that preserves step counts exactly connects the high-level proofs to the machine program, so the interpreter is the only cost model to trust. An unverified native implementation shows the algorithm's practical cost.
tldr: The paper presents a worst-case constant-time order-maintenance data structure assembled from published components and formally verified in Lean 4 down to a cost-counting random-access machine model.
motivation: Order maintenance—maintaining a sequence under insertions/deletions and answering precedence queries—is a classical data-structure problem; the authors aim to provide a fully verified implementation with exact, trustworthy worst-case cost guarantees rather than relying on informal complexity arguments.
method: The algorithm is a deeply embedded RAM program in Lean 4 whose interpreter counts every instruction; a verified, step-count-preserving translation links high-level proofs to the machine program, and proofs establish correctness against a reference specification plus fixed per-operation step bounds and bounded word size.
result: They prove every query matches the simple reference specification, each operation takes a constant number of steps independent of sequence length and history, and after N operations all computed values fit in O(log N) bits; an unverified native implementation demonstrates practical performance.
conclusion: The work delivers a machine-checked, cost-accurate verification of a worst-case-constant-time order-maintenance algorithm, showing that fine-grained complexity guarantees can be certified in a proof assistant.

title: Pooled Testing Under Congestion: Operational Scaling Laws For Pool-Size Selection
authors: Johan van Leeuwaarden Ioannis Dimitriou
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37729v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical pooled-testing rules choose pool sizes to reduce the number of tests. In practice, however, samples arrive over time, pools take time to form, testing capacity is finite, and positive pools create bursts of follow-up work. These operational features can make the test-efficient pool size far from the delay-efficient one. We formulate pooled testing with stochastic arrivals and finite testing capacity as a queueing system, and derive exact performance representations and asymptotic scaling laws for fixed-batch Dorfman testing and a dynamic two-threshold policy. The analysis reveals three distinct design regimes. When test usage is the main concern, the classical Dorfman rule is recovered and the optimal pool size scales with the inverse square root of prevalence. When delay accumulated while the laboratory is busy testing another batch matters, positive pools create service-time variability that grows more rapidly with pool size than the mean retesting burden, and the optimal scale shifts to the inverse cube root of prevalence. When waiting to assemble a pool is itself costly, the optimal fixed pool size remains bounded even as prevalence becomes very small. Under severe capacity scarcity, congestion remains relevant at the classical Dorfman scale: the square-root law survives, but with a capacity-dependent constant. Dynamic pooling separates two operational decisions that fixed pool sizes conflate. A lower threshold determines when routine testing should begin, while an upper threshold limits pooling when backlog is high. The lower threshold follows the cube-root scale, whereas the upper threshold primarily acts as congestion control. The results show how prevalence, capacity, and delay jointly determine pooling decisions and explain why operationally optimal pools can be much smaller than those suggested by test-efficiency calculations alone.
tldr: The paper models pooled (group) testing with stochastic sample arrivals and finite testing capacity as a queueing system, deriving scaling laws that relate optimal pool size to disease prevalence, delay, and capacity.
motivation: Classical Dorfman pooled-testing rules minimize the number of tests but ignore operational realities such as arrival dynamics, batch formation time, finite laboratory capacity, and follow-up retesting bursts, which can make test-efficient pool sizes far from delay-efficient ones.
method: The authors formulate fixed-batch Dorfman testing and a dynamic two-threshold pooling policy as queueing systems, obtaining exact performance representations and asymptotic scaling laws across different design regimes.
result: Three regimes emerge: optimal pool size scales as the inverse square root of prevalence when test usage dominates, as the inverse cube root when delay during busy periods matters, and stays bounded when pool-assembly waiting is costly; under severe capacity scarcity the square-root law survives with a capacity-dependent constant, and the dynamic policy's lower threshold follows cube-root scaling while the upper threshold acts as congestion control.
conclusion: Prevalence, capacity, and delay jointly determine operationally optimal pooling decisions, and operationally optimal pools can be substantially smaller than those suggested by pure test-efficiency calculations.

title: Optimality Of Threshold Policies For Heat Storage Optimization And A Policy Gradient Algorithm
authors: Florian D\"ottling Nicole B\"auerle
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37853v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the optimal control of a stylized finite-horizon heat-storage system operated by a prosumer who can buy heat from and sell heat to a district heating network. Heat production and consumption are uncertain, and charging and discharging decisions have to be taken before the subsequent heat balance is observed. The resulting problem is formulated as a Markov decision process with continuous state and action spaces. We first establish a structural characterization of the optimal policy as a two-parameter threshold policy. Under additional regularity assumptions, we prove differentiability and Lipschitz properties of the value functions. Exploiting the threshold structure, we parameterize the policy by the time-dependent lower and upper thresholds and derive a pathwise stochastic-gradient estimator. We then propose a projected stochastic policy-gradient algorithm, establish a constrained Kurdyka-\L ojasiewicz inequality and derive global finite-sample bounds for both the objective optimality gap and the distance to the optimal threshold vector. Finally, numerical experiments for a non-stationary heat-balance process illustrate the evolution of the threshold parameters.
tldr: The paper studies optimal control of a finite-horizon heat-storage system for a prosumer trading heat with a district heating network, proving threshold-optimal policies and proposing a projected stochastic policy-gradient algorithm with finite-sample bounds.
motivation: Prosumers interacting with district heating networks face uncertain production and consumption and must commit to charging/discharging decisions before observing the heat balance, motivating a principled optimal-control treatment of storage.
method: The problem is cast as a Markov decision process with continuous state and action spaces; the authors prove the optimal policy is a two-parameter threshold policy, establish differentiability and Lipschitz properties of the value functions, and derive a pathwise stochastic-gradient estimator combined with a projected policy-gradient algorithm and a constrained Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz inequality.
result: Global finite-sample bounds are derived for both the objective optimality gap and the distance to the optimal threshold vector, and numerical experiments on a non-stationary heat-balance process illustrate the evolution of the threshold parameters.
conclusion: Threshold-structured policies are optimal for this stylized heat-storage control problem, and the proposed policy-gradient scheme comes with provable convergence guarantees, making it practically attractive for stochastic energy-management settings.

title: Hybrid CutFEM-IFEM Model For Embedded And Immersed Interfaces With Triply-cut Cells For The 2d Poisson Problem
authors: Christopher Kees Darsh Nathawani
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38271v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a hybrid CutFEM--IFEM method for 2D Poisson problems with an immersed fluid--fluid interface and an embedded fluid--solid interface on a single unfitted mesh. The proposed method leverages the strengths of both unfitted finite element methods and immersed interface techniques to handle complex interface geometries and strong discontinuities efficiently. A composite equivalent polynomial representation of the Heaviside and Dirac delta functions is used to integrate on triply-cut cells. Moreover, the IFEM basis functions are enriched with the lift functions exactly representing solution and flux jumps. Numerical examples show optimal convergence for linear and quadratic elements, with accuracy comparable to that of a mesh fitted to both interfaces.
tldr: The paper introduces a hybrid CutFEM-IFEM finite element method for 2D Poisson problems with immersed and embedded interfaces on an unfitted mesh.
motivation: It aims to combine unfitted finite element methods with immersed interface techniques to handle complex interface geometries and strong discontinuities efficiently.
method: The method uses a composite equivalent polynomial representation of Heaviside and Dirac delta functions for integration on triply-cut cells and enriches IFEM basis functions with lift functions to represent solution and flux jumps exactly.
result: Numerical examples demonstrate optimal convergence for linear and quadratic elements, with accuracy comparable to a mesh fitted to both interfaces.
conclusion: The hybrid approach is effective for interface problems but is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Nonlinear Springs With Orbits In Radicals: A Solvability Criterion
authors: Unnikrishna Pillai
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37730v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An odd polynomial oscillator has a periodic orbit given by a quadrature. When the zeros of the energy polynomial are all simple or all of even multiplicity, that quadrature is elementary exactly when the polynomial is a perfect square, and the time is a sum of inverse tangents. Recovering the displacement inverts that relation, algebraic when their coefficients are commensurate, making a closed form a Galois question. This paper identifies the group as the monodromy group of a rational map, computes its branch data from the parameters, and shows the branch value at the phase-angle singularity never vanishes, so every decomposition pairs the amplitudes reciprocally. In the commensurate family with distinct real factors, the orbit is radical exactly when the primitive inversion degree is at most four, or when reciprocal pairs leave a reduced spring of that degree. Radical orbits occur at the fifth, ninth, thirteenth and seventeenth force orders, the last only for reciprocal members, an expression recorded for each. The multiplicity hypothesis cannot be dropped. Factoring the energy polynomial into square and squarefree parts turns the quadrature into a differential of the third kind on a hyperelliptic curve, where elementarity is a torsion condition on the divisor of its poles with a vanishing holomorphic remainder. The first nonsquare elementary member appears at the ninth force order, and the power pullback inverts in closed form at every such order, giving a radical orbit for a confining spring of arbitrarily high degree with a sufficient condition for positive coefficients.
tldr: A classical-mechanics/algebraic-geometry paper characterizing when the periodic orbit of an odd polynomial (nonlinear spring) oscillator admits a closed-form expression in radicals.
motivation: The quadrature for the period of a polynomial oscillator is elementary only under special conditions, and inverting it to recover the displacement raises a Galois-type question about solvability by radicals; the paper aims to give a complete solvability criterion.
method: The author identifies the relevant Galois group as the monodromy group of a rational map, computes its branch data from the spring parameters, and recasts the quadrature as a differential of the third kind on a hyperelliptic curve whose elementarity becomes a torsion condition on the pole divisor.
result: Radical orbits exist exactly when the primitive inversion degree is at most four or reciprocal pairs reduce the spring to such a degree, occurring at fifth, ninth, thirteenth and seventeenth force orders; the first nonsquare elementary case appears at ninth order, and the multiplicity hypothesis is shown to be necessary.
conclusion: The work provides a sharp algebraic solvability criterion for nonlinear spring orbits and constructs confining springs of arbitrarily high degree with radical orbits, giving a sufficient condition for positive coefficients.

title: A Stochastic LineseArch Method (slam) For Minimizing Expectation Residuals: Weakening Boundedness Of Gradient
authors: Qi Wang, Uday V. Shanbhag, Yue Xie
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37947v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish convergence guarantees for the Stochastic LineseArch Method (SLAM) proposed and analyzed in Wang et al. (arXiv:2512.14979) for nonconvex composite stochastic optimization, retaining the iteration and sample complexity orders of the original analysis assuming neither the boundedness of true gradients nor the Lipschitz continuity of the convex nonsmooth term [MATH]. ChatGPT was used to assist in developing a key intermediate result. Under uniformly Lipschitz continuous and unbiased sampled gradients with uniformly bounded variance with mini-batch sizes proportional to the iteration budget, SLAM achieves an iteration complexity [MATH] and a sample complexity [MATH] for obtaining an iterate whose expected proximal-gradient residual norm is at most [MATH].
tldr: This paper proves convergence guarantees for the Stochastic LineSearch Method (SLAM) in nonconvex composite stochastic optimization without requiring boundedness of true gradients or Lipschitz continuity of the nonsmooth term.
motivation: Prior analyses of line-search stochastic methods rely on restrictive assumptions such as bounded gradients and Lipschitz continuity of the proximal term; the authors aim to weaken these assumptions while preserving complexity orders.
method: The analysis assumes uniformly Lipschitz continuous, unbiased sampled gradients with uniformly bounded variance and mini-batch sizes proportional to the iteration budget, and derives iteration and sample complexity bounds for the expected proximal-gradient residual norm.
result: SLAM retains its original iteration and sample complexity orders under the weakened assumptions, achieving an iterate whose expected proximal-gradient residual norm is small.
conclusion: The work broadens the applicability of SLAM to settings lacking gradient boundedness and nonsmooth-term Lipschitz continuity, at no cost in complexity.

title: Neural Stream Function Method For Electrical Impedance Tomography With Lipschitz Conductivities
authors: Xiaosheng Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38064v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electrical impedance tomography (EIT) reconstructs the conductivity inside an object from voltage and current measurements on its boundary. The resulting inverse problem is nonlinear and severely ill-posed. Neural networks offer a flexible computational approach, but training physics informed neural networks for EIT and relating their training loss to reconstruction accuracy remain challenging. We develop a novel constrained neural stream function method for planar EIT with Lipschitz conductivities. The method builds the conductivity constraints and prescribed boundary voltages into the neural trial functions and replaces the second order conductivity equation with a first order system in strong form. The measured current is also used to construct a fixed baseline for the stream function. For this formulation, we derive error estimates that relate the sampled neural objective to errors in the physical boundary currents and the reconstructed conductivity. The error estimates separate the contributions from neural approximation, measurement noise, and sampling. Numerical experiments further demonstrate that the proposed method achieves high reconstruction accuracy with both exact and noisy boundary data.
tldr: A constrained neural stream function method with rigorous error estimates is developed for solving the ill-posed planar electrical impedance tomography inverse problem with Lipschitz conductivities.
motivation: Physics-informed neural networks for EIT are flexible but lack a clear link between training loss and actual reconstruction accuracy, so the authors aim to derive rigorous error bounds.
method: The conductivity constraints and prescribed boundary voltages are built directly into the neural trial functions, the second-order conductivity equation is recast as a first-order strong-form system, and the measured current defines a fixed baseline for the stream function.
result: Error estimates are derived that connect the sampled neural objective to errors in boundary currents and reconstructed conductivity, separating neural approximation, measurement noise, and sampling contributions; numerical experiments show high accuracy with exact and noisy data.
conclusion: The framework provides a principled, theoretically grounded neural approach to EIT reconstruction, though the work lies entirely outside quantum information science.

title: Boxing Problem
authors: April Niu, Santanu Dey, Oktay G\"unl\"uk, Jisun Lee
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38085v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the , which seeks a subset of points in \(^d\) maximizing the total reward of a selection of points minus the width of its axis-aligned bounding box. We also investigate the associated , defined by the epigraph of the width function over binary selection variables. Although the width function is not submodular in general, we restore submodularity by fixing an anchor point. After anchoring, we establish a connection to the intersection of mixing sets with a linking constraint, which yields a polynomial-time optimization algorithm and a polynomial-size extended formulation. We then study the polyhedral structure of the Boxing Set and show that its facets admit laminar families of tight sets and can be obtained by sequential lifting. For the one-dimensional case, we provide a complete description of facet-defining inequalities together with a strongly polynomial-time separation algorithm.
tldr: The paper studies the Boxing Problem, a combinatorial optimization problem maximizing rewarded point selections minus bounding-box width, and analyzes the polyhedral structure of the associated Boxing Set.
motivation: The width function governing the objective is generally not submodular, which obstructs standard optimization techniques; the authors seek tractable structure by anchoring a point.
method: After fixing an anchor point, they restore submodularity, connect the problem to the intersection of mixing sets with a linking constraint, and derive a polynomial-time algorithm and polynomial-size extended formulation; they also analyze facets via laminar families of tight sets and sequential lifting.
result: They obtain polynomial-time solvability with a compact extended formulation, characterize facet-defining inequalities through laminar tight-set families, and for the one-dimensional case give a complete facet description with a strongly polynomial separation algorithm.
conclusion: The work provides a polyhedral and algorithmic understanding of the Boxing Problem and its associated set, extending mixing-set theory to this anchored setting.

title: Randomized Algorithms In Numerical Linear Algebra For Scientific Computing
authors: Ethan N. W. Epperly, Daniel Kressner, Yuji Nakatsukasa
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38157v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Randomized numerical linear algebra (RNLA) has fundamentally changed the landscape of scientific computing over the last twenty to thirty years. While early breakthroughs focused primarily on low-rank approximation and least-squares problems, randomized techniques are now used to solve a broad range of linear algebra problems, supporting applications spanning data science, optimization, and computational engineering. This paper surveys some of the main ideas of RNLA, focusing on methods that are effective in practice and on simple theoretical bounds that can be used to understand them. We highlight the core benefits of randomization: improved scalability, algorithmic simplicity, and---contrary to what the name may suggest---remarkable reliability and numerical stability. Topics include sketching, low-rank approximation, least squares, orthogonalization and approximate orthogonalization, randomized Krylov subspace methods, preconditioning, trace and spectral density estimation, row and column selection algorithms, posterior error estimation, randomized regularization, and tensor-structured randomness.
tldr: This paper surveys randomized numerical linear algebra methods for scientific computing, covering sketching, low-rank approximation, least squares, randomized Krylov methods, preconditioning, and related topics.
motivation: Randomized numerical linear algebra has become a broad and practical tool in scientific computing, but its main ideas and theoretical guarantees are spread across specialized literature.
method: The authors provide a survey of core RNLA techniques, emphasizing practically effective algorithms and simple theoretical bounds that explain their performance, scalability, reliability, and numerical stability.
result: The survey organizes topics such as sketching, low-rank approximation, least squares, orthogonalization, randomized Krylov subspace methods, preconditioning, trace and spectral density estimation, row/column selection, posterior error estimation, randomized regularization, and tensor-structured randomness.
conclusion: RNLA offers scalable, simple, and reliable approaches for a wide range of linear algebra problems in data science, optimization, and computational engineering.

title: Bound-preserving And Mass-conserving Projection Bcfd Methods For Incompressible Miscible Displacement In Porous Media
authors: Xiaoying Wang, Shusen Xie, Hongfei Fu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38219v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we propose and analyze two novel structure-preserving projection schemes for the incompressible miscible displacement problem in porous media. These schemes are specifically designed to preserve two essential physical properties--concentration bounds and the mass balance identity, and are accompanied by a rigorous error analysis for the projection approach. Both schemes are second-order accurate in space but differ in temporal accuracy: one is first-order and the other is second-order. Methodologically, both schemes comprise a prediction step for the concentration variable, based on a second-order modified upwind discretization together with an implicit-explicit finite difference approximation, followed by a projection (or correction) step that enforces the desired physical constraints, namely bounds and mass conservation. For the first-order temporal scheme, the velocity and pressure are solved at the first step on staggered spatial grids with explicit treatment of concentration. In contrast, for the second-order scheme, to ensure well-posedness and to suppress non-physical oscillations in the simulation, the velocity and pressure are solved at the final step with the concentration treated implicitly. A rigorous numerical theoretical framework is established for the first-order scheme, encompassing optimal-order error estimates, stability, and proofs of the existence and uniqueness of the numerical solutions. The numerical analysis framework is further extended to the more involved second-order scheme, and the corresponding theoretical results are briefly outlined. Finally, numerical examples, including some 'real' simulations, are presented to verify the theoretical findings and demonstrate the strong performance of the proposed schemes. In particular, the occurrence of viscous fingering is successfully captured and confirmed by the numerical results.
tldr: The paper develops two structure-preserving projection schemes for incompressible miscible displacement in porous media that conserve concentration bounds and mass balance, with rigorous error analysis and numerical verification including viscous fingering simulations.
motivation: Standard numerical schemes for miscible displacement can violate physical constraints such as concentration bounds and mass conservation, producing non-physical oscillations; the authors aim to design schemes that preserve these properties while retaining accuracy.
method: A prediction step using second-order modified upwind discretization with implicit-explicit finite differencing is followed by a projection/correction step enforcing bounds and mass conservation; staggered grids are used, with velocity and pressure solved at the first step (first-order scheme) or final step with implicit concentration (second-order scheme).
result: Optimal-order error estimates, stability, and existence/uniqueness are proven for the first-order scheme, with the framework extended to the second-order scheme; numerical tests confirm second-order spatial accuracy and capture viscous fingering.
conclusion: The proposed bound-preserving and mass-conserving projection schemes are accurate, stable, and physically consistent, offering a rigorous numerical framework for porous-media flow simulation.

title: Notes On Orlicz Spaces And Interpolation
authors: Wilfredo Urbina-Romero M. Vali Siadat
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38455v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Orlicz spaces are a natural generalization of classical Lebesgue spaces. They are built upon convex growth functions and provide a flexible framework for studying integrability conditions beyond power-type behavior. In this survey paper, we present the basic definitions, main properties, and fundamental results concerning Orlicz spaces, and also discuss the Marcinkiewicz interpolation result for Orlicz spaces.
tldr: A survey of Orlicz spaces, their basic properties, and Marcinkiewicz-type interpolation results for these spaces.
motivation: Orlicz spaces generalize Lebesgue spaces via convex growth functions, offering a flexible framework for integrability beyond power-type behavior, and a consolidated survey of their fundamentals and interpolation theory is useful for analysts.
method: Expository survey presenting definitions, main structural properties, and fundamental theorems of Orlicz spaces, followed by a discussion of the Marcinkiewicz interpolation theorem in the Orlicz setting.
result: The paper consolidates standard results on Orlicz spaces and describes how interpolation arguments (Marcinkiewicz type) extend to this generalized integrability framework.
conclusion: The survey serves as an accessible reference for Orlicz space theory and interpolation, but remains purely within classical functional analysis with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Local Hardy And Bmo Spaces On Filtered Lie Groups
authors: Elena Rizzo Mattia Calzi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38562v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a theory of local Hardy and [MATH] spaces on a connected Lie group with polynomial growth whose Lie algebra is endowed with a filtration. Under suitable assumptions, we prove that the local Hardy spaces enjoy an appropriate atomic decomposition, are compatible with Calder\'on--Zygmund operators, and can be identified with certain Triebel--Lizorkin spaces, as it happens in the classical settings.
tldr: The paper develops a theory of local Hardy and BMO spaces on connected Lie groups with polynomial growth and filtered Lie algebras, proving atomic decompositions and Calderón–Zygmund compatibility.
motivation: Classical local Hardy and BMO theory on Euclidean spaces is well established, but a corresponding theory on filtered homogeneous Lie groups is missing and needed for harmonic analysis in that setting.
method: Under suitable assumptions on the filtration and group growth, the authors construct local Hardy spaces, establish atomic decompositions, and identify them with certain Triebel–Lizorkin spaces.
result: Local Hardy spaces on filtered Lie groups admit atomic decompositions, are preserved by Calderón–Zygmund operators, and coincide with appropriate Triebel–Lizorkin spaces, mirroring the classical Euclidean picture.
conclusion: The work extends classical real-variable harmonic analysis to filtered Lie groups, providing a coherent framework that parallels the Euclidean theory.

title: Market Attention And Information Quality In On-Chain Prediction Markets: Evidence From Polymarket
authors: Davide Mancino, Hasret Ozan Sevim, Luca Pennella, Huy Hoang Le
