abstract: ArXiv:2610.37669v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper asks whether the leading on-chain prediction market, Polymarket, behaves more as an information market, in which monetary stakes compress dispersed beliefs into a price that tracks the truth, or more as an attention market, in which capital flows toward the most visible contracts rather than the most informative ones. Using trade-level data from Polymarket's central-limit-order-book (CLOB) markets from January 2024 through March 2026, and a one-sided exchange-contract convention that avoids double-counting maker and taker fills, we study the top 1,000 markets by taker-side dollar volume. For each, we build an attention score from the within-sample percentile ranks of volume, transaction count, and active trader wallets, and an information-quality score on resolved Yes/No markets equal to one minus the absolute distance between the YES-token price seven days before resolution and the realised outcome. Placing markets on this attention/information plane answers the question in favour of the information-market reading: 68.2% of analysis-sample volume sits in well-calibrated markets (average 7-day error of 0.03, falling to 0.02 one day before resolution), spread across 515 of 679 contracts. A narrower, identifiable cluster of 19 high-attention/low-information contracts captures 22.1% of analysis-sample volume, but 79% of that mass is the 2024 US Presidential Election, the single closest macro-political event of the window. Polymarket is therefore primarily an information aggregator; the attention component is real but small and concentrated in a handful of headline contracts whose outcomes are hardest to forecast ex ante.
tldr: An empirical study of Polymarket on-chain prediction markets asking whether prices behave as information aggregators or as attention-driven flows, concluding the information-market reading dominates.
motivation: Prediction markets are claimed to compress dispersed beliefs into truth-tracking prices, but capital may instead chase visible, headline contracts; the authors test which mechanism prevails on the leading on-chain venue.
method: Using CLOB trade-level data from January 2024 to March 2026 for the top 1,000 markets by taker-side volume, they construct a composite attention score (percentile ranks of volume, transaction count, active wallets) and an information-quality score defined as one minus the 7-day pre-resolution price error on resolved Yes/No markets.
result: 68.2% of analysis-sample volume lies in well-calibrated markets (mean 7-day error 0.03, shrinking to 0.02 one day out) across 515 of 679 contracts, while a 19-contract high-attention/low-information cluster holds 22.1% of volume, 79% of which is the 2024 US Presidential Election.
conclusion: Polymarket functions primarily as an information aggregator, with a real but small and concentrated attention component tied to a handful of hard-to-forecast headline contracts.

title: Generation, Not Selection: Llm Proposals For Certified Access-Control Policy Mining
authors: Gautam Kumar (indian Institute Of Technology Kharagpur, India), Ravi Sundaram (northeastern University, USA), Shamik Sural
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37716v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) policy mining---recovering a compact, auditable policy from an access log---is posed as minimum set cover and solved greedily, which enjoys an [MATH] guarantee. That guarantee is on a precondition the literature never states: the candidate pool handed to greedy must contain the optimal rules. Generation, not selection, is the binding constraint, and existing generators are purely ---they surface a rule only when enough log records witness it, so they fail on precisely the rare exception rules that fill a heavy-tailed policy. We replace the generator with a language model proposing rules , from attribute names, and keep the combinatorial selector to carry the guarantee: every proposal is filtered against the observed denials, so soundness is independent of the proposal mechanism and an unreliable proposer can only waste candidates, never grant access. Over five seeds on each of two enterprise domains, adding semantic proposal to a syntactic miner dominates it on runs---strictly better on seven---with near-optimal policies ([MATH]--[MATH] rules against [MATH], versus [MATH]--[MATH]) and false grants cut four- to sevenfold. Replacing the syntactic miner rather than augmenting it wins only where witnesses are scarce. An anonymization ablation isolates the mechanism: opaque attribute names cost two thirds of the model's rule recovery while leaving the syntactic baselines provably unmoved, and cost nothing where witnesses are plentiful. Semantic knowledge and log evidence are substitutes.
tldr: This paper reframes attribute-based access control (ABAC) policy mining as a generation problem, using LLM-proposed candidate rules combined with a greedy set-cover selector to recover compact, auditable policies.
motivation: Existing ABAC miners rely on syntactic generators that only surface rules witnessed by many log records, so they miss the rare exception rules characteristic of heavy-tailed enterprise policies.
method: The authors replace the rule generator with a language model that proposes candidate rules directly from attribute names, while retaining the combinatorial minimum-set-cover selector; proposals are filtered against observed denials so soundness is independent of the proposer.
result: Across five seeds on two enterprise domains, semantic proposal augmented with the syntactic miner strictly improves seven runs, yielding near-optimal policy sizes and four- to sevenfold reductions in false grants; an anonymization ablation shows opaque attribute names cost two thirds of rule recovery.
conclusion: Semantic knowledge and log evidence act as substitutes, and generation rather than selection is the binding constraint in certified access-control policy mining.

title: FVH-Bench: Evaluating Image Generator Safety Beyond Overtly Harmful Imagery
authors: Zihao Zhu, Yuhan Liu, Siwei Lyu, Baoyuan Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37722v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern image generators can produce complex visual artifacts, including diagrams, interfaces, and records that combine text, graphics, and layout to convey detailed information. They may refuse requests for overtly harmful imagery yet still generate artifacts that guide dangerous actions or support deception. We call the risk arising from what such images enable, rather than only what they depict, functional visual harm (FVH). Existing safety benchmarks focus largely on overtly harmful content, such as pornography and graphic violence, leaving image generators' safety alignment against FVH insufficiently evaluated. To address this gap, we introduce FVH-Bench, comprising 669 prompts across five harmful visual functions and ten risk domains. The 11 evaluated image generators rarely refuse these requests and frequently generate artifacts that fulfill the targeted harmful functions. High scores for target harm realization and harmful artifact usability further indicate that these outputs can support the intended harmful purposes. A further analysis finds that existing safety detectors also provide limited coverage of FVH, indicating gaps in their ability to recognize harmful visual functions. Together, these findings show that evaluating image-generator safety alignment requires considering not only what images depict, but also what they may enable.
tldr: FVH-Bench is a 669-prompt benchmark evaluating whether image generators produce artifacts that enable harmful actions (functional visual harm) rather than merely depicting harmful content.
motivation: Existing safety benchmarks focus on overtly harmful imagery such as pornography or graphic violence, leaving unevaluated the risk that generated diagrams, interfaces, and records can support dangerous actions or deception.
method: The authors construct 669 prompts spanning five harmful visual functions and ten risk domains, and evaluate 11 image generators plus existing safety detectors on refusal behavior, target-harm realization, and artifact usability.
result: Evaluated generators rarely refuse these requests and frequently produce usable artifacts satisfying the targeted harmful functions, while existing safety detectors provide only limited coverage of such functional harms.
conclusion: Safety alignment of image generators must account for what images enable, not just what they depict, motivating function-oriented benchmarks and detectors.

title: When Skills Tell Agents Not To Ask: A Large-Scale Study Of Oversight Directives In Agent Skills
authors: Yuan Tian Timofey Sanko
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37734v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent skills, reusable instruction packages centred on a SKILL.md file, extend AI agents on demand, and a single line in a widely copied skill reaches every agent that loads it. Some lines are oversight-loosening directives: they tell the agent to proceed without approval, to bypass checks with --no-verify, or to keep working without checking in. Although such directives can remove a checkpoint from every agent that loads them, no prior work has examined them. We present the first large-scale study of oversight-loosening directives, analyzing 1.53 million English skills from GitSkills. We split skills into units (sentences, bullets, table cells, and code lines), develop a codebook that labels oversight directives by polarity, mechanism, and scope, label 2,097 units by hand, and train a detector to scale the analysis. Our results show that about one in seventeen skills (about 88,000 skills) contains a loosening directive. These directives most often loosen oversight through permission flags, and most of them (70.1%) apply unconditionally rather than only in specific contexts such as CI. Compared with skills that have the same amount of oversight language, skills that run shell code, install packages, or use sudo have 1.7-1.8 times the odds of containing a loosening directive, an association that holds across all our robustness checks, and they do not compensate with more tightening. Loosening spreads through a few upstream skills rather than through edits by their adopters: 2.4% of the skill families that carry loosening account for half of all copies of loosening-carrying skills, and 1.1% of distinct loosening units for half of all loosening occurrences. Open-source skill scanners catch at most 46% of loosening directives, with a precision below 0.4, while the LLM behind them, prompted with our codebook instead, catches 61% at a precision of 0.71.
tldr: A large-scale empirical study of 'oversight-loosening' directives embedded in 1.53 million AI agent skill files, quantifying their prevalence, mechanisms, and spread.
motivation: Agent skills are widely copied instruction packages, so a single permissive line can strip approval checkpoints from every agent that loads it — yet no prior work has characterized such directives.
method: The authors split 1.53M English skills from GitSkills into sentence/bullet/table-cell/code-line units, hand-label 2,097 units with a codebook covering polarity, mechanism and scope, and train a detector to scale the labeling; they also benchmark open-source scanners and an LLM using their codebook.
result: About 1 in 17 skills (~88,000) contains a loosening directive, 70.1% unconditional, concentrated in permission flags; skills running shell code, installing packages, or using sudo have 1.7–1.8× the odds of loosening without compensating tightening, and 2.4% of skill families account for half of all copies.
conclusion: Oversight-loosening spreads through a few upstream skills rather than adopter edits, existing scanners catch at most 46% of directives at precision below 0.4, while an LLM prompted with the codebook reaches 61% at precision 0.71.

title: Poisoned Skills: Propagating Jailbreaks Through Agent Markdown Files
authors: Murali Emani Kashyap R Manjusha
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37738v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern agent frameworks allow users to provide Markdown files containing system prompts, tool descriptions, and skill definitions (e.g., SKILL.md), which are incorporated into the agent's context during initialization. In this work, we investigate whether this configuration mechanism can also serve as an injection channel: can a jailbreak embedded in a Markdown skill file propagate through an agent and induce prohibited behavior? To answer this question, we construct a LangChain-based question-answering agent whose system prompt is assembled from a user-provided Markdown file. We embed a jailbreak combining persona manipulation with a GPTFUZZER-based attack and evaluate its effectiveness across seven contemporary open-weight models using 270 forbidden questions spanning nine harm categories. Under a benign system prompt, the models exhibit near-complete refusal behavior, with a mean attack success rate (ASR) of just 0.5%. In contrast, the injected skill file raises the mean ASR to 45%, reaching 68.9% for individual models. We further evaluate two payload obfuscation strategies: an invisible zero-width character-based stealth payload and a phonetic payload based on grapheme-to-phoneme transformations. Neither outperforms the plain-text injection; notably, the phonetic variant reduces mean ASR to 30%. These findings identify Markdown skill files as an underexplored attack surface for AI agents and suggest that vulnerability to configuration-based jailbreaks depends more strongly on the underlying model than on the specific payload obfuscation technique.
tldr: Markdown skill files used to configure LLM agents can serve as a jailbreak injection channel, raising mean attack success rates from 0.5% to 45% across seven open-weight models.
motivation: Agent frameworks ingest user-supplied Markdown files (system prompts, tool descriptions, SKILL.md) into the agent context, and the authors ask whether this configuration mechanism is itself an exploitable injection surface.
method: A LangChain-based QA agent is built whose system prompt is assembled from a user-provided Markdown file; a jailbreak combining persona manipulation with a GPTFUZZER-based attack is embedded and tested on 270 forbidden questions across nine harm categories, plus two obfuscation payloads (zero-width characters, phonetic G2P).
result: Benign prompts yield a mean ASR of 0.5%, while the injected skill file raises mean ASR to 45% (up to 68.9% for individual models); neither obfuscation strategy outperforms plain text, and the phonetic variant drops ASR to 30%.
conclusion: Markdown skill files are an underexplored attack surface for AI agents, and vulnerability depends more on the underlying model than on the payload obfuscation technique.

title: Agentic Backdoors Via Pretraining Poisoning
authors: Xinyan Hu, Pingbang Hu, Chloe Loughridge, Xuanli He, Nicholas Carlini, Matthew Jagielski, Javier Rando, Yiming Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37741v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models are pretrained on vast, uncurated corpora scraped from the public web. This creates a security risk from attackers who plant poisoned content in the pretraining data. We show for the first time that such poisoning can plant a remote code execution backdoor in an agent, causing it to execute attacker-chosen commands on the user's machine. To measure the threat end to end, we pretrain Qwen3 models from scratch at sizes 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B, and then post-train each into a CLI agent using a clean pipeline. Poisoning only 0.1% of the pretraining corpus with our new poison design implants the backdoor: the deployed agent executes the malicious command when the trigger is present while behaving normally on clean inputs. The attack success rate (ASR) increases with model scale, with the 4B model reaching roughly 92% ASR at a 0.1% poison rate and staying positive even when the poisoning rate drops to 0.0005%. Our code is available at [URL].
tldr: The paper demonstrates that poisoning 0.1% of a pretraining corpus can implant a remote-code-execution backdoor in a CLI agent built from Qwen3 models, with attack success rising with model scale.
motivation: LLMs are pretrained on uncurated web data, creating a risk that adversaries can plant poisoned content that survives post-training and manifests as dangerous agent behavior.
method: The authors pretrain Qwen3 models from scratch at 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B parameters on corpora containing a novel poison design at rates from 0.1% down to 0.0005%, then post-train each with a clean pipeline into a CLI agent and measure trigger-conditional command execution.
result: The backdoor is successfully implanted, with attack success rate scaling with model size — roughly 92% ASR at 0.1% poison for the 4B model, and still positive at 0.0005% poison rate — while clean-input behavior remains normal.
conclusion: Pretraining-data poisoning is a practical, scalable vector for agentic backdoors, implying that data provenance and pretraining-time defenses are needed for deployed agents.

title: Structured Security Explanations For Learning-Based Vulnerability Detection
authors: Fares Trad, Yizhou Chen, Hung Viet Pham, Zeyu Sun, Gias Uddin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37797v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Software vulnerability detection remains difficult because existing approaches rely on predefined analysis rules, learn vulnerability patterns implicitly from code and labels, or use large language models (LLMs) to make the final security judgment. It remains unclear whether structured descriptions of security-relevant program behavior can improve supervised detection. We present VulnLens, an explanation-augmented framework for binary C/C++ vulnerability detection that separates program-behavior analysis from the final decision. A label-blind LLM-based Explainer examines each function from seven fixed perspectives: data flow, memory access, object lifetime, arithmetic and type behavior, control flow, shared state, and external-resource access. Without receiving vulnerability labels or CWE information, it generates structured explanations. A supervised Detector combines source code and explanations through sequential cross-attention. We evaluate VulnLens on a PrimeVul-derived dataset covering ten CWE categories and test transfer to SecVulEval without retraining. On the 526-function PrimeVul test set, VulnLens achieves 75.5% accuracy and 77.2% F1, exceeding DeepSeek V4 Pro by 4.2 percentage points in accuracy and Gemini 2.5 Pro by 2.2 points in F1. Matched explanations improve F1 by 7.3 points over a separately trained code-only detector. On SecVulEval, VulnLens achieves 66.4% accuracy and 65.8% F1, outperforming DeepSeek V4 Pro by 7.6 points in accuracy and 20.0 points in F1, and Gemini 2.5 Pro by 16.6 points in accuracy and 7.8 points in F1.
tldr: VulnLens is an explanation-augmented framework that uses a label-blind LLM to produce structured program-behavior explanations, which a supervised cross-attention detector combines with source code to detect binary C/C++ vulnerabilities.
motivation: Existing vulnerability detectors rely on hand-crafted rules, implicit pattern learning, or LLM judgments that are opaque, so it is unclear whether structured security-relevant behavioral descriptions can improve supervised detection.
method: An LLM-based Explainer analyzes each function from seven fixed perspectives (data flow, memory access, object lifetime, arithmetic/type behavior, control flow, shared state, external-resource access) without labels or CWE information, and a Detector fuses code and explanations via sequential cross-attention.
result: On a 526-function PrimeVul-derived test set VulnLens reaches 75.5% accuracy and 77.2% F1, beating DeepSeek V4 Pro by 4.2 points in accuracy and Gemini 2.5 Pro by 2.2 points in F1, with matched explanations adding 7.3 F1 points over a code-only detector; it also transfers to SecVulEval (66.4% accuracy, 65.8% F1).
conclusion: Structured LLM-generated explanations of program behavior materially improve supervised vulnerability detection and generalize across datasets without retraining.

title: TensorBound: Characterizing Tensor Binding Failures In Ai Compiler And Runtime Stacks
authors: Wen Li (utah State University), Yongxi Sha (utah State University), Baihong Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37838v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI compiler and runtime stacks must preserve bindings between tensor values and their operations, storage, and execution state. These bindings can fail while the underlying objects remain present, with symptoms appearing in another layer. We present TensorBound, an empirical study of tensor binding failures in IREE and the XLA and PyTorch ecosystems. The study analyzes 264 reports and reconstructs 149 distinct repaired causes through source tracing and comparisons of pre-fix and repaired revisions. Each reconstruction connects the first invalid decision to its violated condition, physical effect, and repair. Missing eligibility checks, incorrect mappings or translations, and lost or omitted relations account for 69.1% of repaired causes. These patterns highlight the need to preserve binding facts and check the conditions for their use. The 101 first invalid decisions in compiler code identify candidate checking points before execution. Four archived IREE diagnostic attempts distinguish effect localization from source-based cause explanation. Together, these findings motivate transition-specific checks that preserve binding facts across representations and enforce the required conditions at consuming decisions.
tldr: TensorBound is an empirical study of tensor binding failures in AI compiler and runtime stacks (IREE, XLA, PyTorch), reconstructing root causes from 264 bug reports.
motivation: AI compiler and runtime stacks must preserve bindings between tensor values and their operations, storage, and execution state; these bindings can silently fail while objects remain present, producing symptoms in a different layer, so a systematic characterization is needed.
method: The authors analyze 264 reports and reconstruct 149 distinct repaired causes via source tracing and comparison of pre-fix and repaired revisions, linking each first invalid decision to its violated condition, physical effect, and repair.
result: Missing eligibility checks, incorrect mappings or translations, and lost/omitted relations account for 69.1% of repaired causes; 101 first invalid decisions in compiler code identify candidate checking points, and four archived IREE diagnostic attempts distinguish effect localization from source-based cause explanation.
conclusion: The findings motivate transition-specific checks that preserve binding facts across representations and enforce required conditions at consuming decisions.

title: Set An Exploit To Catch An Exploit: Compiling Public Proofs Of Concept Into Threat Hunting Rules
authors: Muhammad Shoaib, Alexander Suh, Joshua Andrew Tomiak, Wajih Ul Hassan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37872v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Public exploit code for a newly disclosed vulnerability usually appears before any published rule that detects its exploitation. Of the 45 CVEs we evaluate, 37 ever received a Sigma, Elastic or Splunk rule; in 33 the exploit came first, by a median of 22 days. Analysts still write every rule by hand. We present Encore, which compiles a public Python proof-of-concept exploit (PoC) into CVE-specific hunting rules over a web service's existing logs, without running it. Encore rests on the PoC Behavior Alignment Principle: a PoC performs the exploit, so its code already provides a rule's HTTP requests, payloads and host operations. That is hard to act on: a PoC is written against libraries and runs on the attacker's machine, while the target's web-server, proxy and host logs record only what arrived and what it did. Encore closes the gap with a map from library calls to the operations they cause, built once per library, keeping only the operations visible on the target. For 12 of the 45, Encore's rule states the exploit's own payload fragment or host operation, which is evidence of the exploit itself, and not of traffic to its endpoint. On matched controls it separates that exploit from the same request with a harmless value, and it raises no alerts across 27,081 legitimate and crawl requests. We never compile the exploit that produced the logs. Most are Splunk's public attack data, recorded by a third party. Without reading a single log, Encore's rules find 43 of the 45. Splunk's log-tested rules cover 30 of the 45, and Encore finds 28 of those, plus all 10 CVEs without an ESCU rule. Where Splunk's rules alert on 20 wrong CVE pairs, Encore's alert on only 2. Hunting can start as soon as a PoC is public, and rules can raise an alert when it provides a payload or host operation.
tldr: Encore compiles public Python proof-of-concept exploits into CVE-specific threat-hunting rules for web-service logs without executing the exploit.
motivation: Public PoCs typically appear well before detection rules (33 of 45 CVEs, median 22 days earlier), and analysts still hand-write every rule, leaving a detection gap.
method: Encore builds a per-library map from library calls to the host/network operations they produce, filters to operations observable in target web-server, proxy and host logs, and derives HTTP requests, payloads and host operations from the static PoC code.
result: Rules find 43 of 45 CVEs without reading any logs, versus 30 for Splunk's log-tested rules; for 12 CVEs the rules cite the exploit's own payload fragment or host operation, alert on only 2 wrong CVE pairs (vs 20 for Splunk), and raise no alerts on 27,081 legitimate and crawl requests.
conclusion: Automated PoC-to-rule compilation enables threat hunting to begin as soon as an exploit is public and yields more precise, exploit-specific detections than vendor rule sets.

title: Scan Before You Install: Detecting And Mitigating Local And Composite Vulnerabilities In Skills
authors: Parth A. Gandhi, Avital Aviv, Prasanna N. Wudali, Yuval Elovici, Asaf Shabtai
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37901v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An agent skill packages natural-language instructions, scripts, and reference files that an LLM-based agent loads for a task. Skills may access the file system, shell, and network under user-authorized permissions; weaknesses can lead to unsafe execution. Existing scanners primarily target malicious skills, not unintended vulnerabilities in public repositories, and analyze skills in isolation, overlooking multi-skill interactions. To address these gaps, we developed a six-module scanner: Content Extraction, Local Analysis, Composite Analysis, Validation, Reporting, and Mitigation. Local Analysis detects unintended vulnerabilities in benign skills. On a 556-case leaderboard subset of SkillTrustBench, it achieved 95.90% recall with a 4.22% false positive rate; on a balanced sample of 1,000 MalSkillBench skills, its F1 was 0.947, outperforming Cisco's Skill Scanner, NVIDIA's SkillSpector, AgentSkillsScanner, and SkillSieve. In 1,587 skills from the 75 most-starred GitHub repositories, three analysts confirmed 53 of 59 findings (89.8% precision) across 23 repositories. We developed proof-of-concept (PoC) attacks for each vulnerability, disclosed 10 medium- and high-severity cases to maintainers, and tested mitigations on the remaining cases. Composite Analysis models dependencies among skills through shared resources, invocations, and instruction-mediated interactions. On SCR-Bench, its F1 score was 0.991 (98.7% precision, 99.6% recall), versus 0.816-0.858 for three SkillsGuard configurations released with CompoSkill. It identified two composite findings on GitHub, validated by PoC attacks. The Mitigation module recommends skill substitution, patches, and configuration changes. For 47 of 55 GitHub findings, mitigations prevented PoC attacks in all trials while preserving tested legitimate functionality.
tldr: A six-module scanner that detects and mitigates unintended local and composite security vulnerabilities in LLM agent skills before installation.
motivation: Existing skill scanners focus on deliberately malicious skills and analyze skills in isolation, missing unintended vulnerabilities in benign public skills and risks arising from multi-skill interactions.
method: The authors build a pipeline of Content Extraction, Local Analysis, Composite Analysis, Validation, Reporting, and Mitigation modules, with composite analysis modeling dependencies via shared resources, invocations, and instruction-mediated interactions; they evaluate on SkillTrustBench, MalSkillBench, SCR-Bench, and 1,587 GitHub skills.
result: The scanner reaches 95.90% recall at 4.22% false positive rate, F1 0.947 on MalSkillBench, and F1 0.991 on SCR-Bench, outperforming several commercial and academic baselines; analysts confirmed 53 of 59 GitHub findings and mitigations blocked PoC attacks in 47 of 55 cases.
conclusion: Systematic, composition-aware scanning plus mitigation substantially improves the security posture of agent-skill ecosystems, though the work lies entirely outside quantum information science.

title: Enumeration Complexity Of Permutation Classes
authors: Mohamed Elsheikh Manuel Bodirsky
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37940v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study classes of permutations that are defined by avoidance of forbidden patterns. For each fixed finite set [MATH] of forbidden patterns, we study the : given an integer [MATH], output all [MATH]-avoiding permutations of length [MATH]. Avoider enumeration is output-polynomial for every fixed [MATH]. However, our main notion of efficiency is polynomial delay. We use the insert-maximum tree as a search tree, in which permutations are built by repeatedly inserting a new maximum while preserving pattern avoidance. This leads to the , which asks if a given permutation has an avoiding descendant at a specified depth. An algorithm for this problem can prune branches that cannot reach the target length. Hence, if this problem is in P, we obtain polynomial-delay enumeration. To investigate this problem, we introduce and study , the maximal finite subtrees of the insert-maximum tree. For fixed [MATH], if there is a polynomial [MATH] such that every pocket rooted at [MATH] has at most [MATH] nodes, then the extension problem is solvable in polynomial time and enumeration has polynomial delay. In particular, a bound on pocket depth depending only on [MATH] suffices. We prove such a bound if the class is well-quasi-ordered, has a regular insertion encoding, or if [MATH] omits one of the three maximum-position types: leftmost, interior, or rightmost. We also prove that extension is in NP for every fixed [MATH], even with binary-encoded target depth. On the negative side, we construct a fixed set of [MATH] forbidden patterns for which extension is NP-complete. Consequently, enumerating valid extensions from a given starting permutation cannot have polynomial delay unless P=NP. This also answers a question of Hanika by showing that the forbidden permutation constraint satisfaction problem can be NP-complete for a fixed forbidden set.
tldr: The paper studies the complexity of enumerating permutations avoiding a fixed finite set of forbidden patterns, introducing the insert-maximum tree, the extension problem, and 'pockets' to characterize when polynomial-delay enumeration is possible.
motivation: Enumeration of pattern-avoiding permutation classes is typically only output-polynomial; the authors want a finer notion of efficiency (polynomial delay) and a structural criterion that guarantees it.
method: They build permutations by repeatedly inserting a new maximum into an avoiding permutation, forming a search tree, and analyze maximal finite subtrees ('pockets'); pruning via a tractable extension problem yields polynomial delay, with bounds proved for well-quasi-ordered classes, regular insertion encodings, and classes omitting a maximum-position type.
result: Polynomial delay is obtained under pocket-size bounds; the extension problem is shown to be in NP for every fixed forbidden set, and a fixed forbidden set is constructed for which extension is NP-complete, ruling out polynomial delay unless P=NP and answering a question of Hanika.
conclusion: The work maps the algorithmic boundary between tractable and intractable enumeration for pattern-avoiding permutation classes, linking pocket structure to the complexity of the forbidden-pattern CSP.

title: AI-Generated Non-Consensual Intimate Imagery Is Configured, Not Built: How General-Purpose Ai Technology Enables Sexual Violence
authors: Julia B. Kieserman, Ashley Phoebe Ishoel, Damon Mccoy, Elissa M. Redmiles, Lucy Qin, Jaron Mink
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37949v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery (AIG-NCII) is an increasingly prevalent form of online abuse, distinguished from AI-generated sexual content (AIG-SC) by the sexualized depiction of a real person's identity without their consent. To understand how offenders may benefit from the tools and resources shared across the broader AIG-SC community, we analyzed 139 R+ guides on CivitAI, a popular platform known to host a disproportionate amount of AIG-SC. We find that AIG-SC guides discuss how to create content generation workflows composed of sexual and identity concepts, the building blocks of AIG-NCII, including one guide that explicitly outlines an AIG-NCII workflow. We identify that ultimately AIG-NCII is enabled by configuration rather than a distinct set of technical tools. We map AIG-NCII threat models across basic and advanced AIG-SC workflows to demonstrate how multiple dual-use technical components can compose NCII outputs in an environment with little to no discussion of ethical implications or responsible use. We conclude by noting that, as most workflows rely on open-weight models, existing technical defenses against AIG-NCII are limited. However, our findings offer a starting point for evaluation of AI-based models and products against realistic attacker behavior required by new EU regulation and suggest that efforts to develop safeguards at the model- and product-levels should focus on generation of identity content.
tldr: An empirical study of 139 CivitAI guides showing that AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery (AIG-NCII) emerges from reconfiguring dual-use components of mainstream AI-generated sexual content workflows rather than from purpose-built tools.
motivation: AIG-NCII is a growing form of online abuse, and understanding how offenders leverage the broader AIG-SC community's shared tools and resources is needed to inform defenses and emerging regulation.
method: The authors qualitatively analyzed 139 publicly posted guides on CivitAI, identifying workflow components (sexual and identity concepts), an explicit AIG-NCII workflow, and mapping threat models onto basic and advanced AIG-SC pipelines.
result: AIG-NCII is enabled by configuration of general-purpose, mostly open-weight model components rather than distinct technical tools, with little ethical or responsible-use discussion in these communities and limited efficacy of existing technical defenses.
conclusion: Model- and product-level safeguards should focus on the generation of identity content, and the findings provide a basis for evaluating AI systems against realistic attacker behavior as required by new EU regulation.

title: Progressive-Observation Physical-Layer Fingerprinting For Efficient Open-Set Ethernet Authentication
authors: Chenming Zhang, Jiaxiang Geng, Aiqun Hu, Azzedine Boukerche, Peng Sun
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38074v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physical-layer fingerprinting (PLF) has emerged as a promising authentication approach for Internet of Things devices. However, most PLF systems acquire and process a fixed-length waveform for every authentication query, burdening resource-constrained edge nodes. To address this issue, we propose a progressive-observation PLF method that adapts the waveform length to each query. Specifically, a lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) first rejects clearly unknown devices from a short observation. Spectral matching then accepts clearly registered devices from a slightly longer observation. Only ambiguous queries proceed to the same matching on the full-length waveform, reducing both data acquisition and computation. Because fingerprints drift across days, we also design an adaptive calibration algorithm to avoid retraining the CNN. The algorithm realigns the features and decision thresholds using a few current-day references from registered devices. We evaluate the method with 100BASE-TX Ethernet devices of two controller types on held-out days. Compared with fixed-length processing, it keeps the false rejection and false acceptance rates equal or lower for both controller types on both days. It also reduces the waveform data per query by 75.1% and the CPU processing time on a Raspberry Pi 5 by 73.7% on average. With the same monitoring bandwidth, an edge node can therefore serve about four times as many authentication queries.
tldr: The paper proposes a progressive-observation physical-layer fingerprinting method for efficient open-set Ethernet device authentication using adaptive waveform-length selection and lightweight CNN-based rejection.
motivation: Most physical-layer fingerprinting systems acquire fixed-length waveforms for every authentication query, which burdens resource-constrained edge nodes and is inefficient when fingerprints drift across days.
method: A lightweight CNN rejects clearly unknown devices from short observations, spectral matching accepts clearly registered devices from slightly longer observations, and ambiguous cases use full-length waveforms; an adaptive calibration algorithm realigns features and thresholds using current-day references.
result: On 100BASE-TX Ethernet devices across two controller types and held-out days, the method maintained equal or lower false rejection and false acceptance rates while reducing waveform data per query by 75.1% and Raspberry Pi 5 CPU processing time by 73.7% on average.
conclusion: Progressive-observation physical-layer fingerprinting can substantially improve the efficiency of edge-node authentication without degrading accuracy, enabling roughly four times as many queries at the same monitoring bandwidth.

title: Toward Understanding The Value Of Anarchy: Empirical Studies On Best Response Dynamics
authors: Philip N Brown Will Wesley
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38081v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study experimental results of best response dynamics (BRD) in randomly generated weighted action networked multiagent optimization problems where agent utility is the agent's marginal contribution to the system objective. We compare those results to the Price of Anarchy (PoA) established in the literature for marginal contribution and to the expected value of randomly choosing from the available equilibria. PoA is used as a metric to describe the performance of various solutions to multiagent optimization problems, but the utility of this metric may be overrated if such worst-case instances are rare in practice. Our study provides evidence to support this doubt, showing that simple best response mechanics tend to out perform the PoA prediction and a uniform random equilibrium selection, even when agents are unable to observe all other agents' actions. In the process of seeking a more ideal metric, we discover that BRD appears to perform better than average. That is, when multiple equilibria exist, BRD appears to be biased toward the higher-performance ones. This evidence also demonstrates that further investigation into a more robust metric for multiagent optimization solutions is warranted and pushes us to understand whether the bias toward better equilibria hold in more general cases.
tldr: An empirical study of best response dynamics in weighted-action networked multiagent optimization problems, comparing observed performance against the Price of Anarchy and random equilibrium selection.
motivation: Price of Anarchy is widely used to characterize worst-case performance of multiagent optimization solutions, but this metric may be misleading if such worst-case instances are rare in practice.
method: The authors run experiments on randomly generated weighted action networked multiagent optimization problems with marginal-contribution utilities, simulating best response dynamics under both full and partial observability of other agents' actions, and compare outcomes to PoA bounds and uniform random equilibrium selection.
result: Best response dynamics tends to outperform the Price of Anarchy prediction and random equilibrium selection, and appears biased toward higher-performance equilibria when multiple equilibria exist.
conclusion: The findings cast doubt on the practical utility of PoA as a worst-case metric and motivate the search for a more robust performance metric for multiagent optimization, with open questions about generality.

title: Is It My Preference? Role Grounding Attack Against Agent's Memory Via Social Interaction
authors: Haoran Bu, Yiting Shen, Litian Zhang, Ruihan Hu, Xi Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38209v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based agents now share experiences on social platforms and remember new preferences to enhance their performance. However, existing memory systems contain a vulnerability in role-to-principal attribution that attackers can exploit. We identify Role Grounding Misattribution, in which an attacker-designed interaction causes the victim agent to incorrectly record a preference from the attacker as a preference of the victim's user. Specifically, we are the first to formalize Role Grounding Attack (RGA), an attack model that exploits this vulnerability through nested conversation structures. In the memory formation stage, an experience-sharing post quoting a conversation between the attacker agent and its user is published, which explicitly identifies its publisher. The inner conversation expresses preferences from the user of the attacker agent. When the victim agent remembers preferences from this nested structure, its memory loses the context binding and grounds the attacker's preference to the victim's user instead. In the memory retrieval stage, the misattributed preference persists and influences the victim agent's decisions when it encounters relevant scenarios. We instantiate RGA as tool selection manipulation and privacy leakage. Tool selection manipulation causes a tool-call preference to be misattributed to the victim's user, steering the victim toward an attacker-controlled tool. Privacy leakage extends this by misattributing both a tool-call preference and a task-requirement preference to the victim's user. The victim selects the attacker's tool, then includes sensitive information in tool arguments to satisfy the task requirement. We evaluate RGA across five mainstream memory systems and six language models. Tool manipulation and privacy leakage both achieve high attack success rates. These results call for stronger role grounding.
tldr: The paper formalizes a Role Grounding Attack in which adversarial social-media interactions cause LLM agents to misattribute an attacker's preferences to the victim's user in memory, enabling tool-selection manipulation and privacy leakage.
motivation: LLM agents that remember user preferences from social platforms lack robust role-to-principal attribution, creating an exploitable security vulnerability in memory formation and retrieval.
method: The authors construct nested conversation structures (an experience-sharing post quoting an attacker-user dialogue) that strip context binding during memory formation, then demonstrate persistence of misattributed preferences in retrieval across five memory systems and six language models.
result: Both tool-selection manipulation and privacy-leakage instantiations achieve high attack success rates across all evaluated memory systems and models.
conclusion: Memory systems require stronger role grounding, and the authors call for defenses against nested-structure preference injection in agent memory.

title: Manifest-Assisted Retrieval In Artificial Intelligence Search: Evidence Gaps And A Security Evaluation
authors: Gangzhen Qian, Kainan Zhou, Chuhong Xu, Hang Xiao, Zhi Jing, Rong Bao, Lu Yi, Zhaoyi Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38361v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The external sources retained in our non-systematic audit did not isolate the incremental security or utility effect of consuming /llms.txt while ordinary retrieval remained fixed. The initial audit covered 39 sources through August 16, 2026, with later targeted updates through October 14. A purposive 15-tool study observed no automatic requests in 45 trials at one endpoint; a non-probability log study found that 97% of domains with detected files received no recorded requests in May 2026. We separate publication, fetch, model use, and action; define five operational threat paths and paired security-utility estimands; and exercise deterministic pre-model controls with 30 author-defined parser fixtures. We also execute a reduced pilot: 24 tasks across eight sites, five conditions, and 120 real model responses, with ordinary evidence held fixed. Frozen automatic scoring identifies attacker-target adoption in [MATH] raw adversarial responses, with one further response unresolved; the adversarial URLs-only condition has no known adoptions and one unresolved response. The pilot measures output changes conditional on supplied evidence, without live retrieval or external actions. Together, the framework and pilot distinguish manifest-content effects from publication, discovery, and downstream execution, while leaving full retrieval and agent evaluation open.
tldr: An audit and pilot study examining whether /llms.txt manifests influence AI search systems, separating publication, fetch, model use, and action, and probing associated security threat paths.
motivation: Practitioners increasingly publish /llms.txt manifests assuming they shape AI retrieval behavior, but evidence that such files are actually requested or used, and the security risks they introduce, is largely anecdotal.
method: A non-systematic audit of 39 sources, a purposive 15-tool study (45 trials at one endpoint), a non-probability log study, plus a reduced pilot of 24 tasks across eight sites, five conditions and 120 real model responses with ordinary evidence held fixed and deterministic pre-model controls with 30 author-defined parser fixtures.
result: No automatic manifest requests were observed in 45 trials at one endpoint, and 97% of domains with detected files received no recorded requests; frozen automatic scoring found attacker-target adoption in some raw adversarial responses while the URLs-only adversarial condition had no known adoptions.
conclusion: The framework and pilot distinguish manifest-content effects from publication, discovery, and downstream execution, but full retrieval and agent-level evaluation remain open.

title: DecisionUnlearn-Bench: Unlearning Probabilistic Decisions Under Changing Schemas
authors: Wei Yang Bryan Lim Tiantong Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38431v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine unlearning aims to reproduce the behavior of a model trained without designated data. For probabilistic decision models, this target also depends on the candidate options supplied at inference. We introduce DecisionUnlearn-Bench, an empirical framework that compares full, unlearned, and retain-only models across deletion granularities, label renderings, and candidate sets. Across 20 eligible model configurations on the BANKING77 dataset, full-to-oracle displacement increases consistently from example to association to class deletion. Replacing semantic option labels with opaque codes nearly eliminates the retrained oracle's recognition of deleted classes, even with successful acquisition of the full model, whereas changing the candidate set alters both the oracle and the measured unlearning progress. SimNPO satisfies the screening criterion in 19 of 20 configurations, but its gains vary substantially across seeds and deletion targets. Development tuning on the CLINC150 dataset does not establish a positive pooled effect across 48 intents. At approximately matched suppression, methods can differ markedly in oracle fidelity. Recovery experiments further distinguish initial forgetting from subsequent adaptation and show conclusions that depend on both architecture and metric. These results show that evaluating decision-model unlearning relative to a schema-specific retraining target, with separate reporting of effect size, utility, robustness, and recoverability.
tldr: DecisionUnlearn-Bench is an empirical benchmark for evaluating machine unlearning in probabilistic decision models when the candidate option set and label schema change at inference time.
motivation: Machine unlearning is typically evaluated against a retrained model, but for decision models the retraining target itself depends on the inference-time candidate options and label rendering, so existing evaluations may misstate unlearning progress.
method: The authors build a framework comparing full, unlearned, and retain-only models across deletion granularities (example, association, class), semantic versus opaque label renderings, and varying candidate sets, using 20 model configurations on BANKING77 and development tuning on CLINC150.
result: Full-to-oracle displacement grows from example to association to class deletion; opaque codes nearly eliminate the retrained oracle's recognition of deleted classes; changing candidate sets shifts both oracle and measured progress; SimNPO passes screening in 19/20 configurations but with high seed variance.
conclusion: Unlearning of decision models should be evaluated against schema-specific retraining targets with separate reporting of effect size, utility, robustness, and recoverability, since conclusions depend strongly on architecture and metric.

title: WebMaze: Defending Against LLM-Powered Web Scanners With Functionality-Coupled Deception
authors: Pengfei Zeng, Changhua Luo, Penghui Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38524v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled more effective vulnerability scanning of web applications. However, these capabilities also make it significantly easier for attackers to automate cyberattacks on the web. In this work, we investigate how to divert malicious LLM-based web scanning, with preservation of genuine functionality as a deployment requirement. We systematically study six LLM-based scanners and summarize how they gather information and iteratively select actions based on observations. Guided by the study, we then present WebMaze, a defense that preserves genuine application functionality while diverting LLM-based scanners to a generated decoy world. WebMaze embeds functionality-coupled traps in genuine pages and constructs view-tailored interactive decoy worlds from the application's existing views. The traps blend into genuine components and expose entry points to decoy worlds that sustain exploration through connected pages and interactions without changing genuine functionality. Across 12 web applications and three LLM-based scanners under the default no-disclosure setting, decoy pages account for an average of 93.0% of the distinct pages requested per run. This demonstrates that WebMaze effectively diverts scanners away from genuine application pages and into the generated decoy worlds. Even when explicitly informed about the decoy mechanism and instructed to avoid decoy pages, scanners continue to explore predominantly decoy pages.
tldr: WebMaze is a web-defense system that diverts LLM-powered vulnerability scanners into generated decoy page worlds while preserving the genuine functionality of the application.
motivation: LLMs make automated web vulnerability scanning cheaper and more effective, so defenders need mechanisms that misdirect such scanners without breaking legitimate application behavior.
method: The authors characterize six LLM-based scanners' information-gathering and action-selection loops, then embed functionality-coupled traps in genuine pages that lead into view-tailored, interconnected decoy worlds built from the application's existing views.
result: Across 12 web applications and three LLM-based scanners, decoy pages made up an average of 93.0% of distinct pages requested per run, and scanners kept exploring decoys even when told about the mechanism and instructed to avoid them.
conclusion: Coupling deception traps to genuine functionality can effectively divert LLM-driven web scanning at deployment time without degrading the real application.

title: Counterfactual Assessment Of Social Media Interventions By Separating Exposure From Engagement
authors: Tommaso Pisani, Pietro Gravino, Giulio Prevedello
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37864v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Social media interventions are usually evaluated in individual-level experiments, which are costly to scale and often miss collective effects. We propose the Exposure--Engagement model, whose parameters separately control what social media users are exposed to (recommendation) and how they engage (behaviour). After fitting it to the Italian Twitter debate (2018--2022), we validate it at individual and collective levels. We simulate behavioural interventions (prebunking and accuracy prompts), calibrated on effect sizes, and a recommender-system intervention (chronological feed), comparing effects on engagement, attention diversity, and segregation. All three reduce engagement. Behavioural interventions slightly reduce diversity, leaving segregation unchanged, whereas the chronological feed increases diversity and reduces segregation. For these interventions, changing recommendation does more for the debate's structure than changing behaviour. We design a recommender-system intervention that increases engagement and diversity while reducing segregation, although with about a tenth of the chronological feed's gains, showing the framework's potential for pro-social intervention design.
tldr: The authors propose an Exposure–Engagement model of social media dynamics, fit it to the Italian Twitter debate (2018–2022), and use it to compare behavioural interventions with recommender-system changes on engagement, attention diversity, and segregation.
motivation: Individual-level experiments for evaluating social media interventions are costly to scale and typically miss collective, system-level effects, so a model-based counterfactual framework is needed.
method: An Exposure–Engagement model separates recommendation-driven exposure from behavioural engagement; it is calibrated on the Italian Twitter debate, validated at individual and collective levels, and then used to simulate prebunking, accuracy prompts, and a chronological-feed recommender intervention.
result: All three interventions reduce engagement; behavioural interventions slightly reduce attention diversity and leave segregation unchanged, while the chronological feed increases diversity and reduces segregation, with a designed pro-social recommender achieving similar but roughly tenfold smaller gains.
conclusion: Changing recommendation structure affects the debate's organisation more than changing individual behaviour, and the framework offers a tool for designing pro-social interventions.

title: Solitary Movement Style Predicts Collective Foraging While Whom To Follow Emerges Only In Company
authors: Hiroshi Higashi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37978v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How far can behaviour inside a group, and the group's performance, be predicted from members measured while alone? We tested this on three public datasets of human collective foraging (621, 128 and 1,133 participants). A low-dimensional individual representation estimated from private-phase movement was mapped onto behaviour inside the group through a mapping learned on other participants. Private information processing was stable between the two halves of a session (split-half reliability, the correlation between the halves, 0.60--0.83) and predicted behaviour inside the group with correlations of 0.30--0.66. Selective social learning, following those who have succeeded or stopped, showed stable individual differences inside the group (reliability 0.45--0.59) yet was not predicted at all from the same person's private behaviour. Group performance was predicted with a correlation of 0.55 in all three datasets by simulations never fitted to group outcomes or by the mean of individually measured performance, a prediction carried by mobility and individual performance rather than by social weights. We found no credible evidence for an effect of how members were combined (equivalence bound 0.06). Whom to follow thus emerges only in company, which delimits what solitary measurements can predict and compose.
tldr: Using three large human collective-foraging datasets, the authors show that individual movement styles measured alone predict in-group behaviour and group performance, but social learning strategies (whom to follow) emerge only in group settings.
motivation: The paper asks how much of group behaviour and collective performance can be predicted from measurements of individuals in isolation, a question about the compositional limits of solitary behavioural measurements.
method: A low-dimensional individual representation is estimated from private-phase movement data and mapped onto in-group behaviour via a mapping learned on other participants; split-half reliability and simulation-based predictions of group performance are evaluated across 621, 128 and 1,133 participants.
result: Private information processing was stable (split-half reliability 0.60–0.83) and predicted in-group behaviour with correlations 0.30–0.66, and group performance was predicted at r=0.55 in all datasets, but selective social learning showed stable individual differences (reliability 0.45–0.59) that were entirely unpredicted by solitary behaviour.
conclusion: Whom-to-follow strategies emerge only in company, delimiting what solitary measurements can predict and compose into collective outcomes.

title: The Interference-Conjugate Transform: The Tightest Interference-Linear Surrogate For Power Control, Scheduling And Beamforming In Wireless Networks
authors: Ahmad Khan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37794v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Closed-form fractional programming (FP), weighted MMSE (WMMSE), and the 2026 surrogate-enhanced methods SEFP and XMMSE all maximize the weighted sum rate by iteratively maximizing a surrogate linear in the interference power. We show that this family admits a unique best member: the interference-conjugate transform (ICT), which replaces each rate term [MATH] by [MATH], where [MATH] is the closed-form partial convex conjugate of the rate in the interference variable and the optimal multiplier is the interference price [MATH]. We prove that, for any fixed price, [MATH] is the pointwise largest own-signal function compatible with a valid interference-linear lower bound, and that tightness at an anchor forces the price. Hence all four benchmark surrogates, which share this price and differ only in their own-signal term, are dominated pointwise by ICT. At SINR [MATH], the benchmarks' own-signal curvature exceeds the true curvature by factors behaving as [MATH] (FP/WMMSE) and [MATH] (SEFP/XMMSE), against [MATH] for ICT, and this ordering carries over to the certified ascent per iteration and the asymptotic linear convergence rate. ICT yields closed-form updates at the benchmarks' per-iteration cost for single-antenna power control, uplink joint scheduling and power control, and multi-cell MISO beamforming, and the first solver-free algorithm for sum-least-[MATH]th-percentile rate maximization, via a [MATH]-dimensional convex dual with closed-form gradient and Hessian and a certified duality gap. In uplink scheduling, ICT improves proportional-fairness utility over FP by +7.03 and over SEFP by +3.35 (60/60 drops) using 18.7 iterations per slot vs. 49.7 and 38.0; in MISO beamforming with [MATH], it reaches 99.9% of its final value in a median of 9 iterations vs. 16 (XMMSE) and 1160 (FP/WMMSE).
tldr: The paper introduces the interference-conjugate transform, a surrogate-based optimization method for power control, scheduling, and beamforming in wireless networks.
motivation: Existing interference-linear surrogates such as fractional programming and WMMSE are widely used but not provably optimal among their family; the paper seeks the tightest such surrogate.
method: It derives a closed-form partial convex conjugate of the rate with respect to interference, proves pointwise dominance over benchmark surrogates, and develops closed-form updates and a solver-free algorithm for sum-percentile rate maximization.
result: The proposed transform yields tighter curvature, faster certified ascent, and improved practical performance in uplink scheduling and MISO beamforming compared with FP, WMMSE, SEFP, and XMMSE.
conclusion: The interference-conjugate transform provides a theoretically optimal and computationally efficient surrogate for interference-limited wireless network optimization.

title: Trajectory-Planning Attitude Control System For Satellites With Magnetic Attitude Control And One Reaction Wheel
authors: Patrick Mckeen, Alex Meredith, Kerri Cahoy
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38029v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Selecting attitude actuators for spacecraft in low earth orbit (LEO) often involves a trade between reaction wheels and magnetorquers. Reaction wheels generally have higher size, weight and power as well as cost, compared with magnetorquers, but have performance advantages. We consider a hybrid system relying on a single reaction wheel and three magnetorquers, using a trajectory planning control method that focuses on meeting pointing goals and minimizing the need to desaturate the reaction wheel. The use of planning allows for intelligent use of the reaction wheel and accommodates time-changing goals and orbit-varying magnetic fields. Preliminary results show trajectories with fractional-degree-accuracy, as well as management of reaction wheel momentum and avoidance of stiction. We also compare to a magnetorquer-only planning-based control system and show better convergence and faster slews.
tldr: The paper presents a trajectory-planning-based attitude control system for LEO satellites combining a single reaction wheel with three magnetorquers to meet pointing goals while managing wheel momentum.
motivation: Spacecraft actuator selection typically trades the performance of reaction wheels against the lower size, weight, power and cost of magnetorquers, motivating hybrid architectures that exploit both.
method: The authors formulate a trajectory-planning control approach that plans attitude trajectories accommodating time-varying pointing goals and orbit-dependent magnetic fields, with explicit consideration of reaction-wheel momentum management and stiction avoidance; they compare it to a magnetorquer-only planner.
result: Preliminary simulations show fractional-degree pointing accuracy, effective reaction-wheel momentum management, avoidance of stiction, and better convergence and faster slews than the magnetorquer-only baseline.
conclusion: Hybrid single-wheel plus magnetorquer systems with planning-based control are a viable, cost-effective option for LEO pointing missions, though results remain preliminary and simulation-based.

title: Convergence Analysis Of An Augmented Dual-mixed Fnite Element Method With Skew-symmetric Nitsche Stabilization For The Generalized Oseen Equations With Mixed Boundary Conditions
authors: Cristian C\'arcamo, Abner Haguit Poza, Ramiro James Rebolledo
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38032v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we propose and analyze a new skew-symmetric Nitsche-augmented mixed scheme for the generalized Oseen equations with non-solenoidal convective fields, subject to mixed boundary conditions. The scheme is based on a continuous pseudostress-velocity augmented dual-mixed finite element formulation, in which the Dirichlet datum is imposed naturally, whereas the prescribed normal trace of the pseudostress is incorporated into the [MATH] stress space. We establish the well-posedness of the continuous formulation by means of a classical lifting argument and its corresponding homogeneous problem. The essential boundary condition is then weakly enforced in the discrete scheme through suitable stabilizing Nitsche terms. We establish the existence and uniqueness of the solution to the discrete scheme, allowing the use of general conforming approximation spaces for both the pseudostress and the velocity. Moreover, in the case of homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions and general Neumann data, we establish the stability of the Nitsche scheme. Under mild regularity assumptions on the exact solution, we prove optimal convergence rates in an energy norm. Finally, numerical experiments in two and three dimensions confirm the theoretical convergence rates and assess the performance of the proposed scheme for non-solenoidal convective fields and solutions exhibiting boundary layers.
tldr: The paper proposes and analyzes a skew-symmetric Nitsche-augmented dual-mixed finite element method for generalized Oseen equations with mixed boundary conditions.
motivation: The authors aim to develop a stable mixed finite element scheme that handles non-solenoidal convective fields and mixed boundary conditions while allowing natural imposition of the Dirichlet datum.
method: A continuous pseudostress-velocity augmented dual-mixed formulation is introduced, with essential boundary conditions weakly enforced via skew-symmetric Nitsche stabilization; well-posedness and convergence are analyzed theoretically and tested numerically.
result: The scheme is shown to be well-posed, stable under homogeneous Dirichlet conditions, and optimally convergent in an energy norm under mild regularity assumptions, with numerical experiments confirming the theoretical rates in two and three dimensions.
conclusion: The proposed Nitsche-augmented mixed finite element method provides a robust and convergent approach for generalized Oseen equations with mixed boundary conditions and non-solenoidal convective fields.

title: The Minimax Complexity Of Federated Optimization Under Interpolation: The Role Of Oracle Models
authors: Kirill Novoselov, Yuriy Dorn, Darina Dvinskikh, Alexander Gasnikov
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38354v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the minimax complexity of smooth convex stochastic optimization with intermittent communication: [MATH] workers run for [MATH] rounds, and between consecutive communication rounds each worker makes [MATH] sequential stochastic gradient queries. We focus on the interpolation regime, in which all sample losses share a common minimizer, so that the gradient noise vanishes at the solution. Let [MATH] be the smoothness of the objective, [MATH] the smoothness of the sample losses, and [MATH] the distance from the initial point to a minimizer. We consider three oracle models that provide increasing information: an unbiased stochastic gradient oracle [MATH] satisfying [MATH], gradients of the sample losses at fresh samples, and repeated gradient queries to stored samples. Up to logarithmic factors, all our results are described by two rates: \[ R^2\min\left\{L,\;{KN},\; {N^2}+{mKN}\right\} \qquad\qquad R^2\min\left\{L,\; }{N^2}+{mKN}\right\}, \] Under the weak growth condition, the first rate is the minimax rate, attained by the best of three simple baselines, as in the classical bounded-variance setting. With repeated access to samples, the second rate becomes the minimax rate for general convex objectives. For general convex objectives with fresh sample gradients, the minimax rate lies between the two rates. Our lower bounds apply to arbitrary randomized intermittent-communication algorithms.
tldr: This paper establishes minimax lower and upper bounds for smooth convex stochastic optimization in an intermittent-communication (federated) setting under the interpolation regime, across three oracle models of increasing information.
motivation: Federated and intermittently-communicating optimization is typically analyzed under bounded gradient variance; the interpolation regime, where noise vanishes at the optimum, admits much faster rates but lacks a complete minimax characterization across realistic oracle models.
method: The authors derive matching upper and lower bounds (up to logarithmic factors) for arbitrary randomized intermittent-communication algorithms, comparing an unbiased stochastic gradient oracle, fresh-sample gradients, and repeated queries to stored samples.
result: Two rate expressions characterize the complexity: under a weak growth condition the first rate is minimax and achieved by the best of three simple baselines, while with repeated sample access the second faster rate is minimax for general convex objectives, and the fresh-sample case lies in between.
conclusion: Oracle access model fundamentally determines achievable complexity in federated interpolation-regime optimization, with repeated sample access enabling strictly better rates than fresh-sample or noisy-gradient oracles.

title: Sparsebleed: Bypassing Attribute-Inference Defenses Via Sparsity Optimizations
authors: Darsh Asher, Farshad Dizani, Joshua Kalyanapu, Ro Cammarota, Aydin Aysu, Samira Mirbagher Ajorpaz
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38110v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are widely deployed in safety- and privacy-critical domains such as healthcare and finance, where models are trained on confidential data. This paper presents the first hardware-level attribute-stealing attack that bypasses state-of-the-art privacy defenses, revealing that accelerator optimizations intended for performance can directly undermine data confidentiality. SparseBleed requires no access to gradients, logits, model weights, ground-truth labels, power traces, DVFS manipulation, shared caches, or other channels. Instead, we show that sparsity-driven execution paths encode stable timing signatures that act as a surrogate for model confidence, enabling high-fidelity attribute inference from a single query. SparseBleed generalizes across heterogeneous backends and hardware engines, including Intel AVX2/AVX-512/AMX, NVIDIA Ampere Tensor Cores with 2:4 sparsity, and nine well-known sparse and dense libraries such as Intel oneDNN, oneMKL SparseBLAS, and NVIDIA cuSPARSE. We evaluate SparseBleed to infer sensitive input attributes and true output labels. On Texas-100X, SparseBleed infers sensitive input attributes such as Sex with 66.39% accuracy and recovers the true output label, Surgical Procedure, with 99.8% accuracy. Finally, we evaluate mitigations. Constant-time execution by disabling sparsity optimizations is expensive (e.g., up to [MATH] higher latency on NVIDIA Sparse Tensor Cores and [MATH] higher power in AMX microbenchmarks). By contrast, a padding defense that equalizes responses to the worst-case time masks timing leakage with only 7.24% average performance overhead across nine libraries on Texas-100X/Adult and near-zero extra energy.
tldr: SparseBleed demonstrates a hardware-level timing side-channel attack that exploits sparsity optimizations in DNN accelerators to infer sensitive input attributes and output labels.
motivation: The paper aims to show that performance optimizations in deep-learning hardware can leak confidential information despite existing attribute-inference defenses, motivating a new class of privacy attacks.
method: The attack uses sparsity-driven execution timing signatures as a surrogate for model confidence, requiring only a single query and generalizing across Intel AVX2/AVX-512/AMX, NVIDIA Ampere Tensor Cores, and sparse libraries.
result: On Texas-100X, SparseBleed infers sensitive attributes such as Sex with 66.39% accuracy and recovers the Surgical Procedure label with 99.8% accuracy; constant-time mitigations are costly, while a padding defense adds only 7.24% average overhead.
conclusion: Sparsity optimizations can undermine data confidentiality in DNN accelerators, and padding-based timing equalization offers a practical mitigation with modest performance cost.

title: Star: Scalable TEE-based Anonymous Rate-limiter
authors: Kosei Akama, Yoshimichi Nakatsuka, Koichi Moriyama, Keisuke Uehara
abstract: ArXiv:2610.38602v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Protecting Internet services from attacks such as TLS/HTTP floods requires rate limiting, yet identifying users to enforce these limits can compromise their privacy. Anonymous rate limiting promises to reconcile these goals, but existing schemes either struggle to scale or assume that services and authorities do not collude. We present STAR, which uses server-side trusted execution environments (TEEs) to overcome these limitations. By enabling lightweight cryptographic operations, TEEs make authentication efficient, but introduce a privacy challenge: malicious services can observe memory-access patterns to infer user secrets. We address this threat through countermeasures against secret-dependent memory accesses and assess our implementation using dynamic analysis. To extend these efficiency gains across servers, we also design a secure sharding mechanism that distributes client requests. We demonstrate that strong privacy guarantees can coexist with efficient authentication at scale; STAR processes authentication requests in tens of microseconds and handles approximately 13.9K requests per second per CPU core.
tldr: STAR is a scalable anonymous rate-limiting system that uses server-side trusted execution environments (TEEs) with hardened memory-access patterns and secure sharding to authenticate users privately at high throughput.
motivation: Internet services need rate limiting to resist TLS/HTTP floods, but identifying users for that purpose erodes privacy; existing anonymous rate-limiting schemes either fail to scale or rely on the assumption that services and authorities never collude.
method: The authors build rate limiting on server-side TEEs so that authentication becomes a lightweight cryptographic operation, add countermeasures against secret-dependent memory-access leakage (verified via dynamic analysis), and design a secure sharding mechanism to distribute client requests across servers.
result: STAR processes authentication requests in tens of microseconds and sustains roughly 13.9K requests per second per CPU core while providing strong privacy guarantees.
conclusion: Strong privacy and efficient authentication at scale can coexist, offering a practical anonymous rate-limiting architecture for Internet services.

title: Residual-based Adaptive Refinement Of hp-Variational PINNs For Elliptic PDEs With Geometric Singularities And Localized Features
authors: Somnath Giri, Muslim Malik, Rishikesh Yadav
abstract: ArXiv:2610.37670v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks approximate the solution of boundary value problems by minimizing the strong-form residual, their accuracy is often limited near corner and crack singularities, sharp layers and localized features and the enforcement of Neumann boundary conditions remains challenging. In hp-Variational Physics-Informed Neural Networks, the problem is formulated in a Petrov-Galerkin weak form, reducing the differentiation order applied to the neural network, while boundary constraints are imposed through penalty terms. The variational residual is evaluated using fixed Gauss quadrature points and the strong-form residual on a fixed collocation set, which may fail to capture regions of rapid variation. To address this issue, we integrate hp-Variational Physics-Informed Neural Networks with Residual-based Adaptive Refinement. During training, the strong-form residual is computed on a dense candidate pool and points with the largest residuals are added adaptively to the collocation set. Since the weak formulation is defined in [MATH], it avoids the [MATH] regularity requirement that fails on cracked and non-convex domains. The proposed method is validated on four two-dimensional elliptic problems and consistently achieves substantial reductions in relative [MATH], absolute [MATH] and relative [MATH] semi-norm errors through adaptive residual-driven point placement.
tldr: This paper develops residual-based adaptive refinement for hp-variational physics-informed neural networks to solve elliptic PDEs with geometric singularities and localized features.
motivation: Physics-informed neural networks often lose accuracy near singularities, sharp layers, and localized features, and Neumann boundary conditions remain challenging to enforce.
method: The authors combine hp-variational PINNs, formulated in a Petrov-Galerkin weak form with penalty boundary constraints, with residual-based adaptive refinement that adds high-residual collocation points from a dense candidate pool during training.
result: Across four two-dimensional elliptic benchmark problems, the adaptive method substantially reduces relative L2 error, absolute L2 error, and relative H1 semi-norm error compared with fixed collocation and quadrature choices.
conclusion: Residual-driven adaptive point placement improves hp-vPINNs for elliptic PDEs with singular and localized solution features, though the work is a numerical methods contribution unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
